title: Blueprint
text:
The blueprint is the detailed reference behind the paper. It follows the theory note doc/theory/exact-front.md statement by statement. For each node it gives the statement, the note’s proof (collapsed), the remarks around it, and the Lean declarations of lean/ZenoFront that formalise it, with a link to their exact source lines. Statements and proofs are cut out of the note, and listings out of the Lean sources, when the site is built, so neither can drift from the repository.
Every node has two badges:
The blueprint has 76 nodes. 23 are machine-checked theorems and 7 are Lean definitions. 14 have formalised parts, and 32 are not in Lean. The library has 3,675 declarations (2,112 theorems) in 42 modules (Lean v4.36.0, Mathlib v4.36.0). Apart from propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, no declaration uses another axiom: no sorry and no native_decide. These counts are from the last local Lean audit; 12 declarations added since then are badged from the #print axioms footers of their commits, which CI re-checks on every push.
The blueprint is also a PDF.

title: Blueprint
text:
The model
The instance, the plans and the Pareto front, as fixed in §1 of the note. Plans are precise objects (routes, journeys, capacity, waiting), and the Lean development transcribes that definition. Definitions are the trusted interface of the whole formalization: every theorem below is about these objects.

Instances
Lean Lean definition · Note definition

Statement (theory note, §1.1).

Cities: \(C_I\) (initial) and \(C_G\) (goal), the hubs, and central cities \(1,\dots,n\).
Flights are undirected: an existing flight joins two distinct cities and has one duration, used in both directions. \(C_I\)–\(i\) lasts \(d_i \ge 0\), \(i\)–\(C_G\) lasts \(\bar d_i \ge 0\), and a central flight \(i\)–\(j\) (\(i \ne j\)), if it exists, lasts \(d_{ij} = d_{ji} \ge 0\). There is no flight \(C_I\)–\(C_G\). \(\mathrm{dur}(a,b)\) denotes the duration of the flight \(a\)–\(b\).
Landing in central city \(i\) costs \(c_i \ge 0\); landing in a hub is free.
\(p \ge 1\) planes and \(t \ge p\) passengers start in \(C_I\) at time 0. A plane carries at most one passenger.
Durations and times lie in an archimedean ordered field \(\mathbb K\) (\(\mathbb Q\) or \(\mathbb R\)), so that \(\lfloor\cdot\rfloor\) is defined. From §7 on, durations are integers.

In Lean. Network holds the durations d, dbar and an arbitrary table dc of central flights; costs are a separate argument c : Fin n → ℕ. Durations, costs and times are natural numbers (format v1); Cert.check_sound_rat extends the checker’s soundness to rational times.
Lean ZenoFront.Network Lean definition
/-- The flight network: durations between `C_I` and each city (`d`), between `C_G` and each city
(`dbar`), and between central cities (`dc`, arbitrary). -/
structure Network (n : ℕ) where
  d : Fin n → ℕ
  dbar : Fin n → ℕ
  dc : Fin n → Fin n → ℕ
lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean, lines 87–92



Plans, cost and makespan
Lean Lean definition · Note definition

Statement (theory note, §1.2).
Definition (plan). A plan on a finite set \(Q\) of planes (all \(p\) planes unless stated otherwise) consists of

for every plane \(k \in Q\), a route: a finite sequence of legs \((k,1),\dots,(k,\nu_k)\), where leg \((k,j)\) uses an existing flight joining \(v_{k,j-1}\) and \(v_{k,j}\), flown from \(v_{k,j-1}\) to \(v_{k,j}\), and departs at time \(e_{k,j}\), with \(v_{k,0} = C_I\), \(e_{k,1} \ge 0\) and \(e_{k,j+1} \ge a_{k,j} := e_{k,j} + \mathrm{dur}(v_{k,j-1}, v_{k,j})\);
for every passenger \(\pi\), a journey: a non-empty sequence of legs whose first leg departs from \(C_I\), whose last leg arrives in \(C_G\), and in which each leg departs from the city where the previous one arrives, no earlier than that arrival, and, if both are legs of the same plane, at a later position of its route;
capacity: the journeys are pairwise disjoint, and none repeats a leg.

Below, “flight” also means a leg when no confusion is possible. The plan is feasible if every route ends in \(C_G\) (\(\nu_k \ge 1\) and \(v_{k,\nu_k} = C_G\)). Its cost \(C = \sum_{k,j} c(v_{k,j})\) sums the landing costs of all flights (hubs are free). Its makespan \(M = \max_k a_{k,\nu_k}\) is the time at which the last plane reaches \(C_G\) for the last time. \(\mathcal A\) is the set of pairs \((C, M)\) of feasible plans.
Waiting is implicit: a departure may be later than the preceding arrival, for planes and for passengers. Boarding and debarking are instantaneous: a passenger changing planes debarks when its flight arrives and boards when the next one departs, and the only constraint is the time inequality of item 2. Several planes may be in a city at once.
Sequence order. “First” and “last” refer to positions in a journey or in a route. With zero durations several events can share a time; the sequences fix their order, and every argument below reads them this way.
A plan is event-ordered if its legs have a total order \(\prec\) that extends every route and every journey and along which departure times do not decrease. Lemma 6.8 and Corollary 6.10 use this notion, and Statement 1.2 relates it to PDDL; Theorem 6.9 does not need it. If every flight has a positive duration, every plan is event-ordered: in a route or a journey the next leg departs after the previous one arrives, hence strictly after it departs, so sorting legs by departure time extends both. Plans of the PDDL domain are event-ordered too (Statement 1.2). With zero durations a plan can fail to be: a passenger may ride a later leg of one plane and then an earlier leg of another at the same instant, in a cycle of dependencies that no execution in time realises. Such plans do not change the front (Corollary 6.10).
The flight time of plane \(k\) is \(F_k = \sum_j \mathrm{dur}(f_{k,j})\). Its flights are sequential, so \(F_k \le a_{k,\nu_k} \le M\).
Planes ending anywhere. In the variant of Theorem 4.9, every plan counts (routes need not end in \(C_G\) and may be empty), journeys still end in \(C_G\), and the makespan \(M'\) is the largest arrival time over all legs; there is at least one leg since \(t \ge 1\). \(\mathcal A'\) is the set of pairs \((C, M')\) of all plans.
In Lean. A plan gives every plane a list of legs (Leg: from, to, departure, arrival, passenger). Feasible requires routes chained from C_I at time ≥ 0 and ending in C_G, legs of exact duration, and every passenger’s legs ordered into a route from C_I to C_G; capacity one holds by construction, since a leg names at most one passenger.

Statement 1.2 (PDDL correspondence)
Lean informal · Note sketch

Statement (theory note, §1.3).
Statement 1.2 (PDDL correspondence, S). A plan of the domain under ε-separation yields a plan of §1.2 with the same cost and a makespan at most its total-time: each plane’s fly actions in time order form its route, each person’s flights between board and debark form its journey, and libre gives capacity one; ordering the fly actions by start time (ties by the plan’s order of actions) shows that this plan is event-ordered. Conversely, an event-ordered plan of §1.2 with makespan \(M\) yields PDDL plans with total-time at most \(M + K\varepsilon\), where \(K\) is its number of fly, board and debark actions: list the actions in the event order (each board just before its leg, each debark just after) and delay the \(r\)-th one by \(r\varepsilon\). So the PDDL front tends to the front of event-ordered plans, which is \(\mathcal F\) under (S) and (A1), and under (S) and (AΔ) (the plans of Theorem 4.1 are event-ordered, Lemma 6.8(c); Corollaries 4.8 and 4.12), and under (A1-NS) (Corollary 6.10). The model’s makespan is thus the PDDL makespan in the limit ε → 0, which is what ZenoSolver reports. Whether PDDL planners and VAL accept zero-duration actions is not checked here. This is argued, not formalised.

Lemma 1.1 (dominating subset)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note

Statement (theory note, §1.5).
Lemma 1.1 (dominating subset). Let \(\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S \subseteq \mathbb K^2\) with \(\mathcal S'\) finite and every point of \(\mathcal S\) weakly dominated by a point of \(\mathcal S'\). Then \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'\), and every point of \(\mathcal S\) is weakly dominated by a point of \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Let \(z \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S\). Some \(y \in \mathcal S'\) has \(y \preceq z\), so \(y = z\), and \(z\) is minimal in \(\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S\). Let \(z \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'\) and \(y \in \mathcal S\) with \(y \preceq z\). Some \(y' \in \mathcal S'\) has \(y' \preceq y \preceq z\), so \(y' = z\) and then \(y = z\). Finally, for \(z \in \mathcal S\), take \(y \in \mathcal S'\) with \(y \preceq z\) and a \(\preceq\)-minimal element of the finite set \(\{y' \in \mathcal S' : y' \preceq y\}\); it lies in \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S' = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S\). \(\square\)

Segments, admissible partitions, link forests
The combinatorial core (§2 of the note). A partition of the landings among the planes can be flown without waiting exactly when it is admissible, a parity condition that is a \(\mathcal T\)-join of the plane-city incidence graph. It is what makes the front computable without fixing a schedule.

Definition 2.2 (admissible partition)
Lean Lean definition · Note definition

Statement (theory note, §2).
Definition 2.2 (admissible partition). Let \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) be a partition of \(X\). A parity matrix for it is \(h \in \{0,1\}^{p\times n}\) such that

(h1) \(h_{k,i} = 1\) implies \(X_k(i) \ge 1\);
(h2) \(h_k := \sum_i h_{k,i} \equiv |X_k| + 1 \pmod 2\) for every plane \(k\);
(h3) \(\sum_k h_{k,i} \equiv 0 \pmod 2\) for every city \(i\).

The partition is admissible if it has a parity matrix. Write \(\eta_k = \{i : h_{k,i} = 1\}\), so that \(|\eta_k| = h_k\), and \(Z(h) = \bigcup_k \eta_k\) for the cities that \(h\) touches. A plane with \(|X_k|\) even is an even plane. An empty group would need \(h_k = 0 \equiv 1\) by (h1)–(h2), so admissible partitions have non-empty groups. Admissibility is decidable by enumerating \(h\) on the support of the groups. This definition replaces the component form of the first version (Lemma 2.4 shows they agree), and is the one to formalise.
In Lean. IsParityWitness X h is (h1)–(h3) with h k : Finset (Fin n), one set of cities per plane; Admissible X is ∃ h, IsParityWitness X h, decidable through witnessCandidates.
Lean ZenoFront.IsParityWitness Lean definition
/-- `h` is a *parity witness* for the grouping `X` (Claim A of the note): `h k` is a set of
cities of `X k` whose size has the parity of `|X k| + 1`, and every city lies in an even number
of the sets `h k`. Equivalently, `{(k, i) | i ∈ h k}` is a `T`-join of the plane–city graph,
`T` being the set of planes with an even number of landings. -/
structure IsParityWitness (X : Groups n p) (h : Fin p → Finset (Fin n)) : Prop where
  /-- Only edges of the plane–city graph are used. -/
  subset : ∀ k, h k ⊆ (X k).toFinset
  /-- Plane `k` has degree `≡ |X_k| + 1 (mod 2)`. -/
  row : ∀ k, (h k).card % 2 = ((X k).card + 1) % 2
  /-- Every city has even degree. -/
  col : ∀ i, Even #{k | i ∈ h k}

Lemma 2.3 (integer form)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.2

Statement (theory note, §2).
Lemma 2.3 (integer form) [A′]. A partition is admissible if and only if some \(\tilde h \in \mathbb N^{p\times n}\) has \(\tilde h_{k,i} \le X_k(i)\), \(\sum_i \tilde h_{k,i} \equiv |X_k| + 1\) for every \(k\), and \(\sum_k \tilde h_{k,i} \equiv 0\) for every \(i\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. A parity matrix is such an \(\tilde h\), by (h1). Conversely, \(h = \tilde h \bmod 2\) satisfies (h1)–(h3): \(h_{k,i} = 1\) forces \(\tilde h_{k,i} \ge 1\), and reduction mod 2 keeps both parity conditions. \(\square\)






Lemma 2.4 (component form)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.2

Statement (theory note, §2).
Lemma 2.4 (component form). Let \(H\) be the bipartite graph on planes and cities with an edge \(\{k,i\}\) iff \(X_k(i) \ge 1\).

The partition is admissible iff every connected component of \(H\) contains an even number of even planes.
If it is admissible, then for every spanning forest \(\Theta\) of \(H\) it has a parity matrix whose support \(\{(k,i) : h_{k,i} = 1\}\) is a set of edges of \(\Theta\).







Proof (theory note)





Proof. By (h1), the support \(J\) of a parity matrix is a set of edges of \(H\). By (h2), \(\deg_J(k)\) is odd exactly at the even planes, and by (h3) \(\deg_J(i)\) is even at every city. So parity matrices are the \(\mathcal T\)-joins of \(H\), for the set \(\mathcal T\) of even planes. If \(J\) exists, the degrees in a component \(K\) sum to \(2|J \cap E(K)|\), so \(K\) has an even number of odd-degree vertices, that is, of even planes. Conversely, assume this parity condition and root every tree of \(\Theta\). For a vertex \(v\) let \(\epsilon(v) \in \{0,1\}\) be the parity of the number of even planes in the subtree of \(v\), and put the edge from \(v\) to its parent in \(J\) iff \(\epsilon(v) = 1\). Then \(\deg_J(v) = \epsilon(v) + \sum_u \epsilon(u)\) over the children \(u\) of \(v\) (without the first term at a root), and \(\epsilon(v) \equiv [v \in \mathcal T] + \sum_u \epsilon(u)\). So \(\deg_J(v) \equiv [v \in \mathcal T]\) at a non-root. At a root, \(\epsilon(v) = 0\) by assumption, so \(\deg_J(v) = \sum_u \epsilon(u) \equiv [v \in \mathcal T]\). \(\square\)

Definition (link forest)
Lean Lean definition · Note definition

Statement (theory note, §2).
Definition (link forest). A link forest for \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) is a forest \(\Lambda\) on the planes (without loops or parallel edges) whose edges carry city labels, such that

(F1) for every plane \(u\) and city \(i\), at most \(X_u(i)\) edges at \(u\) are labelled \(i\);
(F2) \(r_u := |X_u| - \deg_\Lambda(u)\) is odd for every plane \(u\).







Remarks in the note





An edge \(\{u, v\}\) labelled \(i\) is a link at \(i\). By (F1) the links at \(u\) can be given distinct copies of landings of \(X_u\): the multiset of their labels is \(\le X_u\). The remaining \(r_u \ge 1\) landings are the free landings of \(u\).

Lemma 2.6 (link forest)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.3, 2.4

Statement (theory note, §2).
Lemma 2.6 (link forest) [LF]. A partition is admissible if and only if it has a link forest. An admissible partition has a link forest with at most one edge of each label at each plane.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. (If.) Let \(\tilde h_{u,i}\) be the number of edges at \(u\) labelled \(i\). Then \(\tilde h_{u,i} \le X_u(i)\) by (F1), \(\sum_i \tilde h_{u,i} = \deg_\Lambda(u) \equiv |X_u| + 1\) by (F2), and \(\sum_u \tilde h_{u,i}\) is twice the number of edges labelled \(i\). Lemma 2.3 applies. This direction holds for any loopless multigraph (a loop would add 2 to the degree but 1 to \(\tilde h_{u,i}\)).
(Only if.) Take a spanning forest \(\Theta\) of \(H\) and a parity matrix with support \(J \subseteq E(\Theta)\) (Lemma 2.4(b)). At each city \(i\), \(\deg_J(i)\) is even. Split the planes \(J\)-adjacent to \(i\) into \(\deg_J(i)/2\) pairs, and for each pair \(\{u, v\}\) add to \(\Lambda\) an edge \(uv\) labelled \(i\). Then \(u \ne v\), since \(J\) has at most one edge per plane and city. At most one edge at \(u\) is labelled \(i\), and only if \((u,i) \in J\), hence \(X_u(i) \ge 1\): (F1) holds. \(\deg_\Lambda(u) = \deg_J(u) = h_u \equiv |X_u| + 1\): (F2) holds.
\(\Lambda\), built so far as a multigraph, has no cycle, and in particular no parallel edges. Take a cycle: a closed trail \(u_0, u_1, \dots, u_{m-1}, u_0\) with \(m \ge 2\) distinct edges \(u_{j-1}u_j\) labelled \(i_j\) (indices mod \(m\)), with distinct vertices if \(m \ge 3\); \(m = 2\) is the case of parallel edges. It gives the closed walk \(u_0, i_1, u_1, i_2, \dots, i_m, u_0\) in \(J\), which never uses the same edge twice in a row, even cyclically. At a city \(i_j\) it arrives from \(u_{j-1}\) and leaves to \(u_j \ne u_{j-1}\). At a plane \(u_j\) it arrives from \(i_j\) and leaves to \(i_{j+1}\); if \(i_j = i_{j+1}\), then \(u_j\) would belong to two different pairs at that city (the two distinct edges of the cycle at \(u_j\)). But a closed walk of positive length in a forest uses some edge twice in a row: at a vertex of the walk farthest from the root of its tree, both neighbours on the walk are its parent. \(\square\)

It does not go through the spanning-forest construction of the note’s proof, which needs Lemma 2.4.

Corollary 2.7
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses \(\lvert X\rvert = s\) · Uses 2.6

Statement (theory note, §2).
Corollary 2.7. If \(|X| = s\), every link forest has at most \(t - p\) edges, and each of its trees has at most \(q_{\max} := \min(p,\ t - p + 1)\) planes.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. By (F2), \(\deg_\Lambda(u) \le |X_u| - 1\). Summing over planes, \(2\#E(\Lambda) \le s - p = 2(t-p)\). A tree with \(q\) planes has \(q - 1\) edges, so \(q - 1 \le t - p\). \(\square\)






Lemma 2.8 (few touched cities)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses \(\lvert X\rvert = s\) · Uses 2.5

Statement (theory note, §2).
Lemma 2.8 (few touched cities) [B′]. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) be admissible with \(|X| = s\).

Every parity matrix touches at most \(t - p\) cities.
A parity matrix with the fewest entries equal to 1 has an acyclic support, as a subgraph of \(H\), and touches at most \(p - 1\) cities.
So some parity matrix touches at most \(w := \min(p-1,\ t-p)\) cities, and it has \(h_k \le \min(|X_k| - 1,\ w)\) for every \(k\).







Proof (theory note)





Proof. (a) By Lemma 2.5, \(\sum_k h_k \le \sum_k (|X_k| - 1) = 2(t-p)\), and by (h3) each touched city carries at least two of these entries.

Parity matrices form a finite non-empty set, so one with the fewest entries exists; let \(J\) be its support. \(H\) is a simple bipartite graph, so each vertex of a cycle of \(H\) meets exactly two of its edges. If \(J\) contained a cycle, setting \(h\) to 0 on it would lower the degree of each of its vertices by 2 and keep (h1)–(h3), with fewer entries. So \(J\) is a forest. Let \(P'\) and \(Z\) be the planes and the cities incident to \(J\). If \(Z = \emptyset\) the bound is \(0 \le p - 1\). Otherwise every city of \(Z\) has \(J\)-degree at least 2, so \(2|Z| \le |J| \le |P'| + |Z| - 1\), and \(|Z| \le |P'| - 1 \le p - 1\).
Apply (a) to the matrix of (b). Then \(h_k \le |X_k| - 1\) by Lemma 2.5, and \(\eta_k \subseteq Z(h)\). \(\square\)




In Lean. Part (b) is proved over ZMod 2: if the edge vectors e_k + e_i of a witness are linearly dependent, removing an even subgraph gives a witness with fewer edges (IsParityWitness.exists_edgeCount_lt); independent edge vectors satisfy #edges + 1 ≤ p + #touched.

Lemma 2.9 (shared city). Let \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) be non-empty groups with \(\sum_k |X_k| \equiv p \pmod 2\). If some city belongs to every even group, the partition is admissible. This holds in particular when all groups contain a common city, and when all even groups are equal.

Lemma 3.1 (cleaning)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note

Statement (theory note, §3).
Lemma 3.1 (cleaning). Every plan can be changed, keeping all routes (hence cost, makespan and flight times), so that every journey is clean: its first flight is its only flight departing from \(C_I\), and its last flight is its only flight arriving in \(C_G\). A clean journey has no flight arriving in \(C_I\) and none departing from \(C_G\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Replace each journey by its part from its last flight departing from \(C_I\) to the first later flight arriving in \(C_G\), which exists since the journey ends in \(C_G\). This is a journey, and capacity only gets looser. In a clean journey, a flight arriving in \(C_I\) would be followed by a flight departing from \(C_I\) other than the first, since the journey ends in \(C_G\). A flight departing from \(C_G\) would follow a flight arriving in \(C_G\) other than the last. \(\square\)



In Lean. Lean does not rewrite journeys: exists_transfer extracts, from every passenger’s route, the leg C_I → x followed by a leg leaving x not towards C_I that the cleaned journey would keep.

Lemma 3.2 (counting)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note

Statement (theory note, §3).
Lemma 3.2 (counting). A feasible plan has at least \(s = 2t - p\) segments, hence at least \(s\) landings in central cities.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. For plane \(k\), let \(D^I_k\) and \(A^I_k\) be its numbers of flights departing from and arriving in \(C_I\), and \(D^G_k\), \(A^G_k\) the same for \(C_G\). The route is in \(C_I\) at its start and after each arrival there, and leaves after each of these visits since it ends in \(C_G\): \(D^I_k = A^I_k + 1\). It is in \(C_G\) only after arrivals, and leaves after each but the last: \(D^G_k = A^G_k - 1\). The first flight of each journey departs from \(C_I\) and the last arrives in \(C_G\); by capacity both maps are injective, so \(\sum_k D^I_k \ge t\) and \(\sum_k A^G_k \ge t\). Segments end exactly at arrivals in hubs, so plane \(k\) has \(A^I_k + A^G_k = D^I_k - 1 + A^G_k\) segments, and the plan at least \(t - p + t = s\). Each segment contains a landing in a central city, and different segments contain different landings. \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





No cleaning and no segment types are needed.

Lemma 3.4 (relaxation)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S) · Uses 3.2, 3.3

Statement (theory note, §3).
Lemma 3.4 (relaxation) [R]. Assume (S). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\) there are non-empty multisets \(Y_1,\dots,Y_p\) with \(\sum_k |Y_k| = s\), \(c(Y_1 + \dots + Y_p) \le C\), and \(\ell(Y_k) \le F_k \le M\) for every \(k\). Hence, with integer durations, \(C \ge L(\lfloor M/2\rfloor)\), where \[L(T) = \min\Big\{c(Y) : Y = Y_1 + \dots + Y_p,\ |Y| = s,\ Y_k \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \delta(Y_k) \le T\ \forall k\Big\}
\quad(\min\emptyset = \infty).\] No assumption on central flights is needed.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. For a segment \(\gamma\), let \(x^\star(\gamma)\) be whichever of its first and last central cities has the smaller \(d\). By Lemma 3.3(a), \(F(\gamma) \ge 2d_{x^\star(\gamma)}\). Every route goes from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), so every plane has a segment, and by Lemma 3.2 the plan has at least \(s \ge p\) segments. Choose one segment per plane and any \(s - p\) others, and let \(Y_k\) collect \(x^\star(\gamma)\) over the chosen segments \(\gamma\) of plane \(k\). Different segments have different landings, and \(x^\star(\gamma)\) is a landing of \(\gamma\), so \(c(Y) \le C\). Also \(\ell(Y_k) = \sum_\gamma 2d_{x^\star(\gamma)} \le \sum_\gamma F(\gamma) \le F_k \le M\). With integer durations, \(\delta(Y_k)\) is an integer at most \(M/2\). \(\square\)

title: Blueprint
text:
Symmetric case: achievability, converse, front
The heart of the note (§4). Theorem 4.1 flies every admissible partition with no waiting; Theorem 4.7 reduces every plan to an admissible partition under (A1); together they characterise the front (Corollary 4.8). All three are machine-checked. Theorem 4.10 proves the same converse under the triangle inequality (AΔ) instead of (A1), so the front characterisation also holds there (Corollary 4.12); Example 4.13 shows that some such hypothesis is needed. These are proved in the note, not in Lean.

Theorem 4.1
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S) · Uses 2.6

Statement (theory note, §4.1).
Theorem 4.1. Assume (S). For every multiset \(X\) with \(|X| = s\) and every admissible partition \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) of \(X\), there is a feasible plan whose central landings are exactly \(X\) (so of cost \(c(X)\)), in which plane \(k\) flies for \(\ell(X_k)\) and picks up at most one passenger, and whose makespan is \(\max_k \ell(X_k)\). The plan uses no central flight, so no assumption on them is needed.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Take a link forest \(\Lambda\) (Lemma 2.6) and root each of its trees at a plane. For a link at \(i\) between a parent \(u\) and a child \(v\), \(u\) will drop a passenger in \(i\) (a segment \(B\)) and \(v\) will pick it up (a segment \(\bar B\)). A non-root plane has exactly one parent link, so every plane picks up at most once. Plane \(u\) uses one copy of \(i\) from \(X_u\) per link at \(u\) labelled \(i\) (F1), and its \(r_u\) free landings, an odd number (F2), for crossings.
Schedule of plane \(k\). Let \(\tau^{\rm dr}_k\) be twice the sum of the durations of its child links (its drop-offs) and \(\tau^{\rm cr}_k\) the load of its free landings.

Its drop-offs, one after the other from time 0: \(C_I \to i \to C_I\), each carrying a new passenger from \(C_I\) and leaving it in \(i\). These never wait.
Its \(r_k\) free landings as crossings \(A, \bar A, A, \dots, A\); each \(A\) carries a new passenger from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\). These never wait.
If \(k\) has a parent link at \(i\): \(C_G \to i \to C_G\), leaving \(i\) once the passenger dropped there by its parent is present, and carrying it to \(C_G\).

Timing. The drop-off of \(u\) at \(i\) reaches \(i\) at a time at most \(\tau^{\rm dr}_u - d_i\). Its child \(v\) reaches \(C_G\) at \(\tau^{\rm dr}_v + \tau^{\rm cr}_v\), arrives in \(i\) at \(\tau^{\rm dr}_v + \tau^{\rm cr}_v + d_i\), leaves at the later of this time and the drop-off’s arrival, and is back at a time at most \(\max(\tau^{\rm dr}_v + \tau^{\rm cr}_v + 2d_i,\ \tau^{\rm dr}_u) = \max(\ell(X_v), \tau^{\rm dr}_u) \le \max(\ell(X_v), \ell(X_u))\). A plane without a parent link finishes at \(\ell(X_k)\). Every plane flies exactly \(\ell(X_k)\), as its segments are simple (Lemma 3.3(c)), so the makespan is \(\max_k \ell(X_k)\).
Passengers. Let \(\Lambda\) have \(N\) links. There are \(\sum_k r_k = s - 2N\) crossings, and each plane makes one more \(A\) than \(\bar A\), so there are \((s - 2N + p)/2 = t - N\) segments \(A\). They and the \(N\) drop-offs carry \(t\) distinct passengers out of \(C_I\), each delivered to \(C_G\) by its \(A\) or by the pick-up linked to its drop-off. Every flight carries at most one passenger, every route ends in \(C_G\), and the central landings are exactly \(X\). \(\square\)



In Lean. The plan is built on a rooted link forest (LTree.routes): each plane drops off its children’s passengers, crosses its free landings, then picks up its parent’s passenger.

Definition 4.2 (role configuration)
Lean Lean definition · Note definition

Statement (theory note, §4.2).
Definition 4.2 (role configuration). A role configuration on a set \(Q\) of planes is a family of multisets of central cities \(\mathrm{Dr}_k\) (drop-offs), \(\mathrm{Pk}_k\) (pick-ups) and \(\mathrm{Cr}_k\) (crossings), \(k \in Q\), with \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k|\) odd and the per-city balance \(\sum_{k\in Q}\mathrm{Dr}_k = \sum_{k\in Q}\mathrm{Pk}_k\). Its passenger count is \(t(\mathrm{cfg}) = \sum_k \big(|\mathrm{Dr}_k| + (|\mathrm{Cr}_k| + 1)/2\big)\), its cost is \(\sum_k c(\mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k)\), and the role load of plane \(k\) is \[\lambda_k = 2\delta(\mathrm{Dr}_k) + 2\bar\delta(\mathrm{Pk}_k) + \delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k) + \bar\delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k).\] With \(X_k = \mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k\), the balance gives \(\sum_k |X_k| = 2t(\mathrm{cfg}) - |Q|\), and under (S), \(\lambda_k = \ell(X_k)\).






Remarks in the note





A plan is simple if each of its flights joins a hub and a central city; all its segments are then simple.

Lemma 4.3 (direct selection)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses simple, clean plan · Uses 2.1, 3.1, 3.3

Statement (theory note, §4.2).
Lemma 4.3 (direct selection) [DS]. (a) In a simple plan with clean journeys, whether or not its routes end in \(C_G\), every journey consists of exactly two flights, \(C_I \to x\) and then \(x \to C_G\), for a central city \(x\).

Let \(P\) be a simple plan on a set \(Q\) of planes, every route ending in \(C_G\), with clean journeys and cost \(C\). Then there is a role configuration on \(Q\) with \(t(\mathrm{cfg}) \ge t\), cost at most \(C\), \(\lambda_k \le F_k\) for every \(k\), and \(\mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k\) a sub-multiset of the central landings of plane \(k\). No assumption on durations is needed.







Proof (theory note)





Proof. (a) The first flight of a journey departs from \(C_I\), so it goes to a central city \(x\). As \(x \ne C_G\), the journey continues with a flight from \(x\), which goes to a hub. That hub is not \(C_I\) (Lemma 3.1), so the flight arrives in \(C_G\), and it is the last flight of the journey (Lemma 3.1).

Journeys. By (a), the first flight of a journey is the first flight of a segment of type \(A\) or \(B\), written \(o(\pi)\), and its second flight is the second flight of a segment at the same city \(x\) of type \(A\) or \(\bar B\), written \(n(\pi)\). A segment has one first flight and one second flight, and by capacity a flight carries at most one passenger, so \(o\) and \(n\) are injective. Passenger \(\pi\) is a hand-off if \(o(\pi) \ne n(\pi)\). A \(B\) is never an \(n(\cdot)\), and a \(\bar B\) never an \(o(\cdot)\).

Counts at a city \(x\). Let \(\beta_x\) be the number of \(B\) segments at \(x\) that are an \(o(\cdot)\), and \(\bar\beta_x\) the number of \(\bar B\) segments at \(x\) that are an \(n(\cdot)\). Among the \(A\) segments at \(x\): \(\theta_x\) are \(o(\pi) = n(\pi)\) for some \(\pi\) (through); \(\omega_x\) are \(o(\pi)\) and \(n(\pi')\) with \(\pi \ne \pi'\) (swaps); \(\alpha_x\) are an \(o(\cdot)\) and no \(n(\cdot)\); \(\bar\alpha_x\) are an \(n(\cdot)\) and no \(o(\cdot)\); the others are empty. Every hand-off at \(x\) has its \(o\) among the \(\beta_x + \alpha_x + \omega_x\) segments counted so, and its \(n\) among the \(\bar\beta_x + \bar\alpha_x + \omega_x\), and each of these segments serves exactly one hand-off at \(x\) in that role. Hence \[\beta_x - \bar\beta_x = \bar\alpha_x - \alpha_x. \tag{1}\] Every passenger has exactly one \(o\), so \[t = \textstyle\sum_x (\theta_x + \omega_x + \alpha_x + \beta_x). \tag{2}\] Let \(z_k\) be the number of non-empty \(A\) segments of plane \(k\). Then \[\textstyle\sum_k z_k = \sum_x (\theta_x + \omega_x + \alpha_x + \bar\alpha_x). \tag{3}\]
Selection. At each city \(x\), let \(\mu_x = \min(\beta_x, \bar\beta_x)\). Select \(\mu_x\) of the \(B\) segments at \(x\) that are an \(o(\cdot)\), and \(\mu_x\) of the \(\bar B\) segments at \(x\) that are an \(n(\cdot)\). For each plane \(k\), let \(z'_k = \max(z_k, 1)\), and select its \(z_k\) non-empty \(A\) segments, \(z'_k - 1\) of its \(\bar A\) segments and, if \(z_k = 0\), one (empty) \(A\) segment. These exist: by Lemma 2.1, plane \(k\) has at least one \(A\), and \(\#\bar A_k = \#A_k - 1 \ge z_k - 1\). Let \(\mathrm{Dr}_k\), \(\mathrm{Pk}_k\) and \(\mathrm{Cr}_k\) be the cities of the selected \(B\), \(\bar B\), and \(A\) or \(\bar A\) segments of \(k\). Then \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k| = 2z'_k - 1\) is odd, and the balance holds since both sides contain \(\mu_x\) copies of \(x\).
Count. By (2) and (3), \(t(\mathrm{cfg}) = \sum_x \mu_x + \sum_k z'_k \ge \sum_x \mu_x + \sum_k z_k = t + \sum_x (\mu_x - \beta_x + \bar\alpha_x)\). By (1), \(\beta_x - \mu_x = (\beta_x - \bar\beta_x)^+ = (\bar\alpha_x - \alpha_x)^+ \le \bar\alpha_x\). So \(t(\mathrm{cfg}) \ge t\).
Loads and cost. The selected segments of \(k\) are distinct and simple, and by Lemma 3.3(c) each lasts exactly its role duration: \(2d_x\) for \(B\), \(2\bar d_x\) for \(\bar B\), \(d_x + \bar d_x\) for \(A\) and \(\bar A\). So \(\lambda_k \le F_k\). Each selected segment contributes its single central landing, so \(\mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k\) is a sub-multiset of the landings of \(k\), and the cost is at most \(C\). \(\square\)



In Lean. Part (b), on the landing records of a feasible plan; it is shared by Theorems 4.7 and 6.1. Part (a) is not a separate Lean statement.

Lemma 4.4 (shrinking) [SH]. If a role configuration on \(Q\) has \(t(\mathrm{cfg}) > t \ge |Q|\), deleting landings gives one on \(Q\) with passenger count \(t(\mathrm{cfg}) - 1\); its cost, its role loads and its groups \(X_k\) do not increase. Proof (theory note)





Proof. If some \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k| \ge 3\), delete two of its crossings. Otherwise every \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k| = 1\), so \(\sum_k |\mathrm{Dr}_k| = t(\mathrm{cfg}) - |Q| > t - |Q| \ge 0\): some plane \(u\) drops off at some city \(x\), and by the balance some plane \(v\) picks up at \(x\). Delete one copy of \(x\) from \(\mathrm{Dr}_u\) and one from \(\mathrm{Pk}_v\). Oddness and balance are kept, and the passenger count drops by one. \(\square\)

Lemma 4.6 (adding a plane) [AP]. Let \((X_k)_{k \in Q}\) be admissible with \(q = |Q|\), \(\sum_k |X_k| = 2t - q\) and \(t \ge q + 1\), and let \(\star \notin Q\) be a further plane. Then some admissible partition \((Y_k)_{k \in Q \cup \{\star\}}\) has \(\sum_k |Y_k| = 2t - q - 1\), \(c(Y) \le c(X)\) and \(\max_k \delta(Y_k) \le \max_k \delta(X_k)\). This corrects case (b) of the first version’s Lemma 4.4, where the support has \(2(t-q)\) entries, not \(t - q\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Fix a parity matrix \(h\). By Lemma 2.5, \(f_k := |X_k| - h_k\) is odd and at least 1. In \(X_k\), call free the \(X_k(i) - h_{k,i}\) copies of each city \(i\) beyond one copy for each \(i \in \eta_k\); there are \(f_k\) of them.
Case (a): some \(f_k \ge 3\). Let \(y, y'\) be two free landings of \(X_k\). Set \(Y_k = X_k - \{y, y'\}\), \(Y_\star = \{y\}\), keep the other groups, and give plane \(\star\) a zero row. (h1) holds as \(Y_k(i) \ge h_{k,i}\) for every \(i\). (h2) holds for \(k\), since \(|Y_k| = |X_k| - 2\), and for \(\star\), since \(|Y_\star| = 1\) and \(h_\star = 0\). (h3) is unchanged. Also \(\delta(Y_\star) = d_y \le \delta(X_k)\) and \(c(Y) = c(X) - c_{y'}\).
Case (b): every \(f_k = 1\). Then \(2t - q = \sum_k (h_k + 1)\), so \(\sum_k h_k = 2(t-q) \ge 2\). Some city \(i\) has a non-zero column, which is even, so \(h_{u,i} = h_{v,i} = 1\) for two planes \(u \ne v\). Set \(Y_u = X_u - \{i\}\), \(Y_v = X_v - \{i\}\) and \(Y_\star = \{i\}\), set \(h_{u,i} = h_{v,i} := 0\), and give plane \(\star\) a zero row. (h1) holds for \(j \ne i\), as \(Y_u(j) = X_u(j)\). (h2) holds for \(u\) and \(v\), whose group size and row sum both drop by one, and for \(\star\). Column \(i\) drops by 2. \(|Y_u| = h_u \ge 1\) (old \(h_u\)), \(\delta(Y_\star) = d_i \le \delta(X_u)\), and \(c(Y) = c(X) - c_i\). \(\square\)

Theorem 4.7 (converse). Assume (S) and (A1). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\), makespan \(M\) and flight times \(F_k\), there is an admissible partition \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) of a multiset \(X\) with \(|X| = s\), \(c(X) \le C\) and \(\ell(X_k) \le F_k \le M\) for every \(k\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Step 1: remove central flights. This step applies to any plan, whether or not its routes end in \(C_G\). Replace a flight \(a \to b\) between central cities, departing at \(e\), by \(a \to C_G\) departing at \(e\) followed by \(C_G \to b\) departing on arrival. The plane reaches \(b\) at \(e + d_a + d_b \le e + d_{ab}\) by (S) and (A1), and waits there until its next departure, which is unchanged. A passenger on board is delivered at \(C_G\): its journey is cut after \(a \to C_G\). Central landings are unchanged (\(C_G\) is free), and no arrival time and no \(F_k\) increases; in a feasible plan the last flight of a route ends in \(C_G\) and is never replaced, so the makespan is unchanged. After finitely many replacements the plan is simple.
Step 2. Clean it (Lemma 3.1).
Step 3. Lemma 4.3(b) on all \(p\) planes gives a role configuration with passenger count at least \(t\), cost at most \(C\) and \(\lambda_k \le F_k\). Lemma 4.4 (\(t \ge p\)) brings the count to \(t\). Lemma 4.5 gives an admissible partition of a multiset of size \(2t - p = s\) with \(\ell(X_k) = \lambda_k \le F_k \le M\). \(\square\)

Theorem 4.9 (bridge) [B3]. Assume (S) and (A1). The front \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A'\) of the variant in which planes may end anywhere and the makespan is the last arrival time (§1.2) equals \(\mathcal F\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. A feasible plan is a plan of the variant with the same cost and makespan, since the last arrival of each route is its latest; so \(\mathcal A \subseteq \mathcal A'\). Conversely, take a plan of the variant with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M'\). We build an admissible partition of a multiset of size \(s\) with cost at most \(C\) and loads at most \(M'\); its point in \(\mathcal X\) (Corollary 4.8) weakly dominates \((C, M')\). So \(\mathcal X \subseteq \mathcal A \subseteq \mathcal A'\) is finite and dominates both sets, and Lemma 1.1 gives \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A' = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X = \mathcal F\).

Apply Step 1 of Theorem 4.7, which applies to any plan. Clean the plan (Lemma 3.1). From every route, delete the flights after its last flight that carries a passenger. Cost and arrival times do not increase.
A route that is not empty now ends with a flight carrying a passenger \(\pi\). That flight joins a hub and a central city, and it cannot arrive in \(C_I\) or depart from \(C_G\) (Lemma 3.1). So either it arrives in \(C_G\), or it is \(C_I \to x\), the first flight of \(\pi\)’s journey, arriving at some time \(a\). In the second case the journey’s second flight is \(x \to C_G\) (Lemma 4.3(a)), departing at some \(e' \ge a\) and arriving at \(e' + \bar d_x \le M'\). Append to the route a flight \(x \to C_G\) departing at \(a\) and carrying \(\pi\); it arrives at \(a + \bar d_x \le M'\), and \(\pi\)’s old second flight becomes empty. Do this for all such routes at once: it only adds flights and empties others, so each inequality \(e' \ge a\) refers to a flight that is still there.
Every route is now empty (an idle plane) or ends in \(C_G\). Let \(Q\) be the set of the \(q\) planes that are not idle; \(q \ge 1\) since \(t \ge 1\), and \(q \le p \le t\). On \(Q\) this is a simple plan with clean journeys, every route ending in \(C_G\), of cost at most \(C\), with \(F_k \le M'\). Lemmas 4.3(b), 4.4 and 4.5 on \(Q\) give an admissible partition over \(Q\) of a multiset of size \(2t - q\), with cost at most \(C\) and loads at most \(M'\).
Lemma 4.6, applied once per idle plane (each time with \(t \ge q' + 1\) for the current number \(q' < p \le t\) of planes), gives a partition over all \(p\) planes of size \(s\), without increasing the cost or the largest load. \(\square\)

Theorem 4.10 (converse without (A1)). Assume (S) and (AΔ). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\), makespan \(M\) and flight times \(F_k\), there is an admissible partition \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) of a multiset \(X\) with \(|X| = s\), \(c(X) \le C\) and \(\ell(X_k) \le F_k \le M\) for every \(k\). More generally, for a feasible plan on any set \(Q\) of planes with \(t \ge |Q|\), the same holds with \(|Q|\) in place of \(p\): an admissible partition \((X_k)_{k \in Q}\) with \(|X| = 2t - |Q|\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. We write the proof for all \(p\) planes. It uses \(t \ge p\) only for Lemma 4.11, through \(s \ge p\), so it holds word for word for any set \(Q\) with \(t \ge |Q|\). Clean the plan (Lemma 3.1); this keeps the routes. For a segment \(\gamma\), let \(R(\gamma)\) be the largest \(d_x\) over its central landings \(x\). By Lemma 3.3(b) and (S), \(F(\gamma) \ge 2R(\gamma)\). Plane \(k\) has \(\sigma_k \ge 1\) segments, and \(\sigma = \sum_k \sigma_k \ge s\) (Lemma 3.2).
A selection is a set of segments, at least one per plane, with for each chosen \(\gamma\) a city \(x(\gamma)\) such that \(d_{x(\gamma)} \le R(\gamma)\), and a central landing \(\pi(\gamma)\) of the plan in \(x(\gamma)\), with \(\pi\) injective. Its groups \(X_k = \{x(\gamma) : \gamma \text{ chosen, of plane } k\}\) satisfy \(\ell(X_k) \le \sum_{\gamma \text{ chosen}} 2R(\gamma) \le \sum_{\gamma} F(\gamma) = F_k \le M\), the last sum running over all segments of \(k\), and \(c(X) = \sum_\gamma c(\pi(\gamma)) \le C\). We build a selection whose groups are admissible with \(|X| \ge s\) and \(|X| \equiv s \pmod 2\). Lemma 4.11 then removes landings two at a time, down to \(|X| = s\), keeping the groups admissible and making them smaller.
Step 1: sharing components. Two planes share a central city if both land in it. Hubs do not count: every plane lands in \(C_G\). Let \(K\) be a connected component of the graph on planes whose edges join planes that share a central city. Let \(q_K\) be its number of planes, \(\sigma_K\) its number of segments, and \(t_K\) the number of passengers whose journey uses a plane of \(K\). A clean journey arrives in a hub only with its last flight. So two consecutive flights of a journey on different planes meet in a central city. The first plane lands there, and so does the second, whose route starts in \(C_I\). Every journey therefore stays inside one component, \(\sum_K t_K = t\), and \(K\) with its passengers is a feasible plan. Lemma 3.2, whose proof does not use \(t \ge p\), gives \(\sigma_K \ge 2t_K - q_K\), even when \(t_K < q_K\); write \(\delta_K = \sigma_K - 2t_K + q_K \ge 0\), so that \(\sum_K \delta_K = \sigma - s\). The number of planes of \(K\) with \(\sigma_k\) even has the parity of \(q_K - \sigma_K\), hence of \(\delta_K\). If \(\delta_K\) is odd, some plane \(\kappa_K\) of \(K\) has \(\sigma_{\kappa_K} \ge 2\); otherwise \(\sigma_K = q_K\) and \(\delta_K = 2(q_K - t_K)\) would be even. Let \(\mathcal T\) be the set of planes with \(\sigma_k\) even, with membership of \(\kappa_K\) flipped for every \(K\) with \(\delta_K\) odd. Every component then contains an even number of planes of \(\mathcal T\). Plane \(\kappa_K\) will leave out one segment, so that \(\mathcal T\) is the set of planes with an even number of chosen segments.
Step 2: links. A link \((\gamma, \gamma', y)\) joins segments \(\gamma, \gamma'\) of two different planes at a city \(y\) with \(d_y \le \min(R(\gamma), R(\gamma'))\). Its ends are \((\gamma, y)\) and \((\gamma', y)\). Each end will carry a payment, a central landing in \(y\), and no landing will pay for two ends. The degree of a plane is the number of ends at its segments. Take a spanning forest of the sharing graph, and in it the \(\mathcal T\)-join \(J\) built as in the proof of Lemma 2.4(b): the edge from a vertex to its parent is in \(J\) iff the vertex’s subtree contains an odd number of planes of \(\mathcal T\). Every tree has an even number of them, so in \(J\) the planes of \(\mathcal T\) have odd degree and the others even degree. For each edge \(\{u, w\}\) of \(J\), pick a central city that \(u\) and \(w\) share, and segments of \(u\) and of \(w\) that land in it, and make a link there. While a segment \(\gamma\) has two ends at one city \(y\), in links \((\gamma, \gamma_1, y)\) and \((\gamma, \gamma_2, y)\), replace them by \((\gamma_1, \gamma_2, y)\), or delete both if \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) belong to the same plane. This keeps every plane’s degree mod 2 and lowers the number of links. At this point every end is at a city in which its segment lands, and no segment has two ends at one city. Pay each end with a landing of its own segment in its city. Later steps move ends to cities their segment does not visit. Only the payments and the bound by \(R\) are tracked from now on.
Re-pairing. Let a segment \(\gamma\) have ends in the links \(\lambda_1 = (\gamma, \gamma_1, y_1)\) and \(\lambda_2 = (\gamma, \gamma_2, y_2)\), with \(d_{y_1} \le d_{y_2}\). Re-pairing them replaces both links by \((\gamma_1, \gamma_2, y_1)\). In it, \(\gamma_1\) keeps its payment from \(\lambda_1\), and \(\gamma_2\) receives the payment of \(\gamma\) in \(\lambda_1\). The payments of \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma_2\) in \(\lambda_2\) are released. If \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) belong to the same plane, both links are deleted instead and all their payments released. A re-pairing keeps the following properties:

every end is within \(R\), as \(d_{y_1} \le d_{y_2} \le R(\gamma_2)\);
payments are in the right city and exclusive;
every plane’s degree mod 2: the plane of \(\gamma\) loses two ends, and the planes of \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) keep one end each, or their common plane loses two;
no segment gains an end.

It also lowers the number of links.
Step 3: one end per segment. For every segment \(\gamma\) fix one of its landings \(z(\gamma)\) in a city of duration \(R(\gamma)\). While some segment \(\gamma\) has \(r \ge 2\) ends, sort them by the duration of their city, putting last the end paid by \(z(\gamma)\) if there is one. This is possible, because every end of \(\gamma\) is within \(R(\gamma)\). Then re-pair the first end with the second, the third with the fourth, and so on. Afterwards \(\gamma\) has at most one end, and never gains another. The loop ends because the number of links decreases.
Claim: no landing \(z(\gamma)\) ever pays for an end of another segment. Payments are only ever moved from one end to another, or released, and a released landing never pays an end again. So a landing of \(\gamma\) can pay for another segment only if \(\gamma\) hands it over, which happens only when \(\gamma\) is the middle segment of a re-pairing. That happens only when \(\gamma\) itself is processed, which is at most once, and only for its ends at odd positions. If \(z(\gamma)\) pays an end of \(\gamma\), that end is at position \(r\): for \(r\) even its payment is released, and for \(r\) odd it is not re-paired.
Step 4: the left-out segments. For each \(K\) with \(\delta_K\) odd, consider \(\kappa = \kappa_K\). If \(\kappa\) has a segment without an end, leave it out. Otherwise two segments \(\gamma, \gamma'\) of \(\kappa\) have one end each, in links \((\gamma, \gamma_1, y)\) and \((\gamma', \gamma_2, y')\) with \(d_y \le d_{y'}\). Replace both by \((\gamma_1, \gamma_2, y)\), or delete both if \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) belong to the same plane. Here \(\gamma_1\) keeps its payment and \(\gamma_2\) receives the payment of \(\gamma\); the payments of \(\gamma'\) and of \(\gamma_2\) at \(y'\) are released. The four properties hold as for a re-pairing, with \(\kappa\) losing two ends. Leave out \(\gamma\): its landing may now pay for \(\gamma_2\), but \(\gamma\) will not be chosen. The segment \(\gamma'\) has no end left and handed nothing over. So the claim still holds for every segment that is not left out.
Step 5: the selection. Choose all segments that are not left out. A chosen segment with an end takes the city of its end and the end’s payment. One without an end takes the city of \(z(\gamma)\) and \(z(\gamma)\), which by the claim pays for no end. This \(\pi\) is injective, and every city is within \(R\). Plane \(k\) has \(m_k = \sigma_k\) chosen segments, or \(\sigma_k - 1\) if \(k\) is some \(\kappa_K\). So \(m_k \ge 1\), and \(m_k\) is even exactly when \(k \in \mathcal T\). Let \(\tilde h_{k,y}\) be the number of chosen segments of \(k\) with an end at \(y\). Then \(\tilde h_{k,y} \le X_k(y)\). The row sum \(\sum_y \tilde h_{k,y}\) is the degree of \(k\), which is odd iff \(k \in \mathcal T\); hence it is \(\equiv m_k + 1 = |X_k| + 1\). The column sum \(\sum_k \tilde h_{k,y}\) is twice the number of links at \(y\). By Lemma 2.3 the groups are admissible. Their size is \(\sigma - \#\{K : \delta_K \text{ odd}\}\), which is at least \(\sigma - \sum_K \delta_K = s\) and has the parity of \(s\). \(\square\)

Lemma 4.11 (shrinking)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.5

Statement (theory note, §4.6).
Lemma 4.11 (shrinking). Let \(X_1,\dots,X_p\) be admissible with \(|X| \ge p + 2\). Two landings can be removed from the groups so that the partition stays admissible, each new group a sub-multiset of the old one.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Take a parity matrix \(h\). By Lemma 2.5, \(f_k = |X_k| - h_k\) is odd. If some \(f_k \ge 3\), remove two of the \(f_k\) copies in \(X_k\) beyond one copy of each city of \(\eta_k\): (h1)–(h3) still hold and \(|X_k| - 2 \ge h_k + 1 \ge 1\). Otherwise every \(f_k = 1\), so \(\sum_k h_k = |X| - p \ge 2\). Some city \(i\) has \(h_{u,i} = h_{v,i} = 1\) for planes \(u \ne v\), as its column is even and non-zero. Remove \(i\) from \(X_u\) and from \(X_v\) and set \(h_{u,i} = h_{v,i} = 0\), as in case (b) of Lemma 4.6. Then (h1) holds; (h2) holds, as row sums and sizes both drop by one; (h3) holds, as column \(i\) drops by 2; and \(|X_u| - 1 = h_u \ge 1\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Remarks.

The proof of Theorem 4.10 uses (AΔ) only through \(F(\gamma) \ge 2d_x\) for every central city \(x\) of a segment \(\gamma\). Corollary 4.12 uses (AΔ) once more, for Theorem 4.9: the rest of a journey from a central city \(b\) lasts at least \(\bar d_b\). Under (S) and (A1) this holds too: a segment visiting \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) lasts at least \(d_{x_1} + \sum_j (d_{x_j} + d_{x_{j+1}}) + d_{x_m} = 2\sum_j d_{x_j}\). So the proof is also a second proof of Theorem 4.7, without Step 1 and without Lemmas 4.3–4.5. More generally, it suffices that no sequence of flights from a central city to a hub is shorter than its hub leg.
Under (S) alone, let \(d'_x\) be the shortest flight time from \(x\) to a hub. It is the same for both hubs, as swapping \(C_I\) and \(C_G\) preserves all durations. Then \(F(\gamma) \ge 2d'_x\) for every central city \(x\) of \(\gamma\), and the proof, unchanged with \(d'\) in place of \(d\), gives an admissible partition with \(|X| = s\), \(c(X) \le C\) and \(2\sum_{x \in X_k} d'_x \le F_k\). So \(E\) computed with the durations \(d'\) is a lower bound under (S) alone, next to \(L\). Under (AΔ) or (A1), \(d' = d\). Example 4.13 shows that \(d\) itself does not give a lower bound in general.
No timing is used: only the flight times \(F(\gamma)\), the landings, and which planes share which cities. Zero durations are allowed. The re-pairing at one segment is the “one chain” contraction of the first version (moving an end to the smaller duration, paid by a landing of the middle segment). Step 3 performs it for all chains at once, by moving payments together with ends and keeping \(z(\gamma)\) for \(\gamma\) itself.

Corollary 4.12. Under (S) and (AΔ), Corollary 4.8, Theorem 4.9, Proposition 7.1, the front statements of Propositions 7.8 and 7.9 hold, and forest gaps (§9) are sound.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Corollary 4.8 uses Theorem 4.7 only through its conclusion, which Theorem 4.10 provides; Lemma 1.1 and Theorem 4.1 need no assumption on central flights. Propositions 7.1 and 7.8 and the forest kind rest on Corollary 4.8 and on the groups of Theorem 4.7, which Theorem 4.10 replaces. For Theorem 4.9, change items 1–3 of its proof. Clean the plan, and delete from every route the flights after its last flight that carries a passenger. Journeys are unchanged. A route that is not empty now ends with a flight carrying a passenger \(\pi\). This flight does not arrive in \(C_I\) (Lemma 3.1). Suppose it arrives in a central city \(b\), at time \(a\). The rest of \(\pi\)’s journey goes from \(b\) to \(C_G\), leaving \(b\) no earlier than \(a\), and by (AΔ), as in Lemma 3.3(b), its flights last at least \(\bar d_b\). Item 4 is unchanged. \(\square\)

plane 1: \(C_I \to 1 \to C_G\) carrying a passenger, then \(C_G \to 4 \to C_G\), which picks up at 4, at time 15, the passenger dropped there by plane 3. plane 2: \(C_I \to 2 \to C_G\) carrying a passenger, \(C_G \to 2 \to C_I\), then \(C_I \to 4 \to C_G\) carrying a passenger, ending at 34;
plane 3: \(C_I \to 4 \to 3 \to C_I\), dropping its passenger at 4 at time 11 and coming back through 3 in \(1 + 9 < d_4\). Then \(C_I \to 3 \to C_G\) carrying a passenger, ending at 39, which sets the makespan.

title: Blueprint
text:
Greedy scheduling is not exact
A natural heuristic fixes the multiset of landings and schedules it greedily, longest flights first onto the least-loaded plane. §5 of the note shows that this misses front points; the smallest counterexample’s front is checked by the Lean kernel. Deciding the least makespan of a multiset is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 8.1), so no polynomial rule of this kind is exact unless P = NP.

The greedy counterexample
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S), (A1) · Uses 4.8

Statement (theory note, §5).

\(d = (6, 10)\), \(p = 2\), \(t = 5\), PPP \(a = (10,10,6,6,6)\), \(\bar a = (10,6,6)\): the greedy gives every plane a 20-crossing first and ends at 52/68. The partition \(\{10,10,10\} \mid \{6,6,6,6,6\}\) gives 60/60. The front point (260, 60) is missed.
\(d = (1,3)\), \(c = (9,5)\), \(t = 4\), \(p = 2\): the point (42, 12) needs the plane making the drop-off to also take the long crossing; the no-duplicate greedy ends at 14.

Deciding \(M(X) \le 2T\) is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 8.1), so no polynomial greedy can be exact unless P = NP.

It contains (260, 60). That the greedy schedule misses this point is the hand computation of the note (52/68 instead of 60/60); it is not a Lean statement.

title: Blueprint
text:
Non-symmetric case
Different durations to the two hubs (§6). Waiting can now be harmful (Proposition 6.5), so role loads alone do not give the front. It is characterised instead by schedulable domination (Theorem 6.9), machine-checked for every plan.

Theorem 6.1 (converse to role configurations)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (A1-NS) · Uses 3.1, 4.3, 4.4

Statement (theory note, §6.1).
Theorem 6.1 (converse to role configurations) [N1]. Assume (A1-NS). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\) there is a role configuration on all \(p\) planes with passenger count \(t\), cost at most \(C\) and \(\lambda_k \le F_k \le M\) for every \(k\). (AΔ) is not needed.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Replace a central flight \(a \to b\) departing at \(e\) by \(a \to h \to b\) through a hub \(h\) with \(\mathrm{dur}(a,h) + \mathrm{dur}(h,b) \le d_{ab}\), which exists by (A1-NS). The plane waits in \(b\) until its next departure, and a passenger on board stays on board through \(h\). Then clean (Lemma 3.1): a journey that passes through \(C_I\) now starts there, one that passes through \(C_G\) ends there. The plan is simple, costs no more, and no \(F_k\) increases. Lemmas 4.3(b) and 4.4 conclude. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.2 (relaxed role loads)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (AΔ) · Uses 2.1, 3.3, 4.4

Statement (theory note, §6.1).
Lemma 6.2 (relaxed role loads). Assume (AΔ). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\) there are multisets \(\mathrm{Dr}_k\), \(\mathrm{Pk}_k\), \(\mathrm{Cr}_k\) (\(k = 1,\dots,p\)) with \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k|\) odd, \(\sum_k |\mathrm{Dr}_k| = \sum_k |\mathrm{Pk}_k|\) (only the totals balance), passenger count \(t\), cost at most \(C\) and \(\lambda_k \le F_k \le M\). So the least cost \(L_{\rm NS}(T)\) of such a family with every \(\lambda_k \le T\) is a lower bound for every plan of makespan at most \(T\), whatever its central flights, including the shuttles and the multi-landing segments of §6.4.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Give each segment \(\gamma\) any of its landings. By Lemma 3.3(b), \(F(\gamma)\) is at least the role duration of its type at that landing, reading \(A\) and \(\bar A\) as crossings, \(B\) as drop-offs and \(\bar B\) as pick-ups. A segment has exactly one flight departing from a hub (its first) and one arriving in a hub (its last). Mapping each passenger to the segment of its first flight (from \(C_I\), so of type \(A\) or \(B\)) and to the segment of its last flight (into \(C_G\), of type \(A\) or \(\bar B\)) is injective by capacity, so \(\#A + \#B \ge t\) and \(\#A + \#\bar B \ge t\). Take all \(A\) and \(\bar A\) segments of plane \(k\) as its crossings, so \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k| = 2\#A_k - 1\) (Lemma 2.1), and \(\min(\#B, \#\bar B)\) of the \(B\) and of the \(\bar B\) segments as drop-offs and pick-ups. The passenger count is \(\min(\#B, \#\bar B) + \#A \ge t\). Shrink as in Lemma 4.4, removing in the second case a drop-off and a pick-up anywhere. \(\square\)






Lemma 6.3 (template)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Uses 3.3

Statement (theory note, §6.2).
Lemma 6.3 (template) [N3]. The template is a schedule, and its makespan is \[M_{\rm tmpl} = \max\Big(\max_k \lambda_k,\ \max_{(u,j;\,v,l) \in \mathcal L \text{ at } i}\ \mathrm{Pre}_u(j) + d_i + \bar d_i + \mathrm{Suf}_v(l)\Big).\] Every schedule of the same configuration, orders and matching has makespan at least \(M_{\rm tmpl}\). So the least makespan of a role configuration is the minimum of \(M_{\rm tmpl}\) over orders and matchings. No assumption on durations is needed.






Proof (theory note)

The first half, and why every configuration of cost 14 and loads \(\le 73\) waits, is the following argument.
Cost-14 configurations at level 73. Write \(1\) and \(2\) for the cities. Loads: a crossing weighs 6 in city 1 and 30 in city 2; a drop-off 6 and 38; a pick-up 6 and 22. A role configuration has \(s = 10\) landings, so cost 14 means one landing in city 1 and nine in city 2. Each plane flies an odd number of crossings, and only one plane, \(v\), can cross in city 1; a plane crossing three times in city 2 weighs 90. So the three other planes cross once, in city 2 (load 30), and with \(\ell\) links (drop-off/pick-up pairs) \(v\) crosses \(10 - 2\ell - 3\) times. For \(\ell \le 2\), \(v\) crosses at least 3 times, two of them in city 2, so it weighs at least 66 and takes no link landing (a pick-up in city 2 adds 22); the other three planes can take one link landing each (30 + 38 or 30 + 22; two would exceed 73), which leaves at least one of the \(2\ell\) link landings unplaced when \(\ell = 2\), and fails the crossing count when \(\ell \le 1\) (\(v\) would weigh \(6 + 4 \cdot 30\) or more). Such a configuration exists, so the role-load bound at level 73 is 14.
Why it waits. Every drop-off reaches city 2 at time \(\ge 19\). Plane \(v\) starts in \(C_I\) with no drop-off, so it crosses first and reaches city 2 for its first pick-up at time \(6 + 11 = 17\); it waits until 19, and its two further pick-ups take 44 more: it finishes at \(19 + 11 + 44 = 74 > 72 = \lambda_v\). The configuration-level form of the conjecture fails on it, and since every cost-14 configuration at level 73 is of this shape, so does the front-level form, as the oracle confirms. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.6 (imbalance-vector DP)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.2

Statement (theory note, §6.3).
Proposition 6.6 (imbalance-vector DP) [N5]. Process the planes in order, with states \((k, j, v)\): \(k\) planes processed, \(j\) landings used, and \(v = \sum_{k' \le k} (\mathrm{Dr}_{k'} - \mathrm{Pk}_{k'}) \in \mathbb Z^n\) the imbalance. A plane option is a triple \((\mathrm{Dr}, \mathrm{Pk}, r)\) with \(r\) odd, of weight \(c(\mathrm{Dr}) + c(\mathrm{Pk}) + G^{\rm cr}[r][T - 2\delta(\mathrm{Dr}) - 2\bar\delta(\mathrm{Pk})]\); it adds \(|\mathrm{Dr}| + |\mathrm{Pk}| + r\) to \(j\) and \(\mathrm{Dr} - \mathrm{Pk}\) to \(v\). With states restricted to \(\|v\|_1 \le t - p\), the shortest path from \((0, 0, 0)\) to \((p, s, 0)\) has weight \(E_{\rm NS}(T)\). There are at most \((p+1)(s+1)\sum_{u \le t-p} 2^u \binom{n}{u}\binom{t-p}{u}\) states, a polynomial in \(n\) and \(s\) for fixed \(t - p\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. A path gives a role configuration whose cost is its weight, with \(G^{\rm cr}\)-optimal crossings: the final imbalance 0 is the balance, and \(|X| = s\) gives the passenger count \((s + p)/2 = t\). Conversely, take a role configuration with passenger count \(t\) and every \(\lambda_k \le T\), and let \(N = \sum_k |\mathrm{Dr}_k|\) be its number of links. From \(s = 2N + \sum_k |\mathrm{Cr}_k| \ge 2N + p\), \(N \le t - p\). For a prefix of \(k\) planes and a city \(i\), let \(D^{\le}(i)\), \(P^{\le}(i)\) count the drop-offs and pick-ups at \(i\) of these planes, and \(D^{>}(i)\), \(P^{>}(i)\) those of the others. By the balance, \(v_k(i) = D^{\le}(i) - P^{\le}(i) = P^{>}(i) - D^{>}(i)\), so \(|v_k(i)| \le D^{\le}(i)\) if \(v_k(i) \ge 0\) and \(|v_k(i)| \le D^{>}(i)\) otherwise. Summing over \(i\), \(\|v_k\|_1 \le N \le t - p\), so the configuration is a path of the restricted graph, of weight at most its cost. To count the vectors \(v\), choose a support of \(u\) cities, signs, and positive values summing to at most \(t - p\). \(\square\)

Definition 6.17 (shuttle triple, split crossing)
Lean informal · Note definition

Statement (theory note, §6.4).
Definition 6.17 (shuttle triple, split crossing). Let \(x \ne y\) be central cities joined by a flight.

A shuttle from \(x\) to \(y\) is a segment \(C_G \to x \to y \to C_I\) (type \(\bar A\)) that carries a passenger from \(x\) to \(y\). A shuttle triple at \((x, y)\) is a drop-off at \(x\) (a segment \(B\)), a shuttle from \(x\) to \(y\), and a pick-up at \(y\) (a segment \(\bar B\)), the three carrying one passenger. This is the \(B\bar A\bar B\) situation of the arXiv paper.
A split crossing at \((x, y)\) is a segment \(C_I \to x \to y \to C_G\) (type \(A\)) whose central flight is empty: its first flight leaves a passenger in \(x\), and its last flight carries another passenger from \(y\) to \(C_G\). It acts as a drop-off at \(x\) and a pick-up at \(y\).







Remarks in the note





A shuttle from \(y\) to \(x\) and a split crossing at \((x, y)\) fly the same three flights in opposite directions. Both last \(d_x + d_{xy} + \bar d_y\), and both take one passenger out of \(y\) and leave one in \(x\). But a split crossing is a crossing, while a shuttle is a return segment, whose plane needs two more crossings (Lemma 2.1). By Lemma 3.3(b), under (AΔ), both last at least \(\max(d_x + \bar d_x,\ d_y + \bar d_y)\).

So either a plane has three crossings, with load at least 12, or each plane has one crossing and there is one link, a drop-off and a pick-up at one city \(x\). Lemma 6.19 (cut bound)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 3.3

Statement (theory note, §6.4).
Lemma 6.19 (cut bound). Let \(\Phi\) be the least flight time of a sequence of flights from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\). For every feasible plan, \(\sum_k F_k \ge (2t - p)\,\Phi\), so its makespan is at least \((2t - p)\Phi/p\). No assumption is needed. Under (AΔ), \(\Phi = \min_x (d_x + \bar d_x)\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Let \(\phi(v)\) be the least flight time of a sequence of flights from \(C_I\) to the city \(v\), so \(\phi(C_I) = 0\), \(\phi(C_G) = \Phi\), and \(|\phi(a) - \phi(b)| \le \mathrm{dur}(a, b)\) for every flight. For a leg \(\ell\) from \(a\) to \(b\) let \(\Delta(\ell) = \phi(b) - \phi(a)\). Along the route of plane \(k\) the \(\Delta\) sum to \(\Phi\). So its upward part \(U_k = \sum_\ell \Delta(\ell)^+\) and its downward part \(D_k = \sum_\ell \Delta(\ell)^-\) satisfy \(U_k - D_k = \Phi\), and \(F_k \ge U_k + D_k = 2U_k - \Phi\). Along the journey of a passenger the \(\Delta\) also sum to \(\Phi\), so the upward parts of its legs add up to at least \(\Phi\). Journeys are disjoint (capacity), so \(\sum_k U_k \ge t\Phi\) and \(\sum_k F_k \ge 2t\Phi - p\Phi\). Every \(F_k\) is at most the makespan. Under (AΔ), take a sequence of flights from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), its first arrival in \(C_G\), and its last visit to \(C_I\) before that. Between them it visits only central cities, and if \(x\) is the last of them, that part lasts at least \(d_x + \bar d_x\) by the induction of Lemma 3.3(b). The sequence \(C_I \to x \to C_G\) attains it. \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





In Proposition 6.7 and in 6.18(a) and (c), the least makespan of all plans is this bound rounded up, \(\lceil (2t-p)\Phi/p \rceil\) (8, 32 and 41), and role configurations stay above it. The relaxed role loads of Lemma 6.2 miss it: in 6.18(a) they allow makespan 14, dropping every linked passenger off in city 1 and picking it up in city 2. Lemma 6.19 is a lower bound for every plan, next to \(L_{\rm NS}\), but it bounds makespans only, not costs. Its proof uses that every route ends in \(C_G\), so it does not cover the variant of §4.5 in which planes may end anywhere; there the independent review found that the least makespan still meets the bound on the instances of Proposition 6.7 and 6.18(a).
What remains for clique instances without (A1-NS): \(L_{\rm NS}\) and Lemma 6.19 are lower bounds, and plans built from role configurations and from the segments above are upper bounds. The flow model and the exhaustive searches of §11 compute the front exactly on small instances. A combinatorial description of the front is open. The searches of §11 show where the difficulty lies. Shuttles never improved a front: wherever the exhaustive search compared them, plans whose only multi-landing segments are shuttles gave the front of role configurations. Split crossings alone completed the front on all but two of 600 random instances, and on those two, segments with more central landings were needed. And on 150 random instances whose hub durations \(d\) and \(\bar d\) order the cities alike, central flights never changed the front, as the mechanism above suggests; whether this holds in general is open.






Lemma 6.8 (event order)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Uses 4.3(a)

Statement (theory note, §6.2).
Lemma 6.8 (event order). The next-leg relation of a plan relates a leg to the next leg on its route and to the next leg of the journey it belongs to, if any.

A plan is event-ordered iff its next-leg relation has no cycle.
In a simple plan with clean journeys, a cycle of the next-leg relation passes through a central city \(x\) with \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\).
The template of a role configuration (§6.2), and the plan of Theorem 4.1, are event-ordered.







Proof (theory note)





Proof. (a) An event order extends the relation, so the relation has no cycle. Conversely, along the relation departure times do not decrease, since the next leg departs no earlier than the previous one arrives; sorting the legs by departure time, ties broken by a topological order of the acyclic relation, gives an event order.

Along each step the next leg departs no earlier than the previous one departs plus its duration, so every leg on a cycle has zero duration. Steps within one plane go forward on its route (§1.2, item 2), so a cycle contains a journey step between two planes. By Lemma 4.3(a) that step goes from a leg \(C_I \to x\) to a leg \(x \to C_G\), both on the cycle, so \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\).
Give the legs of a plane’s drop-offs phase 1, of its crossings phase 2 and of its pick-ups phase 3. A step of the relation either stays on one plane and goes forward on its route, or follows a link from the first leg of a drop-off (phase 1) to the second leg of a pick-up (phase 3). Phases never decrease along the relation, and they increase at every step between two planes. A cycle therefore has no such step and stays on one route, which is impossible. The plan of Theorem 4.1 has the same three phases. \(\square\)




In Lean. EventOrdered is the definition; EventOrdered.of_eoOK proves sound a computable test for the order (departure, phase, plane, position). Parts (a)–(c) are not stated in Lean: Theorem 6.9 for every plan does not need them.
Formalised parts. These declarations cover part of the statement; the node keeps the status of the note.
Part ZenoFront.EventOrdered Lean definition
/-- **Event-ordered plans** (§1.2 of the note). The legs have a total order (`rank`, injective)
that extends every route and some journey of every passenger, and along which departure times
do not decrease. Every plan with positive durations is event-ordered, and so is every PDDL plan.
This is the scope of Theorem 6.9 when a city has `d = d̄ = 0`. -/
def EventOrdered (P : Plan n t p) : Prop :=
  ∃ rank : LegId P → ℕ, Function.Injective rank ∧
    (∀ k (i j : Fin (P k).length), i < j → rank ⟨k, i⟩ < rank ⟨k, j⟩) ∧
    (∀ x y, rank x < rank y → (legAt P x).dep ≤ (legAt P y).dep) ∧
    ∀ π : Fin t, ∃ js : List (LegId P), (js.map (legAt P)).Perm (paxLegs P π) ∧
      IsRoute .ci 0 (js.map (legAt P)) ∧ finalLoc .ci (js.map (legAt P)) = .cg ∧
      js.Pairwise fun x y => rank x < rank y

Theorem 6.9 (schedulable domination)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (A1-NS) · Uses 2.1, 3.1, 3.3, 4.3(a), 4.4, 6.1, 6.3

Statement (theory note, §6.2).
Theorem 6.9 (schedulable domination) [SD]. Assume (A1-NS). Let a feasible plan have cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\). Then there are a role configuration on all \(p\) planes with passenger count \(t\) and cost at most \(C\), orders of its drop-offs and pick-ups, and a link matching whose template has makespan at most \(M\). Neither an event order, nor (AΔ), nor (AΔ-path) is needed.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Step 1: a simple plan with clean journeys. Replace central flights and clean, as in the proof of Theorem 6.1; cost, arrival times, flight times and makespan do not increase. By Lemma 4.3(a), every journey is now a leg \(\alpha_\pi : C_I \to x\) followed by a leg \(\beta_\pi : x \to C_G\), which departs no earlier than \(\alpha_\pi\) arrives. Every route is a sequence of segments, one per landing. For a segment \(\gamma\) at a city \(x\), let \(a(\gamma)\) be the time its first leg arrives in \(x\) and \(e(\gamma)\) the time its second leg departs, so \(a(\gamma) \le e(\gamma)\). From here on only the routes and the pairs \((\alpha_\pi, \beta_\pi)\) matter: the moves below keep the routes valid, but need not keep a plan in the sense of item 2 of §1.2.
Step 2: rewiring. Next to the routes, keep a set of loops, empty at first: closed walks whose legs all depart and arrive at one time \(\tau\), so last \(0\), and alternate between hubs and central cities, so that a loop is made of segments too. A passenger is carried through if \(\alpha_\pi\) and \(\beta_\pi\) are the two legs of one segment, of a route or of a loop. Otherwise it is a hand-off, from the segment \(\gamma\) of \(\alpha_\pi\) to the segment \(\gamma'\) of \(\beta_\pi\), both at its city \(x\). While one of these moves applies, apply it.

Exchange. \(\gamma\) is on the route of \(u\), \(\gamma'\) on the route of \(v \ne u\), and \(a(\gamma') \le e(\gamma)\): \(v\) is in \(x\) before \(u\) leaves. Give \(u\) the legs of \(v\) from \(\beta_\pi\) on, and \(v\) the legs of \(u\) after \(\alpha_\pi\). Both routes stay valid: \(\beta_\pi\) departs after \(\alpha_\pi\) arrives, and the second leg of \(\gamma\) departs after the first leg of \(\gamma'\) arrives.
Cut. \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\) are on one route, \(\gamma'\) before \(\gamma\). The route gives \(e(\gamma') \le a(\gamma)\) and the journey \(a(\gamma) \le e(\gamma')\), so every leg from \(\beta_\pi\) to \(\alpha_\pi\) departs and arrives at \(\tau = e(\gamma')\) and lasts \(0\); in particular \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\). These legs form a closed walk at \(x\). Remove it from the route, which keeps the first leg of \(\gamma'\) and the second leg of \(\gamma\), a segment at \(x\) since \(a(\gamma') \le \tau \le e(\gamma)\). The walk becomes a loop; its segments are \((\alpha_\pi, \beta_\pi)\) and the segments strictly between \(\gamma'\) and \(\gamma\).
Splice. One of \(\gamma, \gamma'\) is a segment \(F\) of a loop at time \(\tau\), the other a segment \(\delta\) of a route, and \(e(\gamma) > a(\gamma')\). Then \(a(\delta) < \tau \le e(\delta)\) or \(a(\delta) \le \tau < e(\delta)\): if \(F = \gamma\), then \(e(\gamma) = \tau > a(\delta)\) and \(\tau \le e(\delta)\) by the journey; if \(F = \gamma'\), then \(a(\delta) \le \tau\) by the journey and \(e(\delta) > \tau\). Insert the loop into the route at \(\delta\): the first leg of \(\delta\), the second leg of \(F\), the loop around to \(F\), the first leg of \(F\), the second leg of \(\delta\). The route stays valid, and \(\pi\) is carried through by the new segment of \(\alpha_\pi\) and \(\beta_\pi\).

Every move keeps the legs, so the cost, and every route’s last leg or exchanges two of them, so the makespan. It keeps the routes valid and the loops closed walks at one time, and it carries one more passenger through. It carries none less: the only segments it breaks are \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\), and a segment carrying another passenger through holds both of that passenger’s legs, so it is neither. So the moves stop, after at most \(t\) of them. Then every hand-off from \(\gamma\) to \(\gamma'\) has \(e(\gamma) \le a(\gamma')\):

between the routes of two planes, the exchange does not apply, so \(e(\gamma) < a(\gamma')\);
on one route, the cut does not apply, so \(\gamma'\) comes after \(\gamma\), and \(e(\gamma) \le a(\gamma')\) along the route;
between a loop and a route, the splice does not apply;
between two loops, at times \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\): \(e(\gamma) = \tau\) is when \(\alpha_\pi\) arrives and \(a(\gamma') = \tau'\) when \(\beta_\pi\) departs.

Step 3: paths. At each city \(x\), draw an arrow from \(\gamma\) to \(\gamma'\) for each hand-off at \(x\); the segments are those of the routes and of the loops. Each leg carries at most one passenger, so every segment has at most one outgoing and one incoming arrow. A \(B\) has no incoming arrow, since its second leg returns to \(C_I\), which clean journeys never reach, and a \(\bar B\) has no outgoing arrow. So the arrows form disjoint paths \(\gamma_0 \to \gamma_1 \to \dots \to \gamma_m\) with \(m \ge 1\), and cycles. The inner segments of a path, and all segments of a cycle, have an incoming and an outgoing arrow, so they are \(A\) segments, each dropping one passenger and picking up another. Along a path, by step 2, \(a(\gamma_0) \le e(\gamma_0) \le a(\gamma_1) \le \dots \le e(\gamma_m)\).
Step 4: selection. Attach each loop to any plane. Take every \(A\) and \(\bar A\) segment of each plane, on its route and its loops, as a crossing. A route from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) has \(\#A - \#\bar A = 1\) (Lemma 2.1) and a closed loop \(0\), so each plane gets an odd number of crossings. For each path from a \(B\) to a \(\bar B\), take its \(B\) as a drop-off and its \(\bar B\) as a pick-up, linked to each other. Take no other segment. The balance holds link by link. A passenger carried through rides an \(A\), which carries no arrow; every other passenger is an arrow of exactly one path or cycle. A cycle of \(k\) arrows consists of \(k\) \(A\) segments. A path with \(m\) arrows contributes its \(m - 1\) inner \(A\) segments, one more for each end that is an \(A\), and one link if it runs from a \(B\) to a \(\bar B\): at least \(m\) in every case. So the passenger count, the number of links plus the number of \(A\) segments, is at least \(t\). Distinct segments have distinct first legs, each a leg of the plan of step 1 landing at the segment’s city, so the selected segments are distinct landings of that plan and the cost is at most \(C\). A route segment is simple and lasts its role duration (Lemma 3.3(c)); a loop segment has role duration \(0\), since its legs last \(0\). So \(\lambda_k \le F_k \le M\), where \(F_k\) is the flight time of the rewired route of plane \(k\): it is valid, starts at time \(\ge 0\) and ends by \(M\).
Step 5: the closed form. The closed form \(M_{\rm tmpl}\) of Lemma 6.3 makes sense for any configuration, orders and matching. Order the drop-offs of each plane with those of its loops first, then those of its route in route order, and its pick-ups with those of its route in route order, then those of its loops. Use the links of step 4. Take a link from the \(j\)-th drop-off \(\gamma\) of \(u\) to the \(l\)-th pick-up \(\gamma'\) of \(v\), at \(x\). If \(\gamma\) is on the route, \(u\) flies its earlier route drop-offs before \(\gamma\), and the loop drop-offs weigh \(0\), so \(\mathrm{Pre}_u(j) + d_x \le a(\gamma)\); if \(\gamma\) is in a loop, \(\mathrm{Pre}_u(j) = d_x = 0\). If \(\gamma'\) is on the route, \(v\) flies \(\bar d_x\) to \(C_G\) after \(e(\gamma')\) and then its later route pick-ups, all by time \(M\), and the loop pick-ups weigh \(0\), so \(e(\gamma') + \bar d_x + \mathrm{Suf}_v(l) \le M\); if \(\gamma'\) is in a loop at time \(\tau\), \(\bar d_x = \mathrm{Suf}_v(l) = 0\) and \(e(\gamma') = \tau \le M\): every leg of a loop was a leg of a route before that route’s last leg, which arrives by \(M\). As \(a(\gamma) \le e(\gamma')\) (step 3), the term of the link is at most \(M\). Together with \(\lambda_k \le M\), \(M_{\rm tmpl} \le M\).
Step 6: shrink. Lemma 4.4 (\(t \ge p\), §1.1) brings the passenger count to \(t\), deleting two crossings of a plane or a drop-off together with a pick-up at its city. Take the pick-up linked to it, so that the remaining links still match drop-offs and pick-ups city by city. With the same orders, deleting crossings only lowers loads, and deleting a link lowers loads and the \(\mathrm{Pre}\) and \(\mathrm{Suf}\) of the other links, so \(M_{\rm tmpl}\) stays at most \(M\). The configuration now has passenger count \(t\), and by Lemma 6.3 its template has makespan \(M_{\rm tmpl} \le M\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





The previous version of this proof kept a feasible, event-ordered plan through step 2. It exchanged only the hand-offs that overlap in the event order, so it needed one, and it left open plans that are not event-ordered on instances with a city of \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\). On such a plan an exchange could leave a journey whose two legs lie on one plane in the wrong order. The cut handles exactly that case: the two legs and everything between them happen at one instant, at a city with \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\), and the template does not need them in the plan’s order, since their segments weigh nothing. checks/sd_zero_check.py runs the three moves and steps 3 to 6 on random plans of this kind (§11).



In Lean. Step 2 works on visits by time (exists_rewired): it exchanges futures, cuts a backward hand-off on one plane into a loop of zero-time visits, and splices such a loop back into a route. Steps 3–6 run with the remaining loops attached to one plane (withLoops). not_schedulableDomination shows that the hypothesis p ≤ t is needed.

Corollary 6.10 (non-symmetric front)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (A1-NS) · Uses 1.1, 6.3, 6.8, 6.9

Statement (theory note, §6.2).
Corollary 6.10 (non-symmetric front). Assume (A1-NS). Let \(m(\mathrm{cfg})\) be the least makespan of a role configuration (§6.2), let \[\mathcal K = \{(c(\mathrm{cfg}),\ m(\mathrm{cfg})) : \mathrm{cfg} \text{ a role configuration on the } p \text{ planes with passenger count } t\},\] and let \(\mathcal A_{\rm eo} \subseteq \mathcal A\) be the set of points of feasible event-ordered plans. Then \(\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A_{\rm eo} = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K\): a feasible plan with cost at most \(C\) and makespan at most \(M\) exists iff some configuration has cost at most \(C\) and least makespan at most \(M\), and then an event-ordered plan does too.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. \(\mathcal K\) is finite, and each of its points is attained by a template, which is a feasible event-ordered plan (Lemma 6.8(c)); so \(\mathcal K \subseteq \mathcal A_{\rm eo} \subseteq \mathcal A\). By Theorem 6.9, every point of \(\mathcal A\) is weakly dominated by a point of \(\mathcal K\). Lemma 1.1 applies to \(\mathcal K \subseteq \mathcal A_{\rm eo}\) and to \(\mathcal K \subseteq \mathcal A\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





By Statement 1.2, the PDDL front tends to \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A_{\rm eo}\) as ε → 0, so under (A1-NS) it is \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K = \mathcal F\) whatever the durations. Plans that are not event-ordered have no PDDL counterpart, and they do not beat the front either.
