title: Blueprint
text:
General flight graphs
An instance on any flight graph can be reduced to a clique instance, one central city per path (§6.6 of the note). The reduction does not keep the front in general: Example 6.11 is a counterexample. Propositions 6.12–6.16 say what the reduction does give, where it is exact, and how to compute the graph’s front directly.

Example 6.11 (the reduction misses the front)
Lean informal · Note refuted · Uses 6.3, 6.10, 6.13

Statement (theory note, §6.6).
Example 6.11 (the reduction misses the front). Let \(U\) be the path \(C_I\)–\(a\)–\(b\)–\(C_G\) with durations \(1, 2, 1\) and \(c_a = c_b = 1\), with \(t = 3\) and \(p = 2\). Then \(f(U)\) has two cities, \(v_a = (C_I a,\ a b C_G)\) with \((d, \bar d, c) = (1, 3, 2)\) and \(v_b = (C_I a b,\ b C_G)\) with \((3, 1, 2)\), and \[\mathcal F_{f(U)} = \{(8, 10)\}, \qquad \mathcal F_U = \{(8, 8)\}.\]






Proof (theory note)





Proof. The reduced front. \(f(U)\) has no central flights, so Corollary 6.10 applies. A role configuration with passenger count 3 on 2 planes has \(s = 4\) landings (Definition 4.2), each of cost 2, so it costs 8. Either one plane has three crossings, and a load of at least 12, or each plane has one crossing (load 4) and there is one link, a drop-off and a pick-up at the same city. These weigh 2 and 6 at \(v_a\), and 6 and 2 at \(v_b\), so some plane has a load of at least 10. By Lemma 6.3 every least makespan is at least 10. The template of a link at \(v_a\), with the drop-off on one plane and the pick-up on the other, reaches 10: the pick-up plane crosses in \([0, 4]\), reaches \(v_a\) at 7, after the drop-off’s arrival at 1, and is back at 10. So \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K = \{(8, 10)\}\).
The graph. Every plan costs at least \(s\kappa^\star = 4 \cdot 2\) (Proposition 6.13). Each edge of the path separates \(C_I\) from \(C_G\). Every passenger flies across it towards \(C_G\) on some leg, and a leg carries at most one passenger, so the planes fly it towards \(C_G\) at least \(t = 3\) times. Each plane ends on the \(C_G\) side, so it flies the edge towards \(C_G\) once more than towards \(C_I\), and the planes fly it towards \(C_I\) at least \(t - p = 1\) time. They thus fly at least \(4 \cdot (1 + 2 + 1) = 16\) in total, one of them at least 8. The following plan costs 8 and has makespan 8 (legs as from → to [departure, arrival]):

plane 1: \(C_I \to a\) [0, 1], \(a \to b\) [1, 3], \(b \to a\) [3, 5], \(a \to b\) [5, 7], \(b \to C_G\) [7, 8];
plane 2: \(C_I \to a\) [0, 1], \(a \to C_I\) [1, 2], \(C_I \to a\) [2, 3], \(a \to b\) [3, 5], \(b \to C_G\) [5, 6], \(C_G \to b\) [6, 7], \(b \to C_G\) [7, 8];
passenger 1 flies plane 2 from \(C_I\) at 2 to \(C_G\); passenger 2 flies plane 1 to \(b\), arriving at 3, and plane 2 from \(b\) at 7; passenger 3 flies plane 2 to \(a\), arriving at 1, and plane 1 from \(a\) at 5 to \(C_G\).

Each plane lands twice in \(a\) and twice in \(b\), and each passenger changes planes at most once. \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





The bound shows what \(f(U)\) cannot do. Beyond one crossing per plane, the planes must fly one more round trip on each edge, \(2 + 4 + 2\) in all. A link of \(f(U)\) gives the round trip on \(C_I\)–\(a\) to one plane and the two others to the other plane (\(v_a\)), or splits after \(b\) (\(v_b\)). The plan above gives \(a\)–\(b\) to plane 1 and the two outer edges to plane 2, \(4 + 4\).
Plane 1 does this in one segment, \(C_I a b a b C_G\): it drops passenger 2 at \(b\) at time 3, flies the central edge \(b \to a\), and picks passenger 3 up at \(a\) at time 5. That is what \(f(U)\) lacks. Its cities have no central flights (\(d_{ij} = \infty\)), and through a hub a plane flies \(\bar d_{v_b} + \bar d_{v_a} = 4\), or \(d_{v_b} + d_{v_a} = 4\), between \(v_b\) and \(v_a\): twice the edge \(a\)–\(b\). This is the short-central-flight mechanism of §6.4, and the reason Proposition 6.15(a) needs (A1-NS). Relaying passengers is not the issue: in the plan above, as in every plan of \(f(U)\) after cleaning (Lemma 4.3(a)), each passenger changes planes at most once. The same routes also let passenger 3 be relayed along three legs of two planes, but that is not needed.
Giving \(f(U)\) its central flights back does not repair the reduction either. Add a central flight of duration 2 between \(v_a\) and \(v_b\). Plane 1’s segment then becomes \(C_I \to v_b \to v_a \to C_G\), but plane 2’s drop-off at \(v_a\) and pick-up at \(v_b\) are no longer paired at one city, and \(f\) charges each of them 2 instead of 1 (Proposition 6.12, cost). The front of this instance is \(\{(8, 10), (10, 8)\}\) (computed, §11).
Bucket brigade. On the same path with durations \(1, 1, 1\), \(t = 4\) and \(p = 3\), the same arguments give \(\mathcal F_{f(U)} = \{(10, 7)\}\) and \(\mathcal F_U = \{(10, 5)\}\). In a plan of makespan 5 each plane flies exactly one edge back and forth, a different edge per plane, so one route is \(C_I a b a b C_G\), the segment of Example 6.11. With the routes \(C_I a C_I a b C_G\), \(C_I a b a b C_G\) and \(C_I a b C_G b C_G\), the passengers can be assigned so that each changes planes at most once (checks/general_graph.py). The same routes also allow a relay through all three planes, one edge each, but it is not needed. With central flights back, \(f(U)\) gives \(\{(10, 7), (12, 5)\}\).
Inner points. The reduction also misses points inside the front. Take the spokes \(C_I\)–1–2–\(C_G\), with durations \(1, 2, 3\), and \(C_I\)–3–4–\(C_G\), with durations \(1, 1, 1\), costs \(c = (3, 4, 5, 5)\), \(t = 3\) and \(p = 2\). The exact front is \((40, 7), (37, 8), (34, 9), (31, 11), (28, 12)\), and \(f(U)\) misses \((31, 11)\). The plan the flow model finds for that point has the route \(C_I\,1\,2\,1\,2\,C_G\), the segment of Example 6.11 on the first spoke (§11). On random tiny graphs the two fronts differ on 342 of 4,000 paths, spokes, cycles and random graphs, 22% of those with \(p \ge 2\) and \(t > p\), and on none of 1,000 clique instances under (A1-NS) (§11).






Proposition 6.12 (the reduced front is attained)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 6.3, 6.10

Statement (theory note, §6.6).
Proposition 6.12 (the reduced front is attained). For every role configuration of \(f(U)\) with passenger count \(t\), every order of its drop-offs and pick-ups and every link matching, \(U\) has a feasible plan with the configuration’s cost and the makespan \(M_{\rm tmpl}\) of its template (Lemma 6.3). Hence \(\mathcal F_{f(U)} \subseteq \mathcal A_U\). No assumption on \(U\) is needed.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Fly the template in \(U\), with each leg between a hub and a city \(v = (w, e)\) replaced by the path it stands for: \(C_I \to v\) by \(w\), \(v \to C_G\) by \(e\), and the opposite legs by the reversed paths. Each path is flown without waiting from the departure of the template leg, so it reaches its last vertex when that leg arrives, and every route ends in \(C_G\) when the template’s does. The passenger of a crossing stays on board through its segment. The passenger of a link from a drop-off to a pick-up at \(v = (w, e)\) flies the drop-off along \(w\) to \(i\), waits there, and flies the pick-up along \(e\) to \(C_G\): the template has the pick-up leave \(v\) no earlier than the drop-off arrives, and the paths keep these times. Every leg of \(U\) carries at most the passenger of the template leg it belongs to. So the plan is feasible, with makespan \(M_{\rm tmpl}\).
Cost. Let \(w = (C_I = u_0, \dots, u_a = i)\) and \(e = (i = x_0, \dots, x_b = C_G)\). The landings in \(U\) of a segment at \(v\) cost:

\(\omega(w) + \omega(e) = c_v\) for a crossing \(A\);
\((\omega(e) + c_i) + (\omega(w) - c_i) = c_v\) for a crossing \(\bar A\), since \(e\) reversed lands in \(x_{b-1}, \dots, x_0\) and \(w\) reversed in \(u_{a-1}, \dots, u_0\);
\(2\omega(w) - c_i\) for a drop-off and \(2\omega(e) + c_i\) for a pick-up.

So \(f\) charges a single drop-off or pick-up wrongly, but a drop-off and a pick-up at the same city cost \(2\omega(w) + 2\omega(e) = 2c_v\) together, as \(f\) charges them. By the balance, the link matching pairs the drop-offs and the pick-ups of every city, so the plan costs what the configuration costs. By Corollary 6.10, whose (A1-NS) holds as \(f(U)\) has no central flights, every point of \(\mathcal F_{f(U)}\) is the cost and least makespan of such a configuration. \(\square\)






Proposition 6.13 (same least cost)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses no edge \(C_I\)–\(C_G\) · Uses 6.10, 6.12

Statement (theory note, §6.6).
Proposition 6.13 (same least cost). Let \(\kappa^\star\) be the least \(\omega\) of a path from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) in \(U\). Every plan of \(U\) costs at least \(s\kappa^\star\), and the cheapest point \((s\kappa^\star, M^\star)\) of \(\mathcal F_{f(U)}\) costs exactly that. Hence \(U\) and \(f(U)\) have the same least cost, and \(\mathcal F_U = \mathrm{Min}\{(C, M) \in \mathcal A_U : M \le M^\star\}\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Take a feasible plan. Let \(Y(a, b)\) be its number of legs from \(a\) to \(b\), and \(Z(a, b)\) the number of these legs that belong to a journey. By capacity, \(0 \le Z \le Y\). Routes and journeys are walks from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), so in the directed graph of \(U\), \(Y\) is an integer flow of value \(p\) and \(Z\) one of value \(t\) from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), and \(Y - Z \ge 0\) is a flow of value \(t - p \ge 0\) from \(C_G\) to \(C_I\). By flow decomposition, \(Z\) is the sum of the arc sets of \(t\) paths from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) and of some cycles, and \(Y - Z\) the sum of those of \(t - p\) paths from \(C_G\) to \(C_I\) and of some cycles. Weight the arc from \(a\) to \(b\) by \(c(b) \ge 0\). The plan costs \(\sum Y(a, b)\,c(b)\). A path from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) weighs its \(\omega\), at least \(\kappa^\star\). A path from \(C_G\) to \(C_I\) weighs the landing costs of its vertices other than \(C_G\), which is \(\omega\) of the reversed path, as both hubs are free. So the plan costs at least \((2t - p)\kappa^\star\).
In \(f(U)\), every city costs \(\omega\) of the walk \(w\) followed by \(e\), at least \(\kappa^\star\): deleting closed sub-walks gives a path and removes landings. A cheapest path from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) has a central vertex, as there is no edge \(C_I\)–\(C_G\), and splitting it there gives a city of cost \(\kappa^\star\). A role configuration with passenger count \(t\) has \(s\) landings (Definition 4.2), so it costs at least \(s\kappa^\star\); \(s\) crossings at that city, split among the planes into odd numbers (\(s \ge p\), \(s \equiv p\)), cost exactly \(s\kappa^\star\). By Corollary 6.10 the cheapest point of \(\mathcal F_{f(U)}\) costs \(s\kappa^\star\), and by Proposition 6.12 it lies in \(\mathcal A_U\). It strictly dominates every point of \(\mathcal A_U\) with makespan above \(M^\star\), and such a point dominates no point with makespan at most \(M^\star\). This gives the last claim. \(\square\)






Proposition 6.14 (dominated cities, Pareto paths)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses no central flights · Uses 1.1, 6.3, 6.10

Statement (theory note, §6.6).
Proposition 6.14 (dominated cities, Pareto paths). Let a clique instance without central flights have cities \(v \ne v'\) with \(c_{v'} \le c_v\), \(d_{v'} \le d_v\) and \(\bar d_{v'} \le \bar d_v\). Removing \(v\) does not change the front. In particular, \(f(U)\) keeps its front when restricted to the pairs \((w, e)\) in which \(w\) is non-dominated among the simple paths from \(C_I\) to \(i\), and \(e\) among those from \(i\) to \(C_G\). Here a path is non-dominated if no other path between the same vertices has \((\omega, \varphi)\) componentwise at most its own and different from it: it is Pareto-minimal, and paths with equal \((\omega, \varphi)\) are all kept.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Both instances satisfy (A1-NS), so by Corollary 6.10 their fronts are \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K'\) and \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K\), with \(\mathcal K' \subseteq \mathcal K\) for the smaller instance. In a role configuration of the larger one, replace every copy of \(v\) by \(v'\), in the drop-offs, the pick-ups and the crossings, keeping the orders and the matching. The balance and the passenger count are kept, the cost does not increase, and neither do the role loads, the prefixes \(\mathrm{Pre}\), the suffixes \(\mathrm{Suf}\) and the durations in the link terms of Lemma 6.3, hence \(M_{\rm tmpl}\). So every point of \(\mathcal K\) is weakly dominated by a point of \(\mathcal K'\), which is finite, and Lemma 1.1 gives \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K'\). If \(w'\) dominates \(w\), both from \(C_I\) to \(i\), then \((w', e)\) dominates \((w, e)\) in this sense, and likewise for \(e\); every city is dominated by one whose two paths are non-dominated, so the other cities can be removed one at a time. \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





The paper justifies this restriction by its sub-path claim, which is not needed. Read with “path in a plan” meaning a plane’s route (the journeys of Example 6.11 are simple paths, so they do not refute it), the claim is false for plans of \(U\). Plane 1’s route in Example 6.11 contains the sub-path \(a\,b\,a\,b\), with \((\omega, \varphi) = (3, 6)\), which the path \(a\,b\), with \((1, 2)\), dominates.






Proposition 6.15 (where the reduction is exact)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1, 6.9, 6.10, 6.12, 6.13

Statement (theory note, §6.6).
Proposition 6.15 (where the reduction is exact). \(\mathcal F_U = \mathcal F_{f(U)}\) in each of these cases:

\(U\) is a clique instance (every central vertex is joined to both hubs) satisfying (A1-NS);
\(p = 1\);
\(t = p\).







Proof (theory note)





Proof. It suffices that every feasible plan of \(U\), with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\), is weakly dominated by a point of the finite set \(\mathcal K\) of Corollary 6.10 for \(f(U)\). Indeed \(\mathcal K \subseteq \mathcal A_U\) by Proposition 6.12, and Lemma 1.1 then gives \(\mathcal F_U = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K = \mathcal F_{f(U)}\).

Read \(U\) as the clique instance with cities \((\mathrm{dur}(C_I, i), \mathrm{dur}(i, C_G), c_i)\) and its central edges as central flights. By Theorem 6.9 there is a role configuration with passenger count \(t\), cost at most \(C\) and a template no later than \(M\). Each of its cities \(i\) is the city \((C_I i,\ i C_G)\) of \(f(U)\), with the same durations and cost, so it is a configuration of \(f(U)\) with the same cost and template.
The journeys of the plan are walks from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) on pairwise distinct legs, so their landing costs sum to at most \(C\). Each has a flight time of at most \(M\): its legs follow one another, and the last one arrives by \(M\). Delete the closed sub-walks of each journey, which does not increase \(\omega\) or \(\varphi\), and split the resulting path at a central vertex. This gives a city of \(f(U)\) that costs at most the journey’s landings and has \(d + \bar d\) at most its flight time. Give each of the \(t = p\) planes one journey’s city as its only crossing, with no links: the passenger count is \(t\), the cost at most \(C\), every load at most \(M\), and \(M_{\rm tmpl} = \max_k \lambda_k \le M\).
With \(Y\) and \(Z\) as in the proof of Proposition 6.13, \(Z\) is the sum of \(t\) paths from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) and of cycles, and \(Y - Z\) the sum of \(t - 1\) paths from \(C_G\) to \(C_I\) and of cycles. These \(2t - 1\) paths have total landing cost at most \(C\) and total duration at most \(\sum Y(a, b)\,\mathrm{dur}(a, b) = F_1 \le M\). Split each path, a reversed one for those from \(C_G\), at a central vertex into a city, and give the single plane these \(2t - 1\) cities as crossings. Their number is odd, the passenger count is \(t\), there are no links, the cost is at most \(C\), and \(M_{\rm tmpl} = \lambda_1 \le M\). \(\square\)










Remarks in the note





Example 6.11 has \(n = 2\), \(p = 2\) and \(t = p + 1\), so (b) and (c) are sharp, and every graph instance with \(n = 1\) is the path \(C_I\)–\(1\)–\(C_G\), a clique instance covered by (a).






Proposition 6.16 (time-expanded flows)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses integer durations \(\ge 1\) · Uses 3.1, 6.13

Statement (theory note, §6.6).
Proposition 6.16 (time-expanded flows). Let the durations be integers at least 1, and \(M\) an integer. In the network with nodes \((x, \tau)\) for the vertices \(x\) of \(U\) and \(0 \le \tau \le M\), waiting arcs from \((x, \tau)\) to \((x, \tau + 1)\), and flight arcs from \((a, \tau)\) to \((b, \tau + \mathrm{dur}(a, b))\) for every edge in both directions, take integer flows \(y\) of \(p\) units and \(z\) of \(t\) units from \((C_I, 0)\) to \((C_G, M)\), with \(z \le y\) on every flight arc and \(z = 0\) on the flight arcs into \(C_I\) and out of \(C_G\). The least of \(\sum y\,c(\text{head})\) over the flight arcs is the least cost \(R(M)\) of a feasible plan of \(U\) with makespan at most \(M\). With \(M^\star\) from Proposition 6.13 and \(R(-1) = \infty\), \(\mathcal F_U = \{(R(M), M) : 0 \le M \le M^\star,\ R(M) < R(M - 1)\}\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. A plan of makespan at most \(M\) can be cleaned (Lemma 3.1) without changing its routes, and moved to integer times: durations are positive, so the plan is event-ordered (§1.2), and giving each leg, in that order, the earliest departure its route and its journey allow yields integer times, each no later than before. Each route, with waiting arcs in \(C_I\) before its first leg, between its legs, and after its last one up to \((C_G, M)\), is a unit path. So is each journey, with waiting arcs in \(C_I\) before its first leg, between its legs, and in \(C_G\) after its last. Journeys use distinct legs, so \(z \le y\); a clean journey has no flight into \(C_I\) and none out of \(C_G\); and the cost is the plan’s. Conversely, every arc moves forward in time, so \(y\) decomposes into \(p\) unit paths, the routes, and \(z\) into \(t\) unit paths. On each flight arc, give the passenger units of \(z\) distinct plane units among those of \(y\); this makes the journeys. Consecutive legs of a journey are joined in space and time, and if they belong to one plane the later one departs after the earlier one arrives, so it comes later on the route, as durations are at least 1. Each leg carries at most one passenger, every route ends in \(C_G\) by \(M\), and the plan costs \(\sum y\,c(\text{head})\).
Front. Every point of \(\mathcal A_U\) is weakly dominated by the point of a plan with integer times, so the points of \(\mathcal F_U\) have integer makespans, at most \(M^\star\) by Proposition 6.13. The argument of Proposition 7.1 then applies to \(R\): a point \((c, M)\) of the front has \(c = R(M) < R(M - 1)\), and conversely such a pair is attained with makespan exactly \(M\) and is dominated by no other point. \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





On clique instances this is the model of checks/flowplan.py (§11); checks/general_graph.py solves it on any graph.

title: Blueprint
text:
The exact algorithm (symmetric case)
§7 of the note turns Corollary 4.8 into a pseudo-polynomial algorithm: the front is the set of breakpoints of \(E(T)\), the least cost of an admissible partition with loads at most \(T\). Both exact dynamic programs are proved equal to \(E(T)\) in Lean, and the verified solver zeno-front is built on them.

Proposition 7.1
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S), (A1) · Uses 4.8

Statement (theory note, §7.1).
Proposition 7.1. Under (S) and (A1), \(\mathcal F = \{(E(T), 2T) : T \in \mathbb N,\ E(T) < E(T-1)\}\) with \(E(-1) = \infty\), makespans in units of \(g\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Here \(M(X)\) is an even integer and \(E(T) = \min\{c(X) : M(X) \le 2T\}\). Let \((c, 2T) \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X\) (Corollary 4.8). Then \(c = E(T)\), otherwise a cheaper \(X\) with \(M(X) \le 2T\) dominates it; and \(E(T-1) > c\), otherwise some \(X\) with \(c(X) \le c\) and \(M(X) < 2T\) dominates it. Conversely, let \(E(T) < E(T-1)\) and let \(X\) attain \(E(T)\); then \(M(X) = 2T\). A point \((c(Y), M(Y)) \in \mathcal X\) dominating it has \(M(Y) \le 2T\), hence \(M(Y) = 2T\) (otherwise \(c(Y) \ge E(T-1) > E(T)\)), and then \(c(Y) = E(T)\). \(\square\)



In Lean. minimal_admissiblePoints_iff: (C, 2T) is a minimal admissible point iff E(T) = C and E(T') > C for every T' < T; with Corollary 4.8 this is the proposition.

Lemma 7.2
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note

Statement (theory note, §7.2).
Lemma 7.2. \(G[m][\tau] = \min\{c(Y) : |Y| = m,\ \delta(Y) \le \tau\}\), and \(G\) is non-increasing in \(\tau\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Induction on \(m\): removing an element \(i\) of an optimal \(Y\) leaves an \((m-1)\)-multiset within \(\tau - d_i\), and adding \(i\) to such a multiset gives an \(m\)-multiset within \(\tau\). \(\square\)

Proposition 7.3
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.6, 7.2

Statement (theory note, §7.3).
Proposition 7.3. \(L(T) \le E(T) \le U_3(T) \le U(T)\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. \(L \le E\): \(E\) minimises over a subset. \(U_3 \le U\): more gadgets. \(E \le U_3\): each gadget with \(G\)-optimal fillers is a link tree satisfying (F1)–(F2). A single plane has odd size and degree 0; in a pair, both planes have even size and degree 1; in a chain, the ends have even size and degree 1 and the middle has odd size and degree 2. A combination is a link forest whose groups have duration at most \(T\), admissible by Lemma 2.6. \(\square\)

Proposition 7.4
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.6, 2.7, 7.3

Statement (theory note, §7.3).
Proposition 7.4. If \(q_{\max} \le 2\), that is \(p \le 2\) or \(t \le p + 1\), then \(E = U\). If \(q_{\max} \le 3\), that is \(p \le 3\) or \(t \le p + 2\), then \(E = U_3\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Take \(X\) attaining \(E(T)\) and a link forest (Lemma 2.6). Its trees have at most \(q_{\max}\) planes (Corollary 2.7), and trees with 1, 2 or 3 vertices are a vertex, an edge and a path. In each, a group consists of its link copies and a filler of the size and budget used in the gadget formula, whose cost is at least the corresponding \(G\) value (Lemma 7.2). So the forest costs at least some combination of gadgets. \(\square\)






Theorem 7.5
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.6, 2.7, 7.2

Statement (theory note, §7.4).
Theorem 7.5. \(\mathrm{For}[p][s] = E(T)\). Given \(G\), the computation takes \(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)\) time and \(O(q_{\max} s T + n q_{\max} s + p s)\) memory per level.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. A rooted structure is a rooted tree on \(q\) planes with city-labelled edges and a group \(X_u\) for each plane, such that the edges at \(u\) have distinct copies in \(X_u\) (F1), \(r_u = |X_u| - \deg(u)\) is odd and \(\delta(X_u) \le T\). In a hanging structure with label \(a\), the root’s group holds one more copy of \(a\), counted in its degree and its duration. Each group splits into its link copies and its free landings, of odd size \(r_u\).
(\(\ge\)) By induction on \(q\), every finite entry is the cost of a structure of its kind, with \(G\)-optimal free landings (Lemma 7.2): \(\mathrm{Sub}_a\) and \(\mathrm{Root}\) add a root with \(r\) free landings within the remaining budget to a multiset of child items, and \(\mathrm{Ch}_q\) adds one item to a multiset of items. The forest behind \(\mathrm{For}[p][s]\) satisfies (F1)–(F2) and has \(p\) planes, \(s\) landings and groups of duration at most \(T\), so it is admissible by Lemma 2.6, and \(\mathrm{For}[p][s] \ge E(T)\).
(\(\le\)) Take \(X\) attaining \(E(T)\) and a link forest (Lemma 2.6); its trees have at most \(q_{\max}\) planes (Corollary 2.7). Root each tree. By induction on subtree size: the child items of a plane \(u\) cost at least \(\mathrm{Ch}_{q-1}[\tau_u][j']\), where \(\tau_u\) sums \(d_b\) over the child links of \(u\) (remove one item and bound its subtree by \(\mathrm{Sub}_b\)); the free landings of \(u\) have size \(r_u\) and duration at most \(T - \tau_u\), less \(d_a\) for a hanging root, so they cost at least the matching \(G\) entry. So each subtree costs at least its \(\mathrm{Sub}\) or \(\mathrm{Root}\) entry, and the forest at least \(\mathrm{For}[p][s]\).
Complexity. \(\mathrm{Ch}\) has \(q_{\max}(T+1)(s+1)\) entries, each a minimum over \(b\), \(q'\) and \(j'\), which is \(O(n\,q_{\max} s)\). \(\mathrm{Sub}\) and \(\mathrm{Root}\) range over \(q\), \(a\), \(\tau\), \(j'\) and \(r\): \(O(n\,q_{\max} T s^2)\). \(\mathrm{For}\) costs \(O(p\,q_{\max} s^2)\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Over the levels \([T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]\) of Proposition 7.10, with \(G\) built once in \(O(n\,s\,T_{\rm hi})\), the whole front takes \(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2\, T_{\rm hi}(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo} + 1))\) time. This is pseudo-polynomial, since \(T_{\rm hi} \le d_{\max}\kappa\).



In Lean. Exactness of the link-forest DP (For ≥ E and For ≤ E); the complexity statement is not formalized.

Theorem 7.6 (σ-DP)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.2, 2.8, 7.2

Statement (theory note, §7.5).
Theorem 7.6 (σ-DP) [Claim C]. The shortest path from \((0, 0, \emptyset)\) to \((p, s, \emptyset)\) has weight \(E(T)\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Paths give admissible partitions. Take a path with options \((m_k, \eta_k)\). Let \(R_k\) be a \(G\)-optimal \((m_k - |\eta_k|)\)-multiset within \(T - \delta(\eta_k)\) and \(X_k = \eta_k + R_k\). Then \(|X| = s\), \(\delta(X_k) \le T\), and \(h_{k,i} = [i \in \eta_k]\) is a parity matrix: (h1) as \(\eta_k \le X_k\); (h2) as \(|\eta_k| \equiv m_k + 1\); (h3) because the final \(\sigma = \eta_1 \triangle \dots \triangle \eta_p\) is empty, so every city lies in an even number of the \(\eta_k\). So the path’s weight is at least \(E(T)\).
Admissible partitions give paths. Take \(X\) attaining \(E(T)\) and a parity matrix touching at most \(w\) cities (Lemma 2.8(c)). With the options \((|X_k|, \eta_k)\), every prefix \(\sigma_k = \eta_1 \triangle \dots \triangle \eta_k \subseteq Z(h)\) has at most \(w\) cities, \(|\eta_k| \le \min(|X_k| - 1, w)\), and \(R_k = X_k - \eta_k\) costs at least \(G[|X_k| - |\eta_k|][T - \delta(\eta_k)]\). So some path has weight at most \(c(X)\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Size. An arc joins sets \(\sigma, \sigma'\) with \(|\sigma|, |\sigma'|, |\sigma \triangle \sigma'| \le w\), so \(|\sigma \cup \sigma'| \le \lfloor 3w/2\rfloor\); there are at most \(N_w = \sum_{u \le \lfloor 3w/2\rfloor} \binom{n}{u} 3^u\) such pairs. The DP takes \(O(p\,s\,\hat m\,N_w)\) time per level: polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(w\), practical only for small \(w\) or few cities. The link-forest DP is the default otherwise.



In Lean. The σ-DP’s states are restricted to subsets of the non-dominated cities of size at most min(p − 1, t − p) (Lemma 2.8); every finite value is attained by groups whose witness sets form a parity witness, so no link forest is needed.

/-- **The σ-DP is exact.** At a level `T ≤ Tmax`, with `1 ≤ p ≤ t`, the bound the checker

Lemma 7.7 (Pareto sets)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1, 7.6

Statement (theory note, §7.5).
Lemma 7.7 (Pareto sets). Let \(\otimes\) be a binary operation on \(\mathbb K^2\) that is monotone in the product order. For finite \(A\) and \(B\), \(\mathrm{Min}(A \otimes B) = \mathrm{Min}(\mathrm{Min}\,A \otimes \mathrm{Min}\,B)\) and \(\mathrm{Min}(A \cup B) = \mathrm{Min}(\mathrm{Min}\,A \cup \mathrm{Min}\,B)\), where \(A \otimes B = \{a \otimes b : a \in A, b \in B\}\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Every \(a \in A\) is weakly dominated by some \(a^\star \in \mathrm{Min}\,A\) (finiteness), so \(a \otimes b\) is weakly dominated by \(a^\star \otimes b^\star \in \mathrm{Min}\,A \otimes \mathrm{Min}\,B \subseteq A \otimes B\). This subset is finite and dominating, and Lemma 1.1 applies. The same argument works for \(\cup\). \(\square\)






Proposition 7.8 (Pareto-set variant)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1, 7.6

Statement (theory note, §7.5).
Proposition 7.8 (Pareto-set variant) [PS]. In the σ-graph, replace the weight of the arc with option \((m, \eta)\) by the finite set \(\mathrm{Opt}(m, \eta) = \mathrm{Min}\{(c(\eta) + G[m - |\eta|][\tau],\ \delta(\eta) + \tau) : 0 \le \tau \le T_{\rm hi} - \delta(\eta)\}\). Combine along paths with \((c, \tau) \otimes (c', \tau') = (c + c', \max(\tau, \tau'))\), and keep at each node the \(\mathrm{Min}\) over its incoming arcs. The set obtained at \((p, s, \emptyset)\) is \(\mathrm{Min}\{(c(X), \max_k \delta(X_k)) : |X| = s,\ X_1,\dots,X_p \text{ admissible},\ \max_k \delta(X_k) \le T_{\rm hi}\}\). Under (S) and (A1), or (S) and (AΔ) (Corollary 4.12), its points \((c, \tau)\) are the front points \((c, 2\tau)\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. \(\otimes\) is monotone. \(\mathrm{Opt}(m, \eta)\) is the \(\mathrm{Min}\) of the points \((c(\eta) + c(R), \delta(\eta) + \delta(R))\) over all \(R\) of size \(m - |\eta|\) within the budget: each such point is weakly dominated by the term with \(\tau = \delta(R)\), and each term is attained or weakly dominated by a \(G\)-optimal \(R\). By Lemma 7.7 and induction over the layers, each node holds the \(\mathrm{Min}\) of the points of all paths reaching it, with arbitrary fillers. By both directions of Theorem 7.6 (with any filler in place of the \(G\)-optimal one, and the restriction \(w\) being independent of the level), these are exactly the points of admissible partitions with \(|X| = s\). The front statement is Corollary 4.8 (Corollary 4.12 under (AΔ)), and every front point has \(\tau \le T_{\rm hi}\) (Proposition 7.10). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Combining sets is no better than sweeping the levels in the worst case. It helps when durations are large and the cost range is narrow.






Proposition 7.9 (dominance)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses — ; fronts: (S), (A1) · Uses 2.2, 7.1

Statement (theory note, §7.6).
Proposition 7.9 (dominance) [DOM]. Let \(i \ne i'\) with \(d_{i'} \le d_i\) and \(c_{i'} \le c_i\). Removing city \(i\) leaves \(E(T)\) and \(L(T)\) unchanged at every \(T\). Under (S) and (A1), it leaves the front unchanged.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Removing a city can only raise \(E\) and \(L\). Conversely, in an optimal \(X\) and its groups, replace every copy of \(i\) by \(i'\): costs and durations do not increase. Nothing else is needed for \(L\). For \(E\), set \(h'_{k,i'} = (h_{k,i} + h_{k,i'}) \bmod 2\) and \(h'_{k,i} = 0\). Row sums keep their parity, column \(i'\) is the sum of two even columns, and \(h'_{k,i'} = 1\) means \(X_k\) contained \(i\) or \(i'\), so the new group contains \(i'\). The instance without \(i\) still satisfies (S) and (A1), and Proposition 7.1 expresses both fronts through \(E\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Applied repeatedly: keep one city per class of equal \((d, c)\), and drop every city dominated by another.

Proposition 7.10 (ends of the front)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S) · Uses 2.9, 3.2, 3.4, 4.1

Statement (theory note, §7.6).
Proposition 7.10 (ends of the front) [END]. Assume (S). Let \(d_{\min} = \min_i d_i\), \(c_{\min} = \min_i c_i\) and \(d_{\rm cheap} = \min\{d_i : c_i = c_{\min}\}\).

Every plan has makespan at least \(M_1 := 2d_{\min}\kappa\), and some plan has makespan \(M_1\).
Every plan costs at least \(s\,c_{\min}\). A plan of cost \(s\,c_{\min}\) has makespan at least \(M_r := 2d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\), and some plan has cost \(s\,c_{\min}\) and makespan \(M_r\). So \((s\,c_{\min}, M_r)\) is the cheapest point of \(\mathcal F\), and every point of \(\mathcal F\) has makespan at least \(M_1\).
With integer durations, \(E(T) < \infty\) iff \(T \ge T_{\rm lo} := d_{\min}\kappa\), and \(E(T) = s\,c_{\min}\) iff \(T \ge T_{\rm hi} := d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\). The same holds for \(L\).

No assumption on central flights is needed, and zero durations and ties are covered. The cost of the first point is not in closed form; under (A1) or (AΔ) it is \(E(T_{\rm lo})\) (Proposition 7.1, Corollary 4.12).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Pigeonhole: \(p\) non-empty groups of total size \(s\) include one of size at least \(\kappa\).

Lemma 3.4 gives such groups with \(\ell(Y_k) \le M\), so \(M \ge 2d_{\min}\kappa\). For the plan, put \(s\) copies of a city of duration \(d_{\min}\) into groups of sizes \(\lfloor s/p\rfloor\) and \(\lceil s/p\rceil\), all non-empty as \(s \ge p\). This is admissible by Lemma 2.9 (\(s \equiv p\), one city), and Theorem 4.1 gives a plan of makespan \(2d_{\min}\kappa\).
By Lemma 3.2 there are at least \(s\) central landings, each costing at least \(c_{\min}\). If \(C = s\,c_{\min}\), the multiset \(Y\) of Lemma 3.4 has \(c(Y) \le s\,c_{\min}\) and \(|Y| = s\), so all its cities cost \(c_{\min}\) and have \(d \ge d_{\rm cheap}\); pigeonhole gives \(M \ge 2d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\). The plan is that of (a) built on a cheapest city of duration \(d_{\rm cheap}\). A point \((C, M) \in \mathcal A\) weakly dominating \((s\,c_{\min}, M_r)\) has \(C = s\,c_{\min}\), hence \(M \ge M_r\).
The same arguments apply to \(E\) and \(L\) directly: every partition has a group of size at least \(\kappa\), and the single-city partitions are admissible. \(\square\)










Remarks in the note





Only the levels \([T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]\) need computing. On generator instances this range is about ten times shorter than \([0, d_{\max}\hat m]\).

title: Blueprint
text:
Complexity
§8 explains why no fast rule that schedules a fixed multiset of landings can be exact, and why the dynamic programs are pseudo-polynomial. None of it is formalized.

Theorem 8.1
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses \(p\) in the input · Uses 2.4

Statement (theory note, §8).
Theorem 8.1. Deciding \(M(X) \le 2T\), with \(d\), \(X\), \(p\) and \(T\) as input, is strongly NP-complete.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Membership: guess the partition and a parity matrix, and check Definition 2.2. Hardness, from 3-Partition, which is strongly NP-complete: given integers \(a_1,\dots,a_{3m}\) with \(B/4 < a_i < B/2\) and \(\sum_i a_i = mB\), can they be split into \(m\) triples of sum \(B\)? Take \(3m\) cities with \(d_i = a_i\), \(p = m\) and \(t = 2m\) (so \(s = 3m\)), \(X\) containing every city once, and \(T = B\). Each city lies in one group, so every component of \(H\) is one plane with its cities, and admissibility makes every group odd (Lemma 2.4). A 3-partition gives \(m\) triples, odd groups of duration \(B\). Conversely, groups of duration at most \(B\) summing to \(mB\) all have duration exactly \(B\); a group of one or two items has duration below \(B\) and one of four or more above \(B\), so all groups are triples. The numbers are those of the 3-Partition instance, so the reduction preserves strong NP-hardness. \(\square\)






Proposition 8.2 (fixed \(p\))
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.2, 2.4

Statement (theory note, §8).
Proposition 8.2 (fixed \(p\)). For \(p = 2\) the problem stays NP-complete, even with positive durations. For every fixed \(p\) it is solvable in time polynomial in \(n\), \(s\) and \(T\). So for fixed \(p\) it is weakly NP-complete.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Hardness, from Partition: given \(a_1,\dots,a_m\) with sum \(2B\), is there a subset of sum \(B\)? Choose an odd \(r \ge m\), add \(2r - m\) zero items, and give each of the \(2r\) items its own city of duration \(a_i + K\), with \(K = B + 1\). Let \(p = 2\), \(t = r + 1\) (so \(s = 2r\)) and \(T = B + rK\). Distinct cities make both groups odd (Lemma 2.4). If a subset of sum \(B\) exists, pad both sides with zero items to \(r\) items each, which \(r \ge m\) allows: two odd groups of duration \(B + rK\). Conversely, the two groups have duration exactly \(B + rK\) each, since they sum to \(2B + 2rK\). A group with \(r + 1\) items or more has duration at least \((r+1)K > B + rK\), so both groups have \(r\) items, and the original items of one of them sum to \(B\).
Algorithm for fixed \(p\): process the cities one at a time, with states made of the group durations (each in \([0, T]\)), the parities of \(|X_k|\) and of \(h_k\), and whether each group is non-empty: \((T+1)^p 8^p\) states. For city \(i\), choose how its \(X(i)\) copies split among the planes (\(O(s^{p-1})\) ways), and an even set of planes that received a copy, on which \(h_{k,i} = 1\) (at most \(2^{p-1}\) ways). Conditions (h1) and (h3) are local to the city, and (h2) is checked at the end. The time is \(O(n\,(T+1)^p\, 8^p\, s^{p-1}\, 2^p)\). \(\square\)






Corollary 8.3
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.5

Statement (theory note, §8).
Corollary 8.3. \(E(T)\), and under (S) and (A1) the front, are computable in pseudo-polynomial time (Theorem 7.5). So computing the front is not strongly NP-hard unless P = NP. Whether deciding \(E(T) \le C\) is NP-hard, with \(t\) in unary as in PDDL, is not established here.

text:
Certificates
§9: a certificate lists one plan per point and one lower bound per gap; four obligations imply that the list is the front. The Lean checker is the executable form of Theorem 9.1, and its soundness theorems are the strongest machine-checked results of the project.

Theorem 9.1 (end to end)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1

Statement (theory note, §9).
Theorem 9.1 (end to end) [X3]. If obligations 1–4 hold, then \(\mathcal F = \{(C_i, M_i) : 1 \le i \le r\}\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Let \((C, M) \in \mathcal A\). By 2, \(M \ge M_1\). Let \(i\) be the largest index with \(M_i \le M\). If \(i < r\), then \(M < M_{i+1}\) and \(C \ge C_i\) by 3; if \(i = r\), then \(C \ge C_r\) by 4. Either way \((C_i, M_i) \preceq (C, M)\). So the list, contained in \(\mathcal A\) by 1, is a finite dominating subset, and by Lemma 1.1, \(\mathcal F\) is its \(\mathrm{Min}\). That is the whole list, which is strictly monotone in both coordinates. \(\square\)



In Lean. Cert.check_sound_rat extends it to plans with rational times and Cert.check_sound_anywhere to planes ending anywhere.

central flight durations that satisfies (A1), or for every table if all gaps are `relaxed`. -/

Lemma 9.2 (potentials)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.6

Statement (theory note, §9).
Lemma 9.2 (potentials) [X2]. In a finite graph with arc weights in \(\mathbb K\), let \(V\) map nodes to \(\mathbb K \cup \{\infty\}\) with \(V(\text{target}) \le 0\) and \(V(u) \le \mathrm{wt}(u,v) + V(v)\) on every arc. Then \(V(\text{source})\) is at most the weight of every path from the source to the target.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Along a path \(u_0, \dots, u_m\) ending at the target, \(V(u_m) \le 0\), and by backward induction \(V(u_j) \le \sum_{j' \ge j} \mathrm{wt}(u_{j'}, u_{j'+1})\). \(\square\)






Lemma 9.3 (default potentials)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.6

Statement (theory note, §9).
Lemma 9.3 (default potentials). At level \(T\), let \(G^a[m] = c_a + G[m-1][T - d_a]\), the cheapest \(m\)-group containing \(a\). Let \(L_{\rm rest}(p, s) = 0\), \(L_{\rm rest}(p, j) = \infty\) for \(j \ne s\), and \(L_{\rm rest}(k, j) = \min_m \big(G[m][T] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m)\big)\). Let \(L^a(p, j) = \infty\) and \(L^a(k, j) = \min_m \min\big(G^a[m] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m),\ G[m][T] + L^a(k+1, j+m)\big)\). Define \(V_0(k, j, \emptyset) = L_{\rm rest}(k, j)\) and \(V_0(k, j, \sigma) = \max_{a\in\sigma} L^a(k, j)\) for \(\sigma \ne \emptyset\). Then \(V_0(\text{target}) = 0\) and \(V_0(u) \le \mathrm{wt}(u, v) + V_0(v)\) on every arc of the σ-graph.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. By induction from \(k = p\), \(L^a \ge L_{\rm rest}\), since \(G^a[m] \ge G[m][T]\); so \(V_0(v) \ge L_{\rm rest}(v)\) at every node \(v\). An arc leaving \((k, j, \sigma)\) with option \((m, \eta)\) has weight at least \(G[m][T]\), and at least \(G^a[m]\) when \(a \in \eta\), because \(\eta\) with its filler is an \(m\)-group of duration at most \(T\). If \(\sigma = \emptyset\): \(V_0(u) = L_{\rm rest}(k, j) \le G[m][T] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m) \le \mathrm{wt} + V_0(v)\). If \(\sigma \ne \emptyset\) and \(a \in \sigma\): when \(a \in \eta\), \(L^a(k, j) \le G^a[m] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m) \le \mathrm{wt} + V_0(v)\); when \(a \notin \eta\), \(a \in \sigma \triangle \eta\), so \(V_0(v) \ge L^a(k+1, j+m)\) and \(L^a(k, j) \le G[m][T] + L^a(k+1, j+m) \le \mathrm{wt} + V_0(v)\). Take the maximum over \(a\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Sparse potential. The certificate lists some nodes \(u\) with values \(V(u)\). The checker sets \(V'(u) = \max(V(u), V_0(u))\) on listed nodes and \(V' = V_0\) elsewhere. It checks \(V'(\text{target}) \le 0\), \(V'(u) \le \mathrm{wt}(u, v) + V'(v)\) on every arc leaving a listed node, and \(V'(\text{source}) \ge C_i\). Arcs leaving other nodes satisfy the inequality by Lemma 9.3, as \(V' \ge V_0\). By Lemma 9.2 and Theorem 7.6, \(E(T^\star_i) \ge C_i\). The listed nodes are those that survive the solver’s pruning.

title: Blueprint
text:
The linear family (default generator)
The generator’s default instances have costs affine in durations. §10 gives their front in closed form, valid whatever the central flights.

Theorem 10.1
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S) · Uses 1.1, 2.9, 3.4, 4.1, 7.2, 7.10

Statement (theory note, §10).
Theorem 10.1. Assume (S), \(d_i = i\) and \(c_i = \alpha - \beta i\) for \(i = 1,\dots,n\), with \(\beta \ge 0\) and \(\alpha \ge \beta n\). Let \(q_0 = \lfloor s/p\rfloor\) and \(\rho = s - pq_0\). For every integer \(T \ge \kappa\), \[L(T) = E(T) = \alpha s - \beta\,\Phi(T), \qquad \Phi(T) = (p - \rho)\min(T,\ nq_0) + \rho\min(T,\ n(q_0+1)),\] and \(L(T) = E(T) = \infty\) for \(T < \kappa\). Consequently, whatever the central flights, the front is \[\mathcal F = \{(\alpha s - \beta\,\Phi(T),\ 2T) : \kappa \le T \le n\kappa\} \text{ if } \beta > 0, \qquad
\mathcal F = \{(\alpha s,\ 2\kappa)\} \text{ if } \beta = 0,\] with makespans in units of \(r_0\). For \(\beta > 0\) it has \((n-1)\kappa + 1\) points.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. (1) Affine cost. \(c(Y) = \alpha |Y| - \beta\,\delta(Y)\). An \(m\)-multiset of cities can have any duration in \([m, nm]\): start from \(m\) copies of city 1 and raise one landing by one at a time. So by Lemma 7.2, \(G[m][T] = \alpha m - \beta\min(T, nm)\) for \(1 \le m \le T\), and \(G[m][T] = \infty\) for \(m > T\).

Convexity. \(m \mapsto \min(T, nm)\) is concave, so \(m \mapsto G[m][T]\) is convex on \([1, T]\). A sum \(\sum_k G[m_k][T]\) with \(\sum_k m_k = s\) is then minimised by the balanced profile, with \(p - \rho\) groups of size \(q_0\) and \(\rho\) of size \(q_0 + 1\): if \(m_u \ge m_v + 2\), moving one landing from \(u\) to \(v\) does not increase the sum. The profile is feasible iff \(\kappa \le T\); otherwise \(L = E = \infty\) by Proposition 7.10(c). So \(L(T) = \sum_k G[m_k][T] = \alpha s - \beta\,\Phi(T)\).
Admissibility. Give every group of size \(m\) the same \(G\)-optimal multiset. Exactly one of \(q_0\) and \(q_0 + 1\) is even, so all even groups are equal, and Lemma 2.9 makes the partition admissible. It costs \(L(T)\), so \(E(T) \le L(T) \le E(T)\).
Front. By Lemma 3.4 a plan with makespan \(M\) costs at least \(L(\lfloor M/2\rfloor) = E(\lfloor M/2\rfloor)\), and Theorem 4.1 achieves \((E(T), 2T)\); both need only (S). \(E\) is constant from \(n\kappa\) on, so the finite set \(\{(E(T), 2T) : \kappa \le T \le n\kappa\} \subseteq \mathcal A\) dominates \(\mathcal A\), and Lemma 1.1 gives \(\mathcal F\). For \(\kappa < T \le n\kappa\), \(\Phi(T) - \Phi(T-1)\) is \(p\) when \(T \le nq_0\) and \(\rho\) when \(nq_0 < T \le n(q_0+1)\); the second range meets \([\kappa, n\kappa]\) only if \(\rho \ge 1\). So for \(\beta > 0\) every such \(T\) is a breakpoint. \(\square\)










Remarks in the note





The count \((n-1)\kappa + 1\) matches the front sizes measured with the prototype on generator instances: 1,090 points for \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\); 540 for \(n = 50\) with the same \(t\) and \(p\); 399 for \(n = 200\), \(t = 3\), \(p = 2\). Neither link structures nor smoothing the free landings of a group are needed for this family.
What the theorem does not cover:

Offset progressions. For \(d_i = a + bi\) with \(a > 0\), \(G[\cdot][T]\) need not be convex and \(L < E\) occurs. With \(d = (5, 7, 9, 11)\), \(c_i = 24 - 2d_i\), \(t = 7\) and \(p = 4\), \(L(20) = 80 < E(20) = 84\) (by enumeration; 4 of 5,904 levels on 150 random offset instances). Contiguity from the step is essential: the two-city instance \(d = (6, 10)\) of §5 is affine as well.
The other generator families (logarithm, square root, \(2^i\), \((5/2)i\)) have no closed form; the general algorithm applies.







Conjecture 10.2
Lean informal · Note open problem · Hypotheses (S), (A1)

Statement (theory note, §10).
Conjecture 10.2. The papers’ per-PPP greedy reaches the front of Theorem 10.1. Evidence: equal fronts on 115 instances with \(n \le 6\), \(p \le 5\) and \(s \le 11\). Correctness does not depend on it, since the front is in closed form.

title: Algorithm
text:
This page explains how zeno computes the Pareto front of a MultiZenoTravel instance, and why the front it prints is exact. It can be read on its own: every symbol is defined here, and every claim cites the result that proves it. A citation links to the entry of the blueprint that states and proves the result; the badge after it says how much of it Lean checks (machine-checked, parts in Lean, Lean definition, or informal when the proof is on paper only). The proofs themselves are in the theory note. For context, see the problem page, which introduces the same example, and the paper section.
The page follows one instance from start to finish. Every number quoted for it, and every value in the figures, is recomputed from the definitions by site/gen_algorithm.py and checked against zeno (how).

title: Algorithm
text:
The setting
Instances and plans. An instance has two hubs, \(C_I\), where every plane and passenger starts, and \(C_G\), where they must all end, and \(n\) central cities \(1, \dots, n\) §1.1 Lean definition. A flight between \(C_I\) and city \(i\) lasts \(d_i\), a flight between city \(i\) and \(C_G\) lasts \(\bar d_i\), and no flight joins the two hubs. Central cities may also be joined by flights of their own. Landing in city \(i\) costs \(c_i \ge 0\); landing in a hub is free. There are \(p\) planes and \(t \ge p\) passengers, and a plane carries at most one passenger at a time. A plan gives every plane a timed route and every passenger a journey. Its cost is the sum of its landing costs, and its makespan is the time at which the last plane reaches \(C_G\) §1.2 Lean definition.
The front. A point \((C, M)\) weakly dominates \((C', M')\) if \(C \le C'\) and \(M \le M'\). The Pareto front \(\mathcal F\) is the set of (cost, makespan) points of feasible plans that no other such point weakly dominates §1.5 Lean definition. zeno prints it as cost makespan lines.
Assumptions §1.4 Lean definition. Most of this page assumes

(S), symmetry: \(d_i = \bar d_i\) for every city, so a flight between city \(i\) and either hub lasts \(d_i\);
and either (A1): every central flight between \(i\) and \(j\) lasts at least \(d_i + d_j\), so it is never faster than going through a hub; or (AΔ): the flight durations satisfy the triangle inequality.

Instances with \(d \ne \bar d\) have their own pipeline, described at the end.

Notation




Symbol
Meaning




\(s = 2t - p\)
the least number of landings in central cities of a feasible plan (step 1)


\(\kappa = \lceil s/p \rceil\)
the size of the largest group when \(s\) landings are spread over \(p\) planes as evenly as possible


\(X\)
a multiset of central cities: the landings. \(X(i)\) is the multiplicity of city \(i\), \(\lvert X \rvert\) the size


\(c(X)\), \(\delta(X)\)
\(\sum_{i \in X} c_i\) and \(\sum_{i \in X} d_i\), counted with multiplicity


\(\ell(X) = 2\delta(X)\)
the load: the flight time of a plane that serves each landing of \(X\) by its own round trip from a hub


\(X_1, \dots, X_p\)
a partition of \(X\): one group per plane, with \(X_1 + \dots + X_p = X\)


even plane
a plane whose group has an even number of landings


\(g\)
the gcd of the durations; durations are divided by it


\(T\)
a level: an integer bound on every \(\delta(X_k)\), hence on every load, \(2gT\) in the original units


\(E(T)\)
the least cost of an admissible partition within level \(T\) (step 4)


\(L(T)\), \(U(T)\), \(U_3(T)\)
a lower bound and two upper bounds on \(E(T)\) (step 7)


\(G[m][\tau]\)
the least cost of \(m\) landings whose durations sum to at most \(\tau\) (step 6)


\(\hat m = s - p + 1\)
the largest group that can occur, every group being non-empty


\(q_{\max} = \min(p,\ t - p + 1)\)
the most planes a useful link tree has (step 3)


\(w = \min(p - 1,\ t - p)\)
the most cities a parity matrix needs to touch (step 9)


\(T_{\rm lo}\), \(T_{\rm hi}\)
the first level with a plan, and the first level at the cheapest cost (step 4)




\(s\), \(\kappa\), \(c\), \(\delta\) and \(\ell\) are the notation of the theory note Notation informal.


The worked example

title: Algorithm
text:
What is computed

Step 1. From plans to landing multisets
Idea. A plan is a timed object, with routes, journeys and waiting, but its point on the front depends on two numbers only. The first step replaces plans by a finite, untimed object: the multiset of central cities the planes land in, split among the planes. Under (S), a landing in city \(i\) served by its own round trip from a hub (\(C_I \to i \to C_G\), \(C_G \to i \to C_I\), \(C_I \to i \to C_I\) or \(C_G \to i \to C_G\)) takes exactly \(2d_i\) Lemma 3.3 informal, parts in Lean. If every landing is flown this way, plane \(k\) flies for \(\ell(X_k) = 2\delta(X_k)\), and the question becomes which landings to make and how to split them.
Results.

Counting. Every feasible plan lands at least \(s = 2t - p\) times in central cities Lemma 3.2 machine-checked. Every passenger needs a flight out of \(C_I\) and a flight into \(C_G\). Cut each route at its visits to the hubs: each piece, a segment, lands in a central city, and a plane leaves \(C_I\) one time more than it returns there. Counting the arrivals in the hubs gives at least \((t - p) + t\) segments.
Achievability. For every multiset \(X\) with \(|X| = s\) and every admissible partition \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) of it (step 2), there is a feasible plan whose central landings are exactly \(X\), hence of cost \(c(X)\), that uses no central flight, in which plane \(k\) flies for \(\ell(X_k)\), and whose makespan is \(\max_k \ell(X_k)\) Theorem 4.1 machine-checked. Step 11 shows the construction.
Converse. Under (S) and (A1), every feasible plan with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\) is matched by an admissible partition of some \(X\) with \(|X| = s\), \(c(X) \le C\) and \(\ell(X_k) \le M\) for every plane Theorem 4.7 machine-checked. The same holds under (S) and (AΔ) Theorem 4.10 machine-checked.
Together. Let \(M(X)\) be the least \(\max_k \ell(X_k)\) over the admissible partitions of \(X\), or \(\infty\) if there is none. Under (S) and (A1), \[\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X, \qquad \mathcal X = \{(c(X), M(X)) : |X| = s,\ M(X) < \infty\},\] where \(\mathrm{Min}\) keeps the points that no other point of the set weakly dominates, and every front point is attained by a plan with exactly \(s\) central landings Corollary 4.8 machine-checked. The same holds under (S) and (AΔ) Corollary 4.12 informal, parts in Lean.

Some condition on the central flights is needed: with fast central flights that satisfy neither (A1) nor (AΔ), a plan can beat every point of \(\mathcal X\) Example 4.13 informal.
In the example. \(s = 4\). The multiset \(\{3, 3, 3, 3\}\) split as \(\{3, 3\} \mid \{3, 3\}\) costs \(4\), each plane has \(\delta = 10\), and the makespan is \(20\): the point \((4, 20)\). The multiset \(\{1, 1, 1, 1\}\) split as \(\{1, 1\} \mid \{1, 1\}\) costs \(36\) with makespan \(8\): the point \((36, 8)\). The four other points come from multisets in between.
In the code. solveFront (src/zeno/solve.cpp) takes symmetric instances and sends the others to solveBracket (below). checkFlights (include/zeno/flights.hpp) decides (A1), (AΔ) and (A1-NS) in exact integer arithmetic. With a central flight table that satisfies neither (A1) nor (AΔ), zeno still prints achieved points but warns that the front may not be exact.


Step 2. Admissible partitions
Idea. Not every split of \(X\) among the planes can be flown with loads \(\ell(X_k)\). In the plans of step 1, every landing is a round trip from a hub of one of four kinds: a crossing \(C_I \to i \to C_G\) carrying a passenger, or its empty return \(C_G \to i \to C_I\); a drop-off \(C_I \to i \to C_I\), which leaves a passenger in city \(i\); and a pick-up \(C_G \to i \to C_G\), which collects one there. A plane starts in \(C_I\) and ends in \(C_G\), so it flies an odd number of crossings, counting both directions Lemma 2.1 informal, parts in Lean. Every drop-off in city \(i\) is matched by a pick-up in city \(i\) Definition 4.2 Lean definition. So a plane with an even number of landings must take part in a hand-off, and hand-offs pair up city by city. The parity matrix records exactly this: \(h_{k,i}\) is the parity of the number of drop-offs and pick-ups of plane \(k\) in city \(i\) Lemma 4.5 machine-checked.
Definition Definition 2.2 Lean definition. A parity matrix for a partition \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) is a 0/1 matrix \(h\) with one row per plane and one column per city such that

(h1) \(h_{k,i} = 1\) only if plane \(k\) lands in city \(i\), that is \(X_k(i) \ge 1\);
(h2) row \(k\) has \(|X_k| + 1\) ones modulo 2: an odd number for an even plane, an even number for an odd plane;
(h3) every column has an even number of ones.

The partition is admissible if it has a parity matrix.
Equivalent forms.

Counting with multiplicities changes nothing: integer entries \(0 \le \tilde h_{k,i} \le X_k(i)\) with the same two parity conditions exist iff a parity matrix does Lemma 2.3 informal. This is the form a link forest produces (step 3).
Component form. Let \(H\) be the bipartite graph on planes and cities with an edge between plane \(k\) and city \(i\) whenever \(X_k(i) \ge 1\). The partition is admissible iff every connected component of \(H\) contains an even number of even planes Lemma 2.4 informal. This is the quickest test by hand.
Every row has at most \(|X_k| - 1\) ones Lemma 2.5 machine-checked: each plane keeps at least one landing outside the hand-offs, and an admissible partition has no empty group.
A sufficient condition: if the groups are non-empty, their sizes add up to \(p\) modulo 2, and some city belongs to every even group, the partition is admissible Lemma 2.9 informal.

In the example (Figure 1). The multiset \(\{2, 2, 3, 3\}\) split as \(\{2, 3\} \mid \{2, 3\}\): both planes are even, so each row needs an odd number of ones, and marking city 2 in both rows gives the column sums \(0, 2, 0\). The split is admissible. It costs \(14\), both planes have \(\delta = 8\), and the makespan is \(16\): the front point \((14, 16)\). The split \(\{1, 3\} \mid \{2, 2\}\) of \(\{1, 2, 2, 3\}\) is not: plane 2 is even and lands only in city 2, so its row must mark city 2; plane 1 is even and lands in cities 1 and 3, so its row marks exactly one of them; column 2 then holds a single one. The graph \(H\) shows it at a glance: plane 2 and city 2 form a component with one even plane. This split is not a candidate in Corollary 4.8, whatever its cost (22) and loads.








Figure 1: An admissible and a non-admissible split for the worked example, with the parity matrix of Definition 2.2 and the graph \(H\) of Lemma 2.4. Cities keep their colours in every diagram of this page. Click to open the full-size drawing.



In the code. zeno never enumerates parity matrices. Its dynamic programs only build partitions that carry a link forest (step 3), which are admissible by construction. Admissibility is still decidable by enumerating \(h\) on the supports of the groups Definition 2.2 Lean definition; gen_algorithm.py does so over every partition of the example to check the figures of this page.


Step 3. Link forests
Idea. A parity matrix says which landings take part in hand-offs, not who hands off to whom. A link forest says it. Draw an edge between planes \(u\) and \(v\), labelled with city \(i\), for each passenger that one of them drops off in city \(i\) and the other picks up there. Each edge uses one landing in \(i\) of both planes. The other landings of a plane are its free landings, flown as crossings.
Definition Definition (link forest) Lean definition. A link forest for \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) is a forest \(\Lambda\) on the planes whose edges carry city labels, such that

(F1) for every plane \(u\) and city \(i\), at most \(X_u(i)\) edges at \(u\) are labelled \(i\);
(F2) \(r_u = |X_u| - \deg_\Lambda(u)\), the number of free landings of \(u\), is odd.

Results.

A partition is admissible iff it has a link forest, and then it has one with at most one edge of each label at each plane Lemma 2.6 machine-checked. In one direction, counting the edges of each label at each plane gives the integer form of Lemma 2.3. In the other, the forest is built from a parity matrix whose ones lie on a spanning forest of \(H\).
With \(|X| = s\), a link forest has at most \(t - p\) edges, so each of its trees has at most \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t - p + 1)\) planes Corollary 2.7 informal. Every plane keeps at least one free landing, so the degrees add up to at most \(s - p = 2(t - p)\).

Forests matter for two reasons. They can be built tree by tree, from the leaves up, by dynamic programming (step 8). And in the plan built from a forest, each plane picks up at most once, from its parent, which is what keeps waiting harmless (step 11).
In the example (Figure 2). \(t - p = 1\), so there is at most one link, and \(q_{\max} = 2\): every tree is a single plane or a pair. For the point \((14, 16)\), one edge labelled city 2 joins plane 1 to plane 2. Each plane keeps one free landing, in city 3: \(r_u = 2 - 1 = 1\), which is odd. In the plan, plane 1 drops passenger 1 in city 2 and plane 2 collects it.








Figure 2: The link forest of the point \((14, 16)\) and the plan built from it. Left: the tree; its edge uses one landing in city 2 of each plane (F1), and each plane keeps one free landing (F2). Right: the plan of Theorem 4.1 on a time axis, as zeno --plans prints it (step 11).



In the code. LinkForest and ForestPlane (include/zeno/forest.hpp) store, for each plane, its filler (the odd number of free landings), its parent, and the label of the edge to it. The group of a plane is its filler, plus its parent’s label, plus one landing per child edge.


Step 4. The level function \(E(T)\) and its breakpoints
Idea. Corollary 4.8 still asks for the Pareto set of a search with two objectives. Turn it into a family of searches with one: fix a budget \(T\) for every plane, and ask for the cheapest admissible way to fit in it. As the budget grows, the least cost can only drop, and each drop is a front point.
Definition. Durations are integers, divided by their gcd \(g\) (rational durations are scaled to integers first). For an integer level \(T \ge 0\), \[E(T) = \min\{c(X) : |X| = s,\ X_1, \dots, X_p \text{ admissible},\ \delta(X_k) \le T \text{ for every } k\},\] with \(\min \emptyset = \infty\). A larger \(T\) allows more partitions, so \(E\) is non-increasing.
Results.

Under (S) and (A1), the front is the set of breakpoints of \(E\) Proposition 7.1 machine-checked: \[\mathcal F = \{(E(T),\ 2gT) : E(T) < E(T - 1)\}, \qquad E(-1) = \infty.\] Under (S) and (AΔ) as well Corollary 4.12 informal, parts in Lean.
Only a bounded range of levels matters Proposition 7.10 informal, parts in Lean. Let \(d_{\min}\) be the smallest duration, \(c_{\min}\) the smallest cost, and \(d_{\rm cheap}\) the smallest duration among the cities of cost \(c_{\min}\). Then \(E(T) < \infty\) iff \(T \ge T_{\rm lo} = d_{\min}\kappa\), and \(E(T) = s\,c_{\min}\) iff \(T \ge T_{\rm hi} = d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\). In the original units, every plan has makespan at least \(2d_{\min}\kappa\), which some plan attains, and the cheapest point of the front is \((s\,c_{\min},\ 2d_{\rm cheap}\kappa)\). Both hold under (S), whatever the central flights. The cost of the fastest point has no closed form: it is \(E(T_{\rm lo})\).

In the example (Figure 3). \(T_{\rm lo} = 2 \cdot 2 = 4\) and \(T_{\rm hi} = 5 \cdot 2 = 10\): seven levels. On \(T = 4, \dots, 10\), \(E\) takes the values 36, 30, 24, 20, 14, 14 and 4. It drops at every level but \(T = 9\), where the cheapest groups within the budget are still \(\{2, 3\} \mid \{2, 3\}\): no plan of makespan 18 is cheaper than the plan of makespan 16. Six breakpoints, six front points.




  
    E(T)
    breakpoint: front point (E(T), 2gT)
    no drop: no new point
  
  



Figure 3: \(E(T)\) for the worked example. Each filled dot is a breakpoint, labelled with its front point; the hollow dot at \(T = 9\) is a level where \(E\) does not drop. Below \(T_{\rm lo}\) no partition fits; from \(T_{\rm hi}\) on, \(E\) is the cheapest cost \(s\,c_{\min} = 4\). title: Algorithm
text:
How zeno computes it
Figure 4 is the map of the symmetric solver, solveFront. The left column runs once per instance. The panel on the right settles one level: it tries the cheap bounds first, and the exact program only when they disagree.








Figure 4: The orchestration of solveFront (src/zeno/solve.cpp), following §7.7 of the theory note. The branch that settles a level is what zeno --stats counts: bracket, pairs, chains, exact, and monotone for the levels that bisection settles (step 8).




Step 5. Reduce the instance
Idea. A city that is no faster and no cheaper than another is never needed: replacing each of its landings by a landing in the other city keeps the partition admissible (merge the two columns of the parity matrix) and raises neither the cost nor a load.
Result Proposition 7.9 informal, parts in Lean. If \(d_{i'} \le d_i\) and \(c_{i'} \le c_i\) for two cities \(i \ne i'\), removing city \(i\) leaves \(E(T)\) and \(L(T)\) unchanged at every level, and under (S) and (A1) it leaves the front unchanged. Applied repeatedly, keeping one city per class of equal \((d, c)\), the cities that remain form a staircase: durations strictly increasing, costs strictly decreasing.
In the example. \(2 < 3 < 5\) and \(9 > 6 > 1\): the cities already form a staircase, and \(g = 1\). Nothing changes.
In the code. reduce (src/zeno/reduce.cpp) merges equal cities, drops dominated ones, divides the durations by \(g\), and computes the level range. zeno --stats prints the result, here levels 4..10 (x1, 7 levels), cities 3, max tree 2.


Step 6. The one-plane table
Idea. Every bound and every exact method below keeps asking one question: what is the cheapest way for a single plane to make \(m\) landings within a budget \(\tau\)? It is a knapsack with exactly \(m\) items, in which each city can be used any number of times, and one table answers it for all \(m\) and \(\tau\) at once.
Result Lemma 7.2 machine-checked. Let \(G[0][\tau] = 0\) for \(\tau \ge 0\), \(G[m][\tau] = \infty\) for \(\tau < 0\), and \[G[m][\tau] = \min_{i:\ d_i \le \tau} \big(c_i + G[m-1][\tau - d_i]\big).\] Then \(G[m][\tau]\) is the least cost of a multiset of \(m\) cities whose durations sum to at most \(\tau\), and it is non-increasing in \(\tau\).
In the example (Figure 5). \(m\) runs up to \(\hat m = 3\) and \(\tau\) up to \(T_{\rm hi} = 10\). For instance \(G[2][8] = 7\): one landing in city 2 and one in city 3, of durations \(3 + 5 = 8\). Replay the fill to see each cell computed from a cell of the row above.

In the code. OnePlaneTable (include/zeno/one_plane.hpp) has two layouts. The dense one stores every cell and takes \(O(n\,\hat m\,T_{\rm hi})\) time to build; zeno uses it up to \(2^{22}\) cells. Beyond, it stores for each \(m\) only the Pareto points (load, cost) where \(G[m][\cdot]\) drops, the dotted cells of the figure, so that memory does not depend on the magnitude of the durations; a lookup is then a binary search.


Step 7. The bracket
Idea. Before solving a level exactly, sandwich \(E(T)\) between a cheap lower bound and cheap upper bounds, \(L \le E \le U_3 \le U\). All three are knapsacks that combine small gadgets (a few planes with their groups) filled with \(G\)-optimal landings. Where the lower bound meets an upper bound, the level is settled.
The bounds. A knapsack over planes and landings combines gadgets, with \(\mathrm{For}[0][0] = 0\) and \[\mathrm{For}[P][J] = \min\big(\mathrm{For}[P - q][J - j] + \text{cost}\big)\] over the gadgets of \(q\) planes, \(j\) landings and that cost; the bound is \(\mathrm{For}[p][s]\).

\(L(T)\): one plane with any number \(m \in [1, \hat m]\) of landings, at cost \(G[m][T]\). Admissibility is ignored, so this is a relaxation. It bounds more than \(E\): under (S) alone, whatever the central flights, every feasible plan of makespan \(M\) costs at least \(L(\lfloor M/2g \rfloor)\) Lemma 3.4 machine-checked.
\(U(T)\): one plane with an odd number \(m\) of landings, at cost \(G[m][T]\); or a pair: two planes of even sizes \(a\) and \(b\) linked at a city \(i\), at cost \[2c_i + G[a-1][T - d_i] + G[b-1][T - d_i].\]
\(U_3(T)\): the gadgets of \(U\), and a chain: three planes of sizes \(a\) (even), \(b\) (odd, at least

and \(b'\) (even), the first two linked at \(i\) and the last two at \(j\), at cost \[2c_i + 2c_j + G[a-1][T-d_i] + G[b-2][T-d_i-d_j] + G[b'-1][T-d_j].\]


Results.

\(L(T) \le E(T) \le U_3(T) \le U(T)\) Proposition 7.3 informal, parts in Lean. Each gadget of \(U\) and \(U_3\) is a link tree with one, two or three planes that satisfies (F1) and (F2), so its groups are admissible by Lemma 2.6.
The upper bounds are exact when useful trees are small: \(E = U\) if \(q_{\max} \le 2\), that is \(p \le 2\) or \(t \le p + 1\), and \(E = U_3\) if \(q_{\max} \le 3\) Proposition 7.4 informal. By Corollary 2.7 the trees of an optimal forest then have at most two or three planes, and such trees are a vertex, an edge or a path: exactly the gadgets.

Moreover \(L = U\) at every level: all seven levels are closed by the bracket, and zeno --stats reports settled: bracket 7, pairs 0, chains 0, monotone 0, exact 0. This is no accident of the numbers. With two planes and four landings, the relaxation either splits them \(1 + 3\), two odd planes, which is always admissible since no component of \(H\) then holds an even plane Lemma 2.4 informal; or \(2 + 2\), where the cheapest choice is the same \(G\)-optimal pair twice: the two groups share a city, which makes them admissible Lemma 2.9 informal.

At \(T = 12\), the cheapest relaxed split is \(\{2, 3\} \mid \{1, 1, 1, 1\}\), of cost 46: two even planes that share no city, so each component of \(H\) holds one even plane, and the split is not admissible (Lemma 2.4). The cheapest admissible split, \(\{1, 1, 2\} \mid \{1, 1, 2\}\), costs \(50 = U(12)\). Levels 12 and 14 stay open, and zeno --stats reports settled: bracket 11, pairs 2: both are settled by \(U\), exact since \(q_{\max} = 2\).

In the code. relaxedCost computes \(L\), and forestCost(r, G, T, q) runs the link-forest program of step 8 restricted to trees of at most \(q\) planes (src/zeno/forest.cpp): with \(q = 2\) and \(q = 3\) it ranges over the same trees as the gadgets of \(U\) and \(U_3\). In sweep mode, bracket() computes \(L\) and \(U\) on every level in parallel, and chains() adds \(U_3\) on the levels left open when \(q_{\max} \ge 3\). Every value is checked to lie inside its bracket.


Step 8. The link-forest DP
Idea. When \(q_{\max} \ge 4\) and \(L < U_3\) at a level, zeno computes \(E(T)\) exactly. By Lemma 2.6 and Corollary 2.7, \(E(T)\) is the least cost of \(p\) groups with \(s\) landings in all, each within \(T\), that carry a link forest whose trees have at most \(q_{\max}\) planes. Root every tree at a plane. The group of a plane is then its free landings (an odd number \(r\)), plus one landing per child edge, plus one for the edge to its parent. The program builds such trees from the leaves up, attaching to each plane the subtrees that hang from it.
Tables, for one level \(T\):

\(\mathrm{Ch}_q[\tau][j]\): the least cost of a multiset of child items. An item is a link label \(b\), with one landing in \(b\) in the parent’s group, and the subtree hanging from that link. The labels’ durations sum to \(\tau\), the subtrees have \(q\) planes in all, and \(j\) counts the landings;
\(\mathrm{Sub}_a[q][j]\): the least cost of a subtree with \(q\) planes and \(j\) landings whose root holds one landing in \(a\) for the link to its parent;
\(\mathrm{Root}[q][j]\): the least cost of a tree with \(q\) planes and \(j\) landings;
\(\mathrm{For}[P][J]\): the least cost of a forest on \(P\) planes with \(J\) landings.

For \(q = 1, \dots, q_{\max}\) in order, with \(r\) odd and \(\tau \in [0, T]\), \[\mathrm{Sub}_a[q][j] = \min_{\tau,\ j' + 1 + r = j} \big(c_a + \mathrm{Ch}_{q-1}[\tau][j'] + G[r][T - d_a - \tau]\big),\] \[\mathrm{Root}[q][j] = \min_{\tau,\ j' + r = j} \big(\mathrm{Ch}_{q-1}[\tau][j'] + G[r][T - \tau]\big),\] \[\mathrm{Ch}_q[\tau][j] = \min_{b,\ 1 \le q' \le q,\ j'} \big(\mathrm{Ch}_{q-q'}[\tau - d_b][j - 1 - j'] + c_b + \mathrm{Sub}_b[q'][j']\big),\] with \(\mathrm{Ch}_0[0][0] = 0\), and finally, with \(\mathrm{For}[0][0] = 0\), \[\mathrm{For}[P][J] = \min_{q \le \min(P, q_{\max}),\ j} \big(\mathrm{For}[P - q][J - j] + \mathrm{Root}[q][j]\big).\]
Result Theorem 7.5 machine-checked. \(\mathrm{For}[p][s] = E(T)\). Given \(G\), the program takes \(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)\) time per level.
In the example, at \(T = 8\). With \(q_{\max} = 2\), a tree is a single plane or a pair.

A single plane with one or three landings: \(\mathrm{Root}[1][1] = G[1][8] = 1\) and \(\mathrm{Root}[1][3] = G[3][8] = 21\).
A leaf hanging from a link at city 2, with one free landing within \(8 - d_2 = 5\): \(\mathrm{Sub}_2[1][2] = c_2 + G[1][5] = 7\).
The parent’s side of that link: \(\mathrm{Ch}_1[3][3] = c_2 + \mathrm{Sub}_2[1][2] = 13\).
The pair, rooted at a plane with one free landing within \(8 - 3 = 5\): \[\mathrm{Root}[2][4] = \mathrm{Ch}_1[3][3] + G[1][5] = 13 + 1 = 14.\]
The forest, a pair or two single planes: \[\mathrm{For}[2][4] = \min\big(\mathrm{Root}[2][4],\ \mathrm{Root}[1][1] + \mathrm{Root}[1][3]\big) = \min(14, 22) = 14 = E(8).\]

The pair is the tree of Figure 2. A link at city 3 with free landings in city 2 gives the same groups and the same cost.
In the code. ForestProgram (include/zeno/forest.hpp, src/zeno/forest.cpp). Instead of dense arrays over \(\tau\), it keeps the child items of a plane as Pareto staircases over \((\tau, \text{cost})\), so its work depends on the sizes of these staircases, not on the magnitude of \(T\). reconstruct() returns an optimal LinkForest, which step 11 turns into a plan. In sweep mode the exact program runs only where the bracket and monotonicity leave a level open. Since \(E\) is non-increasing, a level between two settled levels \(a < b\) has \(E(b) \le E \le E(a)\), which tightens its bracket, and equal values at both ends settle every level between them (monotone in --stats). bisect() evaluates up to threads evenly spaced open levels exactly, and recurses on the pieces.


Step 9. The σ-DP
Idea. A second exact method works with parity matrices directly. Process the planes one at a time, choosing for each its number of landings and its row of the parity matrix, and remember only the set \(\sigma\) of cities whose column has an odd number of ones so far. At the end, \(\sigma\) must be empty, which is (h3). Some parity matrix touches few cities, so \(\sigma\) stays small.
Results.

For an admissible partition with \(|X| = s\), some parity matrix touches at most \(w = \min(p - 1, t - p)\) cities, and its rows have at most \(\min(|X_k| - 1, w)\) ones Lemma 2.8 machine-checked.
The σ-graph at level \(T\) has nodes \((k, j, \sigma)\): \(k\) planes processed, \(j\) landings used, and \(\sigma\) a set of at most \(w\) cities. An arc gives plane \(k + 1\) a size \(m\) and a row \(\eta\) with \(|\eta| \equiv m + 1 \pmod 2\), \(|\eta| \le \min(m - 1, w)\) and \(|\sigma \triangle \eta| \le w\); it leads to \((k + 1, j + m, \sigma \triangle \eta)\) and weighs \(c(\eta) + G[m - |\eta|][T - \delta(\eta)]\). The shortest path from \((0, 0, \emptyset)\) to \((p, s, \emptyset)\) weighs \(E(T)\) Theorem 7.6 machine-checked. It takes \(O(p\,s\,\hat m\,N_w)\) time per level, where \(N_w\) bounds the pairs of sets an arc can join: polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(w\).
A variant carries Pareto sets of points \((c(X),\ \max_k \delta(X_k))\) along the arcs instead of one level at a time, and yields the whole front in one pass Proposition 7.8 informal.

In the example, \(w = 1\). At \(T = 8\), plane 1 takes \(m = 2\) landings with the row \(\eta = \{2\}\): an arc of weight \(c_2 + G[1][8 - 3] = 7\) from \((0, 0, \emptyset)\) to \((1, 2, \{2\})\). Plane 2 takes the same option, \(\sigma\) becomes \(\{2\} \triangle \{2\} = \emptyset\), and the path ends at \((2, 4, \emptyset)\) with weight \(14 = E(8)\).
In the code. The C++ solver uses the link-forest DP. The σ-DP belongs to the Lean tools: the verified solver zeno-front machine-checked and the Lean checker compute \(E\) with it, or with the link-forest DP when useTreeDP estimates that cheaper (Lean tools).


Step 10. Finding the breakpoints
Idea. Proposition 7.1 needs \(E\) only where it drops. Since \(E\) is non-increasing, an interval of levels whose two ends have equal values is constant and holds no breakpoint, so a search can skip it whole.
The search breakpoints (include/zeno/breakpoints.hpp). It starts from \(E(T_{\rm lo})\) and the closed form \(E(T_{\rm hi}) = s\,c_{\min}\). Every open interval \((a, b)\) with \(E(a) > E(b)\) is split at up to threads evenly spaced levels, evaluated in parallel; pieces with equal ends are dropped, and a piece \((a, a + 1)\) has its breakpoint at \(a + 1\). With \(r\) breakpoints this evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels. Each level is evaluated by the cascade of Figure 4: \(L\) and \(U\), then \(U_3\), then the exact program, each only if the previous ones do not settle it.
--levels sweep brackets every level and runs the exact program only where needed (step 8); --levels search runs the search above; the default, auto, sweeps up to \(2^{12}\) levels and searches beyond, so on wide level ranges the number of levels evaluated grows with the logarithm of the range.
In the example. Seven levels: auto sweeps them. With --levels search --threads 1, zeno evaluates \(T = 4\), then \(7\), then \(5\) and \(8\), then \(6\) and \(9\); \(T = 10\) is the closed form. On so few levels the search saves nothing. It pays off on ranges of thousands of levels with few breakpoints.


Step 11. Plans
Construction Theorem 4.1 machine-checked. Take a link forest of the partition and root each tree. Every plane flies, in this order:

its drop-offs, \(C_I \to b \to C_I\), one per child edge labelled \(b\), each leaving a new passenger in city \(b\), from time 0;
its free landings as alternating crossings: \(C_I \to x \to C_G\) carrying a new passenger, then \(C_G \to x \to C_I\) empty, and so on, ending in \(C_G\); there is an odd number of them by (F2);
if it has a parent edge labelled \(a\), its pick-up \(C_G \to a \to C_G\), leaving city \(a\) once the passenger its parent dropped there has arrived.

No drop-off and no crossing ever waits. A plane picks up at most once, from its parent, whose drop-offs come first; the timing argument of the theorem shows that each pick-up ends by the larger load of the two planes. So every plane flies exactly \(\ell(X_k)\) and the makespan is \(\max_k \ell(X_k)\). A forest with \(N\) edges hands off \(N\) passengers, and the crossings carry the other \(t - N\).
In the example. The plan of \((14, 16)\), as zeno --plans prints it; a leg reads from->to[depart,arrive], followed by the passenger it carries:
plane 1: CI->c2[0,3]p1 c2->CI[3,6] CI->c3[6,11]p2 c3->CG[11,16]p2
plane 2: CI->c3[0,5]p3 c3->CG[5,10]p3 CG->c2[10,13] c2->CG[13,16]p1
Plane 1 is the root: it drops passenger 1 in city 2 and returns, then crosses through city 3 with passenger 2. Plane 2 crosses through city 3 with passenger 3, flies empty from \(C_G\) to city 2, and brings back passenger 1, who has waited there since time 3. Both planes finish at \(16 = 2 \cdot 8\) (Figure 2).

In the code. For each front point, FrontSolver::plans (solve.cpp) takes the level \(T = M/2g\), reruns ForestProgram with trees of at most 2, then 3, then \(q_{\max}\) planes, and keeps the first whose value equals the point’s cost. reconstruct() gives its link forest, and buildPlan (include/zeno/plan.hpp) the plan of Theorem 4.1. checkPlan then re-simulates every plan against the model, sharing no code with buildPlan; a plan whose cost or makespan differs from its point stops the solver.


Step 12. Certificates
Idea. A front can be checked without trusting the solver that found it. A certificate lists the points, a plan for each, and, for each gap between consecutive points, the name of a lower bound that the checker recomputes.
Result Theorem 9.1 machine-checked. Let \((C_1, M_1), \dots, (C_r, M_r)\) have increasing makespans and decreasing costs. The list is the front if

every listed plan is feasible, with cost \(C_i\) and makespan \(M_i\): the checker simulates it;
no plan is faster than \(M_1\): the checker verifies \(M_1 = 2d_{\min}\kappa\) Proposition 7.10 informal, parts in Lean;
for every \(i < r\), every plan of makespan below \(M_{i+1}\) costs at least \(C_i\): a lower bound at the level \(T^\star_i = \lfloor \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/2 \rfloor / g \rfloor\) reaches \(C_i\) (for a front point, \(T^\star_i = T_{i+1} - 1\));
no plan is cheaper than \(C_r\): the checker verifies \(C_r = s\,c_{\min}\), since every plan lands at least \(s\) times Lemma 3.2 machine-checked.

Obligation 3 names one of two bounds:

relaxed: \(L(T^\star_i) \ge C_i\). Sound under (S) alone, whatever the central flights Lemma 3.4 machine-checked;
forest: \(E(T^\star_i) \ge C_i\), recomputed with the link-forest DP. Sound under (S) and (A1) Theorem 4.7 machine-checked, or (S) and (AΔ) Theorem 4.10 machine-checked.

zeno writes relaxed whenever \(L\) reaches the cost, so a certificate whose gaps are all relaxed holds for every table of central flights.
