title: Algorithm
text:
Non-symmetric instances
When \(d \ne \bar d\), the duration of a landing depends on how it is flown, and step 1 no longer gives the front. zeno then computes a certified bracket instead (solveBracket, include/zeno/ns.hpp).
Roles. A landing in city \(i\) is flown as a crossing \(C_I \to i \to C_G\) or back, which lasts \(d_i + \bar d_i\); as a drop-off \(C_I \to i \to C_I\), which lasts \(2d_i\); or as a pick-up \(C_G \to i \to C_G\), which lasts \(2\bar d_i\). A role configuration gives every plane its drop-offs, pick-ups and crossings, with an odd number of crossings per plane and, city by city, as many drop-offs as pick-ups. The role load \(\lambda_k\) of plane \(k\) sums the durations of its roles Definition 4.2 Lean definition.
What carries over, and what does not.

Under (A1-NS), central flights at least as long as \(\min(d_i + d_j,\ \bar d_i + \bar d_j)\), every plan is weakly dominated by a role configuration with the same number of passengers, no larger cost, and role loads at most its makespan Theorem 6.1 machine-checked. So the least cost of a role configuration within a load bound is a lower bound.
A configuration need not fly within its largest role load: a pick-up can reach a city before the passenger it collects has been dropped there, and wait. That waiting can be harmful. On an instance with two cities, the cheapest role configuration with loads at most 73 costs 14, while no plan of makespan at most 73 costs less than 18 Proposition 6.5 informal. Role loads alone do not give the front.
For fixed orders of the drop-offs and pick-ups and a fixed matching of drop-offs to pick-ups, the template schedule (drop-offs first, then crossings, then pick-ups, each waiting for its passenger) is optimal, and its makespan has a closed form Lemma 6.3 informal, parts in Lean. If every plane picks up at most once, or every plane drops off at most once, the template finishes within the largest role load, provided that no hub leg of a city is longer than the detour through another city and the other hub, (AΔ-path) Corollary 6.4 informal.
Under (A1-NS), every plan is dominated by a role configuration whose template finishes no later, without any assumption on the order of events Theorem 6.9 machine-checked. Hence the front is the Pareto set of (cost, least template makespan) over role configurations Corollary 6.10 informal, parts in Lean.

The bracket.

Upper points. Plans built from link forests in which every plane picks up at most once, or, by time reversal, drops off at most once, and from the cheapest balanced role configurations found inside gaps. All are scheduled and simulated with their waiting, so every printed point is a real plan.
Lower bounds per gap, for every plan of makespan below the next point:

relaxed: the relaxation of Lemma 3.4 machine-checked with each landing weighted \(\min(2d_i, 2\bar d_i)\), which needs no assumption on central flights;
roles: the role relaxation, in which each plane flies an odd number of crossings and the loads add up to the crossing weight of the landings (Theorem 6.1, so (A1-NS));
lagrangian: a Lagrangian relaxation of the per-city balance, with one multiplier per city (A1-NS);
balanced: the exact program over balanced role configurations, a shortest path over the planes on the vector of per-city imbalances Proposition 6.6 informal, parts in Lean. It is exponential in \(t - p\) and stops at the roleStates and roleWork limits;
search: the exhaustive search over the role configurations cheaper than the gap’s cost, each with every drop-off order and matching, the closed form of Lemma 6.3 giving its makespan. It rests on Theorem 6.9 and Corollary 6.10, stops at searchWork, and is the only kind that closes gaps opened by harmful waiting.

Report. The front is exact when the fastest makespan is certified and every gap is closed. Otherwise zeno lists each open gap with its proved lower bound and the reason it stays open, rather than print a front it cannot prove (command line). The refinement of open gaps stops after refineSeconds.

On 1,800 random tiny non-symmetric instances checked against a brute-force oracle, every bracket closes and equals the oracle’s front (README.md).

title: Algorithm
text:
Complexity
From §8 of the theory note, with \(\hat m = s - p + 1\), \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t - p + 1)\), \(w = \min(p - 1, t - p)\) and \(N_w\) as in step 9:



Step
Time




One-plane table \(G\), all levels
\(O(n\,\hat m\,T_{\rm hi})\)


\(L\) and \(U\), per level
\(O(p\,s^2 + n\,\hat m^2)\)


\(U_3\) chains, per level
\(O(n^2\,\hat m\,s + p\,s^2)\)


Link-forest DP, per level (Theorem 7.5)
\(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)\)


σ-DP, per level (Theorem 7.6)
\(O(p\,s\,\hat m\,N_w)\)


Plan for one point
\(O(s + n + p)\), up to union–find



How hard the problem is.

Deciding whether a fixed multiset \(X\) has an admissible partition with every \(\delta(X_k) \le T\), that is \(M(X) \le 2T\), is strongly NP-complete Theorem 8.1 informal, by a reduction from 3-Partition. So a method that fixes the multiset first and then schedules it, for instance greedily with the longest landing first onto the least-loaded plane, cannot be exact in general unless P = NP, and that greedy does miss front points (§5) informal, parts in Lean. The link-forest DP never fixes the multiset: it chooses the landings and their split together.
With two planes the decision stays NP-complete; for every fixed \(p\) it takes time polynomial in \(n\), \(s\) and \(T\), so it is weakly NP-complete Proposition 8.2 informal.
\(E(T)\), and under (S) and (A1) the front, are computable in pseudo-polynomial time (Theorem 7.5), so computing the front is not strongly NP-hard unless P = NP Corollary 8.3 informal. Whether deciding \(E(T) \le C\) is NP-hard, with \(t\) written in unary, is open.

The bounds of the table are those of the dense algorithm. The staircase layouts make the table and the forest DP independent of the magnitude of the durations in practice, and the breakpoint search evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels instead of all of them. Measured scaling is on the results and size guidance pages.

python3 site/gen_algorithm.py
The script needs nothing else. For the worked example and the contrast instance, it recomputes from their definitions the table \(G\), and at every level \(L\), \(U\), \(U_3\), and \(E\) three ways: by the link-forest DP, by the σ-DP, and by brute force over every partition of every multiset of \(s\) landings, with the parity matrix of Definition 2.2 deciding admissibility. It checks that these agree with one another and with zeno: the breakpoints of \(E\) are the front zeno prints, the levels the bracket closes are those --stats counts, the gap kinds are those of the certificate zeno writes, and every number this page quotes still holds. It then writes the data of the figures and the tables into site/algorithm/. The three drawings are hand-made SVG files in the same directory.

title: Certificate format
text:
A certificate lists one plan per front point and one lower bound per gap between consecutive points. A checker that verifies its four obligations has proved that the list is the Pareto front, without trusting the solver (Theorem 9.1). zeno --certificate FILE writes one, zeno check FILE verifies it (command line), and so does the Lean checker zeno-check, whose acceptance is backed by a kernel-checked soundness theorem (Lean tools).
The rest of this page is doc/certificate-format.md, the specification both checkers follow, included as it stands in the repository.

title: Certificate format
text:
A small certificate
zeno -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 -d tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat --certificate lpt.cert writes, for \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\):
zeno-certificate 1
instance 2 5 2
d 6 10
dbar 6 10
c 40 20
assume S
front 6
320 48
280 56
260 60
240 64
200 72
160 80
plan 1 2
plane 1 …
…
lower-bounds 5
…
end
The points are listed by increasing makespan. assume S only: every gap of this front is closed by the relaxation \(L\), so the certificate holds for central flights of any duration. Both checkers accept it:
$ zeno check lpt.cert
certificate accepted, assuming S
$ lake exe zeno-check lpt.cert
accepted: the 6 points are the Pareto front (all gaps relaxed: for every central flight table; ZenoFront.Cert.check_sound)

title: Certificate format
text:
The specification
zeno --certificate FILE writes, next to the front, a certificate that a checker can verify without trusting the solver. The reference checker is zeno check FILE; the Lean checker in lean/ (lake exe zeno-check FILE), whose soundness is proved in Lean, reads the same format. This page defines the format and what a checker must verify. The proofs behind each obligation are in doc/theory/exact-front.md.

What a certificate proves
For an instance with symmetric durations and a front \((C_1, M_1), \dots, (C_r, M_r)\) with \(M_1 < \dots < M_r\) and \(C_1 > \dots > C_r\), the certificate shows that this list is exactly the Pareto front:

Achieved. For every \(i\), the plan given for point \(i\) is feasible and has cost \(C_i\) and makespan \(M_i\). The checker simulates it.
Nothing is faster than \(M_1\). \(M_1 = 2\, d_{\min} \lceil s/p \rceil\), where \(s = 2t - p\). Every plan has at least \(s\) segments (counting lemma), some plane flies at least \(\lceil s/p \rceil\) of them, and under (S) each lasts at least \(2 d_{\min}\).
Nothing in a gap is cheaper. For every \(i < r\), every plan with makespan \(< M_{i+1}\) costs at least \(C_i\). Such a plan has \(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor \le h = \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/2 \rfloor\); with \(g\) the gcd of the durations, its groups fit in level \(T = \lfloor h / g \rfloor\) of the instance with durations divided by \(g\) (for a front point \(M_{i+1} = 2gT_{i+1}\), so \(T = T_{i+1} - 1\)). As \(E\) and \(L\) are non-increasing, it suffices that the bound at level \(T\) is at least \(C_i\). The certificate names how the checker establishes this bound:

relaxed: recompute the relaxation \(L(T)\) (no admissibility). Lemma R gives \(\text{cost} \ge L(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor)\) for every plan under (S) alone, whatever the central flights.
forest: recompute \(E(T)\) with the link-forest dynamic program (trees of at most \(\min(p, t-p+1)\) planes). This relies on a converse theorem: every plan is dominated by an admissible partition. It holds when the central flights satisfy (A1) (Theorem 4.7) or the triangle inequality (AΔ) (Theorem 4.10, Corollary 4.12), and the certificate must list the assumption A1 (or its synonym A1|AD, below).

Nothing is cheaper than \(C_r\). \(C_r = s \cdot c_{\min}\): every plan lands at least \(s\) times.

Then every plan \((C, M)\) is weakly dominated by a listed point: \(M \ge M_1\) by 2; if \(M_i \le M < M_{i+1}\) then \(C \ge C_i\) by 3; if \(M \ge M_r\) then \(C \ge C_r\) by 4. Together with 1, the list is the front.
A certificate whose gap bounds are all relaxed is valid for every symmetric instance, whatever its central flights: it needs neither (A1) nor (AΔ).
The assumptions on central flights, from §1.4 of the theory note: (A1) \(d_{ij} \ge d_i + d_j\) for every central flight (no faster than through a hub); (AΔ) \(\mathrm{dur}(a,b) \le \mathrm{dur}(a,x) + \mathrm{dur}(x,b)\) whenever the three flights exist. A certificate does not contain the central flights, so no checker can test them: assume states the instances the certificate is claimed for.


Syntax
A text file of lines. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. Tokens are separated by spaces. All numbers are non-negative integers.
zeno-certificate 1
instance <n> <t> <p>
d <d_1> ... <d_n>
dbar <dbar_1> ... <dbar_n>
c <c_1> ... <c_n>
assume <assumption>...
front <r>
<C_1> <M_1>
...
<C_r> <M_r>
plan <i> <p>
plane <k> <m>
<from> <to> <depart> <arrive> <passenger>
...
lower-bounds <r - 1>
<i> <kind>
...
end

d: durations between \(C_I\) and each central city; dbar: between \(C_G\) and each central city; c: landing costs.
assume: the assumptions the solver used. A checker refuses an obligation that needs an assumption the certificate does not list. Version 1 knows:

S: symmetric durations, i.e. d = dbar.
A1: the token of forest gaps. Its name comes from (A1), central flights at least as long as through a hub, but the gaps it allows are sound when the central flights satisfy (A1) or (AΔ). Both checkers are proved sound for both. In the theory note, this is Theorem 4.7 under (A1), and Theorem 4.10 with Corollary 4.12 under (AΔ). In Lean, it is Cert.check_sound_A1 under (A1) and Cert.check_sound_ATri under (AΔ), with the variants Cert.check_sound_anywhere_ATri (planes ending anywhere), Cert.check_sound_rat_ATri (rational times) and Cert.check_sound_minimal_ATri.
A1|AD: the same scope, spelled out, (A1) or (AΔ). zeno check accepts it for forest gaps like A1. The Lean checker reads only A1, so it rejects the forest gaps of a certificate that lists A1|AD alone.

What zeno writes and reports:

zeno --certificate lists A1 when a gap needs the forest bound and the instance’s central flights satisfy (A1) or (AΔ). The default table (\(\max(d_i, \bar d_i) + \max(d_j, \bar d_j) + 100\)) satisfies (A1), and --metric tables satisfy (AΔ). When the central flights satisfy neither and a gap needs the forest bound, it writes no certificate (Example 4.13 shows such a gap can hide a cheaper plan). Without a forest gap, it lists S only.
zeno check reports that the forest gaps relied on A1|AD, i.e. (A1) or (AΔ).

front: the points by increasing makespan.
plan <i> <p>: the plan of point \(i\) (1-based), for the \(p\) planes, in order \(i = 1..r\). Each plane <k> <m> (k = 1..p, in order) is followed by its \(m\) legs, in flight order.
A leg: locations are 0 for \(C_I\), 1..n for the central cities, n+1 for \(C_G\); times are integers; passenger is 1..t, or 0 when the plane flies empty.
lower-bounds: one line per gap \(i = 1..r-1\), in order, with its kind, relaxed or forest.
Limits of the reference reader: every number at most \(2^{36}\), \(n, t, p \le 10^5\), at most \(10^7\) legs in all.



Plan semantics (obligation 1)
A plan is feasible when:

every plane starts in \(C_I\) at time \(\ge 0\); each leg leaves the location where the previous one arrived, no earlier than that arrival; each leg is a flight between a hub (\(C_I\) or \(C_G\)) and a central city, lasting d (via \(C_I\)) or dbar (via \(C_G\)) — there is no \(C_I\)–\(C_G\) flight, and version 1 has no central-to-central legs; every plane ends in \(C_G\);
every passenger \(1..t\) starts in \(C_I\) at time 0 and rides a chain of legs, each leaving where the previous one arrived and no earlier, ending in \(C_G\);
a leg carries at most one passenger (by construction of the format).

Boarding and debarking take no time. The cost is the sum of c over the legs that land in a central city; the makespan is the last arrival.


Example
zeno -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 -d tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat --certificate lpt.cert writes a certificate for the instance \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\), whose front has six points; zeno check lpt.cert verifies it.


Version 2: non-symmetric instances
zeno --certificate FILE on a non-symmetric instance writes a version 2 certificate when its bracket is exact (every gap closed). Version 2 differs from version 1 in four places.

The header is zeno-certificate 2, and dbar may differ from d. assume lists S only for symmetric durations, and A1-NS when a bound below needs it (Theorem 6.1 of the theory note: every plan is weakly dominated by a role configuration with the same cost and loads at most its makespan, if central flights are useless). zeno writes no certificate that needs A1-NS for an instance whose central-flight table violates it, such as a --metric --hubs apart instance with short central flights; (AΔ) alone does not suffice for non-symmetric instances, since short central flights can beat every role configuration (Proposition 6.7 of the theory note).
Levels are in units of the gcd g of all durations, and are full loads: a crossing \(C_I \to i \to C_G\) or back weighs \(d_i + \bar d_i\), a drop-off \(2 d_i\), a pick-up \(2 \bar d_i\). A plan of makespan \(< M_{i+1}\) fits in level \(T = \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/g \rfloor\). (For symmetric durations, version 1’s half-loads and level \(\lfloor (M_{i+1}-1)/(2g) \rfloor\) are kept.)
A line fastest <kind> after the front names the bound that rules out plans faster than \(M_1\): the bound at level \(\lfloor (M_1 - 1)/g \rfloor\) must be infinite. Kinds: closed (symmetric only, as in version 1), relaxed, roles, balanced, search.
Gap kinds, in addition to relaxed (lemma R with weight \(\min(2d_i, 2\bar d_i)\) per landing, no assumption) and forest (symmetric, A1 or A1|AD):

roles (A1-NS): each plane flies an odd number \(\ge 1\) of crossings and its other landings weigh at least \(\min(2d, 2\bar d)\); all loads add up to the crossing weight of the landings, so the largest is at least that over \(p\).
lagrangian mu_1 ... mu_n (A1-NS): with one signed integer multiplier per city, a drop-off in \(i\) costs \(c_i + \mu_i\) and a pick-up \(c_i - \mu_i\); the balance of drop-offs and pick-ups city by city drops out and the planes decouple. Every \(\mu\) gives a lower bound, so the checker only evaluates the bound at the listed \(\mu\).
balanced (A1-NS): the checker reruns the exact program over balanced role configurations (a branch and bound against the cost \(C_i\)) and requires that it finishes.
search (A1-NS): the checker reruns the exhaustive search over role configurations of cost below \(C_i\) with exact schedules (every order of drop-offs, matching and pick-up order) and requires that none finishes before \(M_{i+1}\). By Corollary 6.10 (schedulable domination, Theorem 6.9) this rules out every feasible plan, also on instances with a city of \(d = \bar d = 0\). Older certificates may list the assumption EO (event-ordered plans) for such instances. Both checkers still read it, but it is no longer needed. This is the only kind that closes gaps opened by harmful waiting (Proposition 6.5). It is also a valid fastest kind.


Obligations 1 and 4 are unchanged. The reference checker (zeno check) reads both versions. The Lean checker (lean/) verifies version 1. Of version 2 it verifies the relaxed, roles, lagrangian, balanced and search gaps, and fastest closed, relaxed, roles, balanced and search. Its soundness theorem Cert2.check_sound is about every feasible plan, with or without a city of \(d = \bar d = 0\) (schedulableDomination_all, lean/README.md). When a certificate lists EO, the Lean checker also tests that every listed plan is event-ordered, and the points are then also the front of the event-ordered plans (Cert2.check_sound_EO).

title: Command line
text:
zeno [front] [instance options] [--threads N] [--levels MODE] [--plans] [--certificate FILE] [--stats]
zeno check CERTIFICATE
zeno pddl [instance options] [-O FILE] [--no-front]
zeno generate [instance options] [-O FILE]
The first argument selects the command; without one, zeno runs front. -h or --help anywhere prints the help below, which is the output of the current build (regenerated with the site). An unknown option is an error.
Exit codes: 0 on success; 1 on an error (the message on stderr starts with zeno:); 2 when zeno check rejects a certificate.

text:
Instance options
All four commands but check build an instance from the same options, and each means what its name says: -C the costs, -D the durations, -E and -W the two duration sides; data files are read as written. The generator page gives the formulas, and the model page the data file formats.

title: Command line
text:
front: the Pareto front
zeno -n 2 -t 3 -p 2
4 8
6 6
8 4
One cost makespan line per front point, by increasing cost (so by decreasing makespan). Costs and durations are integers, and so is every makespan.
Symmetric instances (durations to \(C_I\) and to \(C_G\) equal, every generated instance without -E/-W): the front is exact. A zeno instance has no central-to-central flights; the front is that of the model in which they exist but are no faster than through a hub, assumption (A1), as in every PDDL file zeno writes (Corollary 4.8 with Proposition 7.1). The note proves that the same front holds for central flights that are faster but obey the triangle inequality (AΔ) (Corollary 4.12, not yet in Lean); with central flights that violate both, it can differ (Example 4.13). When every gap of the front is closed by the relaxation \(L\), the same front holds for central flights of any duration; the certificate then lists only relaxed gaps.
Non-symmetric instances (-E/-W, or a 3-line data file with different lines): zeno computes a certified bracket (algorithm). Stdout lists the points achieved by simulated plans, and stderr reports which gaps between them a lower bound closes:
zeno -n 4 -t 3 -p 2 -E 3 -W 2 -r 10 > front.txt
non-symmetric instance: 12 achieved points; fastest makespan certified; 11 of 11 gaps certified; the front is exact, assuming A1-NS
When the fastest makespan is certified and every gap is closed, the printed points are the exact front, under the listed assumption (A1-NS) when a bound needs it. Otherwise the report says the front is a bracket and lists each open gap:
  open gap between makespans M1 and M2: a plan with makespan < M2 costs at least B (achieved: C; REASON)
where the reason is either “a cheaper balanced configuration exists, no schedule found within the gap” or “the exact balanced program gave up” (a limit of SolveOptions was reached, below).

Solver options

--threads N

Worker threads for the level evaluations. Default 0: all hardware threads.

--levels MODE

How the levels \(T\) (half makespans, in units of the gcd of the durations) are visited. sweep brackets every level between \(T_{\rm lo}\) and \(T_{\rm hi}\), then runs the exact DP on the open ones. search bisects for the breakpoints of \(E\), which evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels for \(r\) breakpoints. auto (the default) sweeps when the range has at most \(2^{12}\) levels and searches beyond. Use search for wide level ranges, for example durations scaled by a large -r.

--plans

After the front, print a plan for every point, each checked by simulation (checkPlan). One block per point, from the cheapest, then one line per plane, legs as from->to[depart,arrive] with pK when passenger \(K\) is aboard. Locations are CI, c1…cn and CG.


# cost 6, makespan 6
plane 1: CI->c2[0,1]p1 c2->CI[1,2] CI->c1[2,4]p2 c1->CG[4,6]p2
plane 2: CI->c1[0,2]p3 c1->CG[2,4]p3 CG->c2[4,5] c2->CG[5,6]p1
Here plane 1 drops passenger 1 in city 2 and returns empty, and plane 2 picks that passenger up on its way back to \(C_G\).

--certificate FILE

Write a certificate of the front to FILE (format): version 1 for symmetric instances, version 2 for non-symmetric ones. A non-symmetric front gets a certificate only when its bracket is exact; otherwise zeno stops with no certificate: the front is a bracket with open gaps. Implies building the plans.

--stats

Print solver statistics on stderr:


levels 2..4 (x1, 3 levels), cities 2, max tree 2
settled: bracket 3, pairs 0, chains 0, monotone 0, exact 0
work: 5 states, 105 relaxations
seconds: table 4.084e-06, bracket 3.9708e-05, chains 0, exact 0, plans 6.6083e-05

levels: the range \([T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]\) of scaled half makespans, the gcd the durations were divided by (x), and the number of levels in the range;
cities: cities left after the dominance reduction; max tree: \(\min(p, t-p+1)\), the largest useful link tree;
settled: how the value of each evaluated level was established. bracket when \(L = U\); pairs when \(U\) is exact (trees of at most 2 planes); chains when \(U_3\) settles it; monotone when \(E\) takes equal values at both ends of an interval; exact counts the link-forest DP evaluations;
work: DP cells written and candidate transitions examined, summed;
seconds: time in the one-plane table, the bracket, the chains bound, the exact DP and the plans.

title: Command line
text:
check: verify a certificate
zeno -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 -d tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat --certificate lpt.cert
zeno check lpt.cert
certificate accepted, assuming S
zeno check reads a certificate of either version and verifies the four obligations of the format. On success it prints the assumptions the accepted obligations needed (S: symmetric durations; A1: central flights no faster than through a hub, needed by forest gaps; A1-NS for the version 2 kinds other than relaxed). On failure it prints one error: line per failed obligation, then certificate rejected, and exits with code 2.
zeno check reuses the solver library’s dynamic programs for the gap bounds, so it is a consistency check of the solver, not an independent proof. The Lean checker zeno-check is the independent one.

title: Command line
text:
pddl: write a PDDL problem
zeno pddl -n 10 -t 8 -p 3            # writes zeno10n8t3pMulti.pddl
zeno pddl -n 10 -t 8 -p 3 -O p.pddl --no-front
Writes the instance as a PDDL 2.1 problem for the domain pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl (PDDL page). The default file name is zeno<n>n<t>t<p>pMulti.pddl; -O FILE sets it. For a symmetric instance the front is solved and appended as comments, unless --no-front. Non-symmetric problems are written without a front.

title: Command line
text:
generate: write a data file
zeno generate -n 4 -t 3 -p 2 -C 2 -D 2 -r 10
20 17 14 10
10 14 17 20
Writes the instance that the options describe as a data file for -d: durations then costs for a symmetric instance, or CI-side durations, CG-side durations, costs otherwise. Without -O FILE it writes to standard output. -t and -p are validated but not written. Reading the output back with -d gives the same instance.

title: Command line
text:
Limits of the non-symmetric bracket
The non-symmetric bracket stops some of its searches at limits set in zeno::SolveOptions (include/zeno/solve.hpp). The command line uses the defaults; the library can change them.








Field
Default
Limits

2,000,000
States of the exact balanced role program, per level.


roleWork

A gap left open by a limit is reported as such (the exact balanced program gave up). It is not an error: the printed points are still achieved by simulated plans, and the reported lower bounds are still proved.

title: Command line
text:
Values and limits

Durations, costs and times are non-negative integers (std::int64_t). The instance is validated: \(n \ge 1\), \(1 \le p \le t\), every vector of length \(n\), every value non-negative.
The certificate reader refuses values above \(2^{36}\), \(n\), \(t\) or \(p\) above \(10^5\), and more than \(10^7\) legs, so no sum in the checker can overflow.
For sizes and running times, see the size guidance.

title: Size guidance
text:
What drives the time
From the algorithm (algorithm) and the measurements:

The number of landings \(s = 2t - p\) and the largest group \(\hat m = s - p + 1\) set the size of the one-plane table and of the knapsacks of the bracket, \(O(p\,s^2 + n\,\hat m^2)\) per level. This is the main cost on the large instances above: \(t\) matters more than \(n\).
The level range \(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo} = (d_{\rm cheap} - d_{\min})\kappa\) multiplies the per-level cost under --levels sweep. Under search (automatic beyond \(2^{12}\) levels), the solver evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels for \(r\) front points, so scaling the durations costs little: \(10^8\) levels take about 4 ms (BM_SolveLargeDurations).
The number of front points \(r\): one plan per point with --plans or --certificate, and a certificate grows with the plans (\(3.9\) MB and 240,000 legs for \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\)).
The cities after reduction. Dominated and equal cities are merged first, so many cities with few distinct (duration, cost) pairs cost little. The default family keeps every city.
Links. The exact link-forest DP runs only on levels the bracket leaves open, and only when link trees can have three planes or more, \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t - p + 1) \ge 3\). Its cost grows with \(q_{\max}^2\). On default-generator instances such as -n 200 -t 100 -p 10, --stats reports every level settled by the bracket (\(L = U\)) and no exact DP call.

--threads parallelises the level evaluations; --stats shows where the time goes (command line).

title: Size guidance
text:
Non-symmetric instances
The non-symmetric bracket is much more expensive. The exact balanced role program has a state space growing like \((2n)^{t-p}\), and the gap search enumerates role configurations with every order and matching. Both stop at limits (2,000,000 states and 50,000,000 transitions per level, 20,000,000 search steps per gap, 30 s of gap refinement; SolveOptions). Beyond them zeno reports the open gaps with their lower bounds instead of an exact front. The instance of Proposition 6.5 (\(n = 2\), \(t = 7\), \(p = 4\)) closes in a few milliseconds. Keep \(t - p\) small for exact non-symmetric fronts.

title: Size guidance
text:
The Lean tools

zeno-check on the certificate of a suite instance takes 26 ms at the median and 2.1 s at most (3.9 MB, \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\)). The σ-DP it uses for forest gaps is exponential in the number of cities that survive the dominance merge. When that is large it switches to the tree DP, and certificates of -n 40 -t 20 -p 8 -C 2 -D 2 -r 100 take 12.5 s.
zeno-front is slower than zeno: 10 s for \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\), against 61 ms. It finishes all 66 suite instances within 60 s (results).

text:
bench/instances/*.txt hold the instances that every solver is timed on. One instance per line, name|arguments, where the arguments are zeno instance options and @DATA@ stands for bench/instances/data/ (data files in the 2-line format). Lines starting with # are comments.



Suite

title: Generator
text: Without -d, zeno builds the instance with a family of generating functions, from the options -n -t -p -C -D -E -W -r -j -k -l -m -x -y (command line). Every option means what its name says: -C sets the costs, -D the durations, -E the \(C_I\)-side and -W the \(C_G\)-side durations. The construction is legacy::buildInstance (src/zeno/legacy_input.cpp).

title: Generator
text:
Construction
For cities \(i = 1, \dots, n\), with \(r\) = -r, \((j, k)\) = -j -k, \((l, m)\) = -l -m and \((x, y)\) = -x -y (defaults \(r = 1\), \(j = l = x = 1\), \(k = m = y = 0\)):

Costs on increasing arguments, durations on decreasing ones: \[c_i = x\,f_C(\lfloor j\,i + k \rfloor) + y, \qquad d_i = x\,f_D(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y.\] With -E and -W (both needed; -D is then ignored) the instance is non-symmetric: \[d_i = x\,f_E(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y, \qquad \bar d_i = x\,f_W(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y.\] Otherwise \(\bar d = d\).
Every value is multiplied by \(r\) and truncated toward zero: \(v \leftarrow \operatorname{trunc}(r\,v)\). -r 100 keeps slowly growing functions such as \(\ln\) from collapsing onto a few integers.

With increasing functions, the first city is the slowest and the cheapest: faster cities cost more, which is what makes the front non-trivial. The order of the cities does not matter to the front.

title: The problem
text: MultiZenoTravel is a planning problem with two objectives. Planes carry passengers from a start hub to a goal hub through intermediate cities. Each landing in an intermediate city has a price, and the cheap cities are the far ones. A plan is judged on its cost, the sum of its landing prices, and on its makespan, the time at which the last plane reaches the goal. No plan is best on both counts, so the answer is a Pareto front: every (cost, makespan) pair that some plan achieves and that no other plan matches or beats on both. ZenoSolver computes it exactly.

title: The problem
text:
The model




MultiZenoTravel, drawn for the example below.




Cities. Two hubs, \(C_I\) where everything starts and \(C_G\) where everything must end, and \(n\) central cities \(1, \dots, n\).
Flights. Central city \(i\) is joined to \(C_I\) by a flight of duration \(d_i\) and to \(C_G\) by a flight of duration \(\bar d_i\); flights can be flown both ways. No flight joins \(C_I\) and \(C_G\), so every trip lands in a central city. Two central cities may be joined. In the instances zeno generates by default, as in the example, such a flight is never faster than going through a hub (assumption (A1)); in metric instances every flight lasts the distance between its ends, so the durations satisfy the triangle inequality instead (assumption (AΔ), §1.4 Lean definition). The instance is symmetric when \(\bar d_i = d_i\) for every city.
Cost. Landing in central city \(i\) costs \(c_i\). Landing in a hub is free.
Planes. \(p\) planes start in \(C_I\) at time 0 and must end in \(C_G\). A plane carries at most one passenger at a time.
Passengers. \(t \ge p\) passengers start in \(C_I\) and must reach \(C_G\). A passenger may leave a plane in a central city and board another one there later: a hand-off. Planes and passengers may wait anywhere.
Objectives. The cost of a plan is the sum of the landing costs of all its flights. Its makespan is the time at which the last plane arrives in \(C_G\). The front is the set of (cost, makespan) pairs of the plans that no other plan dominates.

The precise definitions are §1.1 Lean definition (instances), §1.2 Lean definition (plans) and §1.5 Lean definition (fronts) of the blueprint. One consequence is used everywhere: a plan lands at least \(s = 2t - p\) times in central cities (Lemma 3.2 machine-checked).

City 1 is close to both hubs and expensive; city 3 is far and cheap. With \(t = 3\) passengers and \(p = 2\) planes, a plan lands at least \(2t - p = 4\) times. Four landings in city 3 cost \(4 \times 1 = 4\), but each plane then flies four legs of 5: makespan 20. Four landings in city 1 cost 36 and take 8. The rest of the front lies in between. The command
build/release/zeno -n 3 -t 3 -p 2 -d site/problem/example.dat --plans

title: The problem
text:
A plan, step by step
Choose a point of the front. The map plays the plan zeno returns for it, and the timeline below shows the same plan with one row per plane. In the plan of cost 20 and makespan 14, shown first, plane 1 takes passenger 1 to city 1, leaves them there and flies back to \(C_I\) for passenger 2. Plane 2 crosses with passenger 3, flies back from \(C_G\) to city 1 and collects passenger 1. Each plan of this front contains one such hand-off.



  
  
  

Timeline: one row per plane, one bar per flight, coloured by the passenger on board. Click to move the time.

The plan viewer needs JavaScript. The plans are in problem/plans.json.


Cost and makespan
The cost counts every landing in a central city, whichever plane makes it; hub landings are free. The makespan is the last arrival in \(C_G\): delivering a passenger early does not shorten it.

In a symmetric instance, a plane whose landings form the multiset \(X_k\) can fly them in exactly \(\ell(X_k) = 2\sum_{i \in X_k} d_i\), one round trip from a hub per landing, and a plan exists whose makespan is the largest of these loads (Theorem 4.1 machine-checked). No plan does better (Theorem 4.7 machine-checked), so the front is a statement about multisets of landings and how they split among the planes (Corollary 4.8 machine-checked).

title: The problem
text:
The whole front
Moving along the front buys time with money. The cheapest plan, (4, 20), makes all four landings in city 3. The fastest, (36, 8), makes all four in city 1. In between, the planes mix cities: at (20, 14) each plane lands once in city 1 and once in city 3, flies \(2 \times (2 + 5) = 14\), and the four landings cost \(9 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 20\). The plan shown above is ringed; click another point, or focus the chart and use the arrow keys and Enter, to show its plan.

title: The problem
text:
Why it is hard

Hand-offs
Passengers can change planes, so a plan is not a set of independent trips. Without a hand-off, a plane that carries two passengers must come back to \(C_I\), which takes at least three landings; in the example no such plan ends before 12. With one hand-off each plane lands twice, and the plan ends at 8. The search therefore ranges over who drops whom where, and who collects them, not only over which cities to use.


Parity: not every split can be flown




The four kinds of segment between two visits to a hub.



Between two visits to a hub, a plane flies a segment. A crossing \(A\) carries a passenger from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), a return \(\bar A\) flies back, a drop-off \(B\) leaves a passenger in a central city, and a pick-up \(\bar B\) collects one. A route from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) has one more crossing than returns (Lemma 2.1 informal, parts in Lean), so a plane that only crosses lands an odd number of times. A plane with an even number of landings must drop off or pick up, and a drop-off in city \(i\) needs another plane’s pick-up in city \(i\).
So a split of the landings among the planes can be flown without waiting only if these parities can be matched. Definition 2.2 Lean definition (admissible partition) states the condition, and Lemma 2.6 machine-checked turns it into a forest of hand-offs between planes. In the example, the split \(\{1, 3\} \mid \{1, 3\}\) is admissible: both planes land twice, and they share city 1, where the hand-off happens. The split \(\{1, 1\} \mid \{3, 3\}\) has the same number of landings but cannot be flown: each plane would drop a passenger that the other plane never visits.


Splitting the landings among the planes
Even for a fixed multiset of landings, the best split is a scheduling problem, and the natural greedy rule, longest landing first onto the least-loaded plane, is not exact. On the instance lpt-counterexample of the catalogue (two cities, \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\)), three landings in the \(d = 10\) city and five in the \(d = 6\) city split as \(\{10, 10, 10\} \mid \{6, 6, 6, 6, 6\}\): both planes fly 60, which gives the front point (260, 60). Longest first ends at 64, a makespan that the cheaper point (240, 64) already reaches (§5 informal, parts in Lean). Deciding whether a multiset can be flown within a given makespan is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 8.1 informal), so no polynomial rule of this kind is exact unless P = NP.


Waiting can cost time
In a symmetric instance, waiting never costs time: the plans of Theorem 4.1 machine-checked end at the largest flight time of a plane. When the two hubs are at different distances (\(\bar d_i \ne d_i\)), a plane can reach a city before the passenger it must collect. Proposition 6.5 informal gives an instance with two cities, \(d = (3, 19)\), \(\bar d = (3, 11)\), \(c = (5, 1)\), \(t = 7\) and \(p = 4\). At cost 14 the flight times of the planes fit within 72, but the plane that collects three passengers in city 2 gets there at time 17, before the first drop-off can arrive at 19. It waits, and the plan ends at 74, which is the front point of cost 14. In this non-symmetric case zeno brackets the front between plans and lower bounds, and says on its standard error whether the two meet.

title: MultiZenoTravel
text: Revised and extended version of arXiv:2304.14659 (2023).

title: MultiZenoTravel
text:
Introduction
The progress of algorithmics, the availability of more & more data and the dramatic increase of computational power drive a fast-pace evolution of the artificial intelligence (AI) field. As part of this change, the need to assess the performances of computational methods and to compare their merits is crucial. Many of the core fields of AI have set up standard benchmarks and competitions, in order to complement expert knowledge and analysis. In that regard, the automated planning community is at the edge of the state of the art, with the well-known International Planning Competition (IPC), hosting a large benchmark and using a common definition language.
A deterministic planning problem consists in selecting a sequence of actions (a plan) having an effect on a state, so that applying the plan on an initial state allows to reach a goal (partial) state, while optimizing a function of the plan’s value. This function is generally the total duration to reach the goal (the makespan), each action having a duration. However, the value function may very well represent another aspect of the problem, such as the cost of the plan, the energy it requires or the uncertainty produced by the actions.
In realistic problems, it is very often the case that several such objective functions exist and are contradictory. For example, a short plan may be costly, while a cheap plan may take a long time. In such a setting, using a linear combination of those objective functions falls back to introducing a bias about the preferences of the operational user. However, preferences cannot always be modelled easily in practice, e.g. the user may decide based on political information. In addition, the knowledge of the feasible compromises between the objectives may, in fact, influence the decision maker simply because it gives additional information about the problem itself. For instance, if the two objectives are a cost and a risk, the decision maker might revise its risk appetite knowing that the increase of the risk by 1% beyond its initial acceptable risk threshold can lead to a 50% cost decrease.
This calls for the use of multi-objective optimization, where the problem is actually modelled with several objective functions, and the output of the solver is a set of solutions that are non-dominated by other solutions, regarding the objectives. The weak dominance of a \(d\)-dimensional point \(\vec a\) over point \(\vec b\) is defined as \(\vec a \preceq \vec b \iff a_j \le b_j\) for \(j = 1, \dots, d\). A set of points \(P \subseteq X\) is then defined as Pareto-optimal if every point of \(X\) is weakly dominated by a point of \(P\), all its points being non-dominated by each other. The output of solving such a problem is thus a set of solutions ordered as a “Pareto front”. That is, for a problem with two objective functions, a set of points ordered along a monotonic function. Operationally, the user is still in charge of taking the final decision, but the complexity of their decision has been drastically reduced to a \(d-1\) dimensional problem.
While real-world problems are often multi-objective in nature, few works actually consider their study in the automated planning area. The well known IPC does not propose benchmarks for such problems [VCM18, CP19] to this date. In fact, PDDL 3.0 explicitly offered hooks for several objectives [GHL+09], but the only organized competition tracks concerned aggregated objectives, tracks which were canceled in 2011.
Despite various work on benchmark generation [LDG+18, ADE+20, BF22] and extension to other planning problems [PF21], no truly multi-objective planning problem has been proposed apart from our line of work.

Previous Works
We have previously proposed a problem instance generator for such multi-objective planning problems [SSV06, KSV+13, QS15], extending the ZenoTravel [PW94] problem with an additional objective. Such problem sets are crucial for benchmarking optimization algorithms, especially when the optimum is known, as it allows for a rigorous comparison of the performances of solvers.
The original ZenoTravel problem [PW94] involves planes moving passengers between cities, while taking care of their fuel. Actions such as flying, boarding, deplaning or refueling take various time to complete, and a plane cannot fly without fuel. The objective is to minimize the makespan, while honoring passengers’ destinations.
The proof-of-concept of the MultiZenoTravel problem is based on a simplified ZenoTravel model [SSV06]. In this model, there are five connected cities (see Figure 1), planes may transport only one passenger at a time and there is only one flying speed. The main addition to the problem is that an additional objective is attached to all actions. This second objective is either a cost, which is additive (each plane has to pay the corresponding tax every time it lands in that city) or a risk (for which the maximal value encountered during the complete execution of a plan is to be minimized). In this first instance, three passengers can be moved across the cities.

The second version of the MultiZenoTravel problem [KSV+13] builds up on the proof-of-concept, allows for 3, 6 and 9 passengers, and a 3-to-2 passengers-to-planes ratio, which makes up for very small instances, due to the combinatorial explosion of the solution space.
In [QS15], we introduced an algorithm to compute the true Pareto fronts of very large instances in reasonable time, and the first version of the ZenoSolver software is described. The article also provides a few typical instances that exhibit very different shapes of Pareto Fronts, for different levels of complexity. Unfortunately, this work suffers from two unrealistic assumptions. First, the distances are assumed to be symmetric around the central cities, that is to say \(\forall i, d_i = \bar d_i\). Second, the proof of the proposition which allows us to find Pareto-optimal plans relies on the following unrealistic assumption: \[\forall (i, j) \in [1, n]^2,\ d_i + d_j < d_{ij}.\] In other words, none of the instances generated under this assumption would respect a triangular inequality. Even if a benchmark does not necessarily have to be realistic by nature, this particular assumption drastically restrains the extrapolation of the performances of a solver observed on the benchmark to real life problems.


Our Contribution
In this work, we introduce a constructive way to find the Pareto-optimal solutions for the MultiZenoTravel problem. Our first contribution is to generalize from the original symmetric clique problem introduced in [SSV06] to a non-symmetric clique version and to a version with no particular assumption on the graph.
As a second contribution, we characterize the Pareto front of the symmetric clique problem when the flights between central cities obey the triangular inequality, as well as under the assumption of [QS15]: every point of the front is reached by a plan landing exactly \(2t - p\) times in central cities, and the lists of cities that can be flown, and how fast, are described by a parity condition on the way they are shared among the planes. This leads to an exact algorithm, pseudo-polynomial in the durations. For the non-symmetric clique problem, the same holds when no flight between central cities is shorter than a detour through \(C_I\) or \(C_G\), provided the makespan of a configuration accounts for the waiting it may force. We also show where the characterization stops: with short flights between central cities, and for the reduction of the general problem to a clique problem, which preserves the front only in some cases, for which we give exact methods on small instances.
In particular, we would like to insist on the fact that the triangular inequality assumption made in this paper contradicts the assumption of [QS15], so that the latter is not a special case of the former; both are covered here. In addition, even the technical implementation of the algorithm has been completely revised.
In addition, we present the ZenoSolver, a C++ implementation of the algorithm to solve MultiZenoTravel. It can output the instance definition in PDDL such that the generated instance can easily be used by other solvers. We demonstrate how to generate instances with different behavior by tuning the input parameters. We provide a theoretical and empirical study of the performances of ZenoSolver. Each front is returned with a certificate that a checker verifies without trusting the solver, and the main theorems, the checker and a solver of their own are formally verified in Lean 4.
Although we think that the primary utility of ZenoSolver is to generate benchmarks with known Pareto Front to study other solvers’ properties and behaviors, we provide a demonstration of the ZenoSolver on a problem using real data. This has been made possible by the extension of the solver capabilities from the symmetric clique problem to non-symmetric instances. Real data also come as arbitrary graphs, and the extension to arbitrary graphs is studied in detail, together with the part of it that is exact.


Outline
The plan of this paper is as follows: in MultiZenoTravel problems, we define three versions of the MultiZenoTravel problem, together with the plans and the assumptions. Symmetric MultiZenoTravel is dedicated to solve the symmetric MultiZenoTravel problem, followed by Non-symmetric and general MultiZenoTravel that focuses on the non-symmetric version of the problem. In the same section, we study how an instance of the general MultiZenoTravel problem can be reduced to a non-symmetric clique version, and when the reduction preserves the Pareto front.
In Pareto Optimal Plans, we detail how to compute the Pareto front and construct Pareto optimal plans, and we introduce the ZenoSolver, a C++ implementation of the algorithm, with its certificates and their verification in Lean. Experiments reports the validation of the solver and of the theory, its performances and examples of instances.
Finally, in Application, we study an (almost) realistic application for MultiZenoTravel and ZenoSolver using the OpenFlights database to find the optimal routes between the two largest airports in the world, and Conclusion and Perspectives closes with the open problems.






Statements, proofs and formal status. Results keep the numbering of the theory note, which gives every proof in full. Each cited result links to its entry in the blueprint and carries a badge derived from the Lean kernel: machine-checked when the whole statement is proved in Lean, Lean definition for a definition, and informal when the proof is written but not formalised. Here, proofs are sketched in a few sentences. A gentler introduction to the problem, on a small example, is on the Problem page.

title: MultiZenoTravel
text:
MultiZenoTravel problems

Instances, plans, Pareto fronts, assumptions and patterns

In this Section, we introduce three versions of the MultiZenoTravel problem: the symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel, the non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel and the general MultiZenoTravel. We then make precise what a plan is, together with its cost and its makespan, and the assumptions on durations used in the rest of the paper. Plans are defined flight by flight, with explicit departure times, so that waiting, passengers changing planes, empty flights and flights between central cities are part of the problem and not excluded by assumption. The characterization of the Pareto-optimal plans comes next: for the symmetric clique problem first, then for the non-symmetric and general problems.

Instances
Let us introduce some notations related to the planning problem briefly presented in the introduction: a non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel instance (schematic view) is defined by the following elements (§1.1 Lean definition):

\(n\) central cities, organized as a clique in which every node is connected to \(C_I\) and \(C_G\), respectively the initial city and the goal city.
\(c \in (\mathbb R^+)^n\), where \(c_i\) is the cost for landing in \(C_i\).
\(D \in (\mathbb R^+)^{n \times n}\), where \(d_{ij}\) is the flying time between \(C_i\) and \(C_j\).
\(d \in (\mathbb R^+)^n\), where \(d_i\) is the flying time between \(C_I\) and \(C_i\).
\(\bar d \in (\mathbb R^+)^n\), where \(\bar d_i\) is the flying time between \(C_i\) and \(C_G\).
\(p\) planes, initially in \(C_I\), that have a capacity of a unique person.
\(t\) persons, initially in \(C_I\).

The goal of MultiZenoTravel is to carry all \(t\) persons, initially in \(C_I\), to \(C_G\) using \(p\) planes, minimizing both the makespan and the cost of the plan.
Flights are undirected: each one has a single duration, used in both directions, and there is no flight between \(C_I\) and \(C_G\). We write \(\mathrm{dur}(a, b)\) for the duration of the flight between \(a\) and \(b\); a flight between central cities may also be missing. Landing in \(C_I\) or \(C_G\) is free. Without loss of generality, all triples \((d_i, \bar d_i, c_i)\) are assumed to be pairwise distinct. Otherwise, the 2 cities can be “merged” and the resulting \(n-1\) cities problem is equivalent to the original \(n\) cities problem, as there exist no city capacity constraints. Finally, we only consider cases where \(t \ge p\), as the problem is otherwise trivial.
An instance of the symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel problem is an instance such that \(d = \bar d\). A general MultiZenoTravel instance is an instance such that the \(n\) central cities are organized as an arbitrary graph; it is defined in the general section.
Throughout the paper, we illustrate the definitions on the symmetric instance with \(n = 3\) cities, \(t = 3\) passengers and \(p = 2\) planes, durations \(d = (2, 3, 5)\), costs \(c = (9, 6, 1)\) and no flight between central cities (the file site/problem/example.dat, also used on the Problem page). Its Pareto front, as (cost, makespan), is \[(4, 20),\ (14, 16),\ (20, 14),\ (24, 12),\ (30, 10),\ (36, 8).\]



\[
\begin{array}{lllllll}
p_1: & C_I & \overset{t_1}{\to} C_2 & \to C_I & \overset{t_2}{\to} C_3 & \overset{t_2}{\to} C_G & \\
p_2: & C_I & \overset{t_3}{\to} C_3 & \overset{t_3}{\to} C_G & \to C_2 & \overset{t_1}{\to} C_G &
\end{array}
\]


Figure 2: Example of an admissible plan to transport 3 travelers via 2 planes, on the instance above. This representation indicates the successive actions for each plane. We noted by \(\overset{t_i}{\to}\) a flight with a traveler.



Figure 2 illustrates an admissible solution, of cost 14 and makespan 16. Note that the makespan for a plan is not necessarily the largest sum of the flights’ duration as some planes might have to wait for others. This would be the case for \(p_2\) waiting for \(t_1\) in \(C_2\), had it reached \(C_2\) before \(p_1\) dropped \(t_1\) there.


Plans
To reason about all plans, including those that wait, hand passengers over or fly between central cities, we fix their semantics (§1.2 Lean definition). A plan on a set \(Q\) of planes (all \(p\) planes unless stated otherwise) consists of

for every plane \(k \in Q\), a route: a sequence of legs \((k, 1), \dots, (k, \nu_k)\). Leg \((k, j)\) flies an existing flight from \(v_{k,j-1}\) to \(v_{k,j}\) and departs at time \(e_{k,j}\), with \(v_{k,0} = C_I\), \(e_{k,1} \ge 0\), and \(e_{k,j+1} \ge a_{k,j} := e_{k,j} + \mathrm{dur}(v_{k,j-1}, v_{k,j})\);
for every passenger, a journey: a non-empty sequence of legs whose first leg departs from \(C_I\) and whose last leg arrives in \(C_G\). Each leg departs from the city where the previous one arrives, no earlier than that arrival, and, if both legs belong to the same plane, at a later position of its route;
capacity: the journeys are pairwise disjoint, and none repeats a leg.

The plan is feasible if every route ends in \(C_G\). Its cost \(C\) is the sum of the landing costs of all legs, with or without a passenger, and its makespan \(M = \max_k a_{k,\nu_k}\) is the time at which the last plane reaches \(C_G\) for the last time. \(\mathcal A\) is the set of pairs \((C, M)\) of feasible plans. The flight time \(F_k\) of plane \(k\) is the sum of the durations of its legs; its flights are sequential, so \(F_k \le M\).
Waiting is implicit: a plane or a passenger may depart later than it arrived. Boarding and deplaning take no time, several planes may be in a city at once, and a passenger may change planes in any city, any number of times. In Figure 2, \(t_1\) changes planes once, in \(C_2\).
Journeys may contain detours that serve nothing, and they can be removed:

Lemma 3.1 informal, parts in Lean Cleaning. Every plan can be changed, keeping all routes (hence its cost, makespan and flight times), so that every journey is clean: its first flight is its only flight departing from \(C_I\), and its last flight is its only flight arriving in \(C_G\).


Sketch. Cut each journey down to the part from its last departure from \(C_I\) to the first later arrival in \(C_G\); this is still a journey, and capacity only gets looser (full proof).

A plan is event-ordered if its legs admit a total order that extends every route and every journey and along which departure times do not decrease. With positive durations every plan is event-ordered. With zero durations, a passenger can ride a later leg of one plane and then an earlier leg of another at the same instant, in a cycle that no execution in time realises; such plans never improve the front (Corollary 6.10 informal, parts in Lean).
Requiring planes to finish in \(C_G\) does not change the front: if planes may end anywhere, with the makespan taken as the last arrival of any leg, the Pareto front is the same under the assumptions of the next section (Theorem 4.9 machine-checked). All the planes may thus be assumed to finish their respective sequence in \(C_G\).
ZenoSolver outputs each instance as a PDDL file1 for the domain pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl: a durative fly action that adds the landing cost to total-cost, instantaneous board and debark actions, and a predicate libre that enforces capacity one. Under \(\varepsilon\)-separation, PDDL plans and event-ordered plans correspond, with the same cost and makespans equal in the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\) (Statement 1.2 informal); this correspondence is argued but not formalised. The Instances section describes the generator and the files.



Planning Domain Definition Language [FL03], almost universally used in AI Planning to describe domains and instances.↩︎




Pareto fronts
For points \(y, z\) of the plane (cost, makespan), \(y \preceq z\) if \(y \le z\) in both coordinates. For a set \(\mathcal S\) of points, \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S\) is the set of \(z \in \mathcal S\) weakly dominated by no other point of \(\mathcal S\), and the Pareto front of an instance is \(\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A\) (§1.5 Lean definition). We look for the front and for one plan per front point.
Every characterization of the front in this paper has two halves: a finite set of points that plans attain, and a proof that every plan is weakly dominated by one of them. The following lemma turns them into an equality of fronts.

Lemma 1.1 informal, parts in Lean Dominating subset. Let \(\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S\) with \(\mathcal S'\) finite and every point of \(\mathcal S\) weakly dominated by a point of \(\mathcal S'\). Then \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'\), and every point of \(\mathcal S\) is weakly dominated by a point of \(\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S\).



Assumptions
The results of this paper use the following assumptions (§1.4 Lean definition), each one only where stated. The first two are the triangular inequality and the symmetry assumption:
Assumption: \(\forall (a, b, x),\ \mathrm{dur}(a, x) + \mathrm{dur}(x, b) \ge \mathrm{dur}(a, b)\) whenever the three flights exist \(\hfill\) (AΔ)
Assumption (Symmetry): \(\forall i \in [1, n],\ d_i = \bar d_i\) \(\hfill\) (S)
The assumption of [QS15], in a non-strict form, and its non-symmetric counterpart state that flights between central cities are useless, that is, never faster than a detour through \(C_I\) or \(C_G\):
Assumption: under (S), \(\forall (i, j),\ d_{ij} \ge d_i + d_j\) for every existing flight \(\hfill\) (A1)
Assumption: \(\forall (i, j),\ d_{ij} \ge \min(d_i + d_j,\ \bar d_i + \bar d_j)\) for every existing flight \(\hfill\) (A1-NS)
Finally, a weak form of the triangular inequality through the hubs is used for waiting:
Assumption: \(\forall (i, z),\ \bar d_i \le d_i + d_z + \bar d_z\) and \(d_i \le \bar d_i + \bar d_z + d_z\) \(\hfill\) (AΔ-path)

implies (AΔ-path), and so does (AΔ) whenever the flight between \(i\) and \(z\) exists. Under (S), (A1) and (AΔ) hold together only when \(d_{ij} = d_i + d_j\): the first allows flights between central cities longer than the detour through a hub, and the second allows them as short as \(|d_i - d_j|\). Every PDDL problem the generator writes is symmetric, and gives a flight between central cities the duration \(d_i + d_j + 100\), so it satisfies (A1).

Notation. We write \(s = 2t - p\), so that \(s \ge p\) and \(s \equiv p \pmod 2\), and \(\kappa = \lceil s/p \rceil\) (Notation informal). For a multiset \(Y\) of central cities, \(Y(i)\) is the multiplicity of \(i\), \(|Y|\) its size, \(c(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} c_w\) its cost, and \(\delta(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} d_w\) and \(\bar\delta(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} \bar d_w\) its durations; under (S), its load is \(\ell(Y) = 2\delta(Y)\). A partition of \(X\) over the planes is a family of groups \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) with \(X_1 + \dots + X_p = X\), group \(X_k\) being the cities in which plane \(k\) lands.


Patterns
Cut the sequence of a plane at every visit to \(C_I\) or \(C_G\). Each piece, from one of them to the next, is a pattern (a segment in the blueprint). As there is no flight between \(C_I\) and \(C_G\), every pattern lands in at least one central city. Depending on the cities it starts and ends in, a pattern is of one of four types, denoted by \(A\), \(\bar A\), \(B\) and \(\bar B\) (Figure 3). A pattern that lands in exactly one central city, of multiplicity 0, consists of two flights; we call it simple. We denote by \(|X|\) the number of the patterns \(X \in \{A, \bar A, B, \bar B\}\) in a given plan, and by \(F(\gamma)\) the flight time of a pattern \(\gamma\).

In the plans built in this paper, a pattern \(A\) carries a passenger from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), a pattern \(\bar A\) flies back empty, a pattern \(B\) leaves a passenger in \(x\) and a pattern \(\bar B\) takes one from \(x\) to \(C_G\). Patterns of larger multiplicity have the same four types.



In Figure 2, \(p_1\) performs a \(B\) in \(C_2\) and an \(A\) in \(C_3\), and \(p_2\) an \(A\) in \(C_3\) and a \(\bar B\) in \(C_2\). Only the patterns \(A\) and \(\bar A\) change from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) or back, and a plane goes from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\), so its patterns of these two types alternate \(A, \bar A, \dots, A\) (Lemma 2.1 informal, parts in Lean). We deduce the following property on the cardinal of each pattern in any feasible plan.
Property II: In every feasible plan,

\(|A| + |B| \ge t\);
\(|A| + |\bar B| \ge t\);
\(|A| = |\bar A| + p\).

Proof: The patterns \(A\) and \(B\) are the only ones that start with a flight from \(C_I\), and the first flights of the journeys are distinct flights from \(C_I\), so a feasible plan has at least \(t\) of those patterns. Apply the same reasoning to \(C_G\) with \(A\) and \(\bar B\), whose last flight arrives in \(C_G\), to prove the second point. The third point is Lemma 2.1, summed over the \(p\) planes. \(\square\)
Corollary II: A feasible plan performs at least \(2t - p\) patterns, hence lands at least \(2t - p\) times in central cities (Lemma 3.2 machine-checked).
Proof: By Property II, the number of patterns is \(|A| + |\bar A| + |B| + |\bar B| = (|A| + |B|) + (|A| + |\bar B|) - p \ge 2t - p\), and each pattern lands in a central city. \(\square\)
With fewer planes than passengers, some planes have to come back to \(C_I\), and every return costs a landing. In Figure 2 the bound is reached: the plan lands \(2t - p = 4\) times. The next section shows that, in the symmetric case, the Pareto front is always reached by such plans, and which lists of \(2t - p\) cities can be flown, and how fast.

title: MultiZenoTravel
text:
Symmetric MultiZenoTravel

Proposition I: the Pareto front is reached with exactly 2t − p central cities

The method to find the Pareto Front of any general MultiZenoTravel instance consists of three steps. First, we provide an efficient algorithm to find the Pareto Front for any symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel instance. Then, we show that for the non-symmetric version of the problem the method still applies when flights between central cities are not shorter than a detour through \(C_I\) or \(C_G\), provided waiting is accounted for, and that it does not otherwise. Last, we study the transformation of any instance of the general MultiZenoTravel problem into a non-symmetric clique version, and the cases in which it preserves the Pareto front. This section covers the first step; it corresponds to §2 to §4 of the theory note.
The following proposition is the cornerstone of the method to identify and construct the Pareto Set of any instance:

Proposition I: Assume (S), and (AΔ) or (A1). Every point of the Pareto front is attained by a plan where exactly \(2t - p\) (possibly identical) central cities are used by a plane.

Under (A1), Proposition I is Theorem 4.7 machine-checked together with Corollary 4.8 machine-checked; under (AΔ), it is Theorem 4.10 machine-checked, from which Corollary 4.12 informal, parts in Lean carries Corollary 4.8 over.
By Corollary II, no plan uses fewer than \(2t - p\) central cities, so Proposition I reduces the search to lists of \(2t - p\) cities. It is a statement about the front: with landing costs of zero, a Pareto-optimal plan may land more often. With one city of duration 1 and cost 0, \(p = 3\) and \(t = 5\), the front is \(\{(0, 6)\}\), attained by planes landing 3, 3 and 1 times; the plane landing once can add a pattern \(\bar A\) and a pattern \(A\) within its slack, and the resulting plan, with 9 landings, still attains \((0, 6)\).
The goal of this section is to establish the proof of Proposition I for the Symmetric case. For that purpose, we first describe which lists of \(2t - p\) cities can be flown, and how fast. We then show that every plan is dominated by one of them, first under the assumption (A1) of [QS15], then under the triangular inequality (AΔ). Precisely, with \[M(X) = \min\Big\{\max_k \ell(X_k) : X_1, \dots, X_p \text{ an admissible partition of } X\Big\},\] the front is the Pareto set of the pairs \((c(X), M(X))\) over the lists \(X\) of \(2t - p\) cities.

Admissible partitions
A list of \(2t - p\) cities does not hold any information about which plane will land in a particular city. Assign to each plane \(k\) the cities \(X_k\) in which it lands: when can the partition \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) be flown with simple patterns? By Lemma 2.1, a plane performs one more \(A\) than \(\bar A\), so a plane that performs only those patterns lands an odd number of times. A plane that lands an even number of times has to perform a pattern \(B\) or \(\bar B\), that is, to leave a passenger in a central city for another plane, or to take one left there by another plane. These hand-offs pair up at each city. Admissibility records exactly this bookkeeping, modulo 2.

Definition 2.2 Lean definition Admissible partition. A parity matrix for \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) is a matrix \(h \in \{0, 1\}^{p \times n}\) such that

(h1) \(h_{k,i} = 1\) implies \(X_k(i) \ge 1\);
(h2) \(\sum_i h_{k,i} \equiv |X_k| + 1 \pmod 2\) for every plane \(k\);
(h3) \(\sum_k h_{k,i} \equiv 0 \pmod 2\) for every city \(i\).

The partition is admissible if it has a parity matrix.

Here \(h_{k,i} = 1\) means that plane \(k\) takes part in an odd number of hand-offs in city \(i\). (h2) asks a plane with an even group, an even plane, to do so in an odd number of cities, and (h3) pairs the hand-offs of every city. An empty group would need an odd number of marked cities in which it does not land, so admissible partitions have non-empty groups. The condition reads more simply on a graph.

Lemma 2.4 informal Component form. Let \(H\) be the bipartite graph on planes and cities with an edge between \(k\) and \(i\) whenever \(X_k(i) \ge 1\). The partition is admissible if and only if every connected component of \(H\) contains an even number of even planes.


Sketch. A parity matrix is a set of edges of \(H\) with odd degree exactly at the even planes, so each component has an even number of them; conversely, such a set is built bottom-up in any spanning forest of \(H\) (full proof).

On the example instance, the groups \(\{2, 3\}\) and \(\{2, 3\}\) are admissible: both planes are even, and they share cities. The groups \(\{1, 1\}\) and \(\{3, 3\}\) are not: each plane is even, but they share no city, so each would have to hand a passenger to a plane that never comes to its city. Two odd groups, such as \(\{1\}\) and \(\{1, 1, 1\}\), are always admissible, and Lemma 2.9 informal shows that a partition with \(\sum_k |X_k| \equiv p \pmod 2\) is admissible as soon as some city belongs to every even group.


(BB̄)-pairings and link forests
A (\(B\bar B\))-pairing in city \(i\) is a pattern \(B\) of one plane and a pattern \(\bar B\) of another plane, both in \(i\), carrying the same passenger: the first plane leaves it in \(i\), the second takes it to \(C_G\). The parity matrix says in which cities the pairings are, but not between which planes. A link forest says both.

Definition (link forest) Lean definition A link forest for \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) is a forest \(\Lambda\) on the planes whose edges carry city labels, such that

(F1) for every plane \(u\) and city \(i\), at most \(X_u(i)\) edges at \(u\) are labelled \(i\);
(F2) \(r_u := |X_u| - \deg_\Lambda(u)\) is odd for every plane \(u\).

An edge between \(u\) and \(v\) labelled \(i\), a link in \(i\), is a \((B\bar B)\)-pairing; the \(r_u\) other landings of \(u\), its free landings, are performed as patterns \(A, \bar A, \dots, A\).


Lemma 2.6 machine-checked Link forest. A partition is admissible if and only if it has a link forest.


Sketch. Counting the labels of a link forest at each plane gives an integer parity matrix, which reduces mod 2 to a parity matrix (Lemma 2.3 informal). Conversely, take a parity matrix supported in a spanning forest of \(H\), pair the planes marked in each city, and check that the pairs form no cycle (full proof).

When \(|X| = 2t - p\), Corollary 2.7 informal bounds the structure: a link forest has at most \(t - p\) links, and each of its trees has at most \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t - p + 1)\) planes.


Constructing the plan

Theorem 4.1 machine-checked Assume (S). For every list \(X\) of \(2t - p\) cities and every admissible partition \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) of \(X\), there is a feasible plan whose central landings are exactly \(X\) (so its cost is \(c(X)\)), in which plane \(k\) flies for \(\ell(X_k)\) and performs at most one pattern \(\bar B\), and whose makespan is \(\max_k \ell(X_k)\). The plan uses no flight between central cities.

The construction roots every tree of a link forest at a plane. For a link in \(i\) between a parent \(u\) and a child \(v\), \(u\) performs the pattern \(B\) and \(v\) the pattern \(\bar B\). The western part of each pairing is performed as early as possible, and its eastern part as late as possible: each plane flies its patterns \(B\) first, from time 0, then its free landings as patterns \(A\) and \(\bar A\), then its pattern \(\bar B\) if it has a parent. A plane has at most one parent, so it performs at most one \(\bar B\), at the end of its sequence. That \(\bar B\) may have to wait for the passenger, but the parent flies its patterns \(B\) first, so the wait ends within the parent’s own duration, and no plane finishes later than its load or its parent’s.

Sketch. The child \(v\) arrives in \(i\) at \(\ell(X_v) - d_i\), and the parent’s drop-off arrives there by \(\tau_u - d_i\), where \(\tau_u \le \ell(X_u)\) is the duration of \(u\)’s patterns \(B\). So \(v\) is back in \(C_G\) by \(\max(\ell(X_v), \ell(X_u))\), and every plane flies exactly \(\ell(X_k)\) (full proof).

The partition is \(X_1 = X_2 = \{2, 3\}\) with one link in \(C_2\), \(p_1\) being the parent: \(p_1\) performs a \(B\) in \(C_2\) and then an \(A\) in \(C_3\), and \(p_2\) an \(A\) in \(C_3\) and then a \(\bar B\) in \(C_2\). \(t_1\) waits in \(C_2\) from time 3 to 13; no plane waits. Both loads are \(2(3 + 5) = 16\).





A lower bound for every plan
A first lower bound on the cost of every plan comes from forgetting admissibility. It needs a bound on the duration of a pattern.

Lemma 3.3 informal, parts in Lean Pattern durations. Let a pattern \(\gamma\) visit the central cities \(x_1, \dots, x_m\) in this order.
(a) Under (S), \(F(\gamma) \ge d_{x_1} + d_{x_m} \ge 2\min(d_{x_1}, d_{x_m})\).
(b) Under (AΔ), for every \(j\), \(F(\gamma) \ge d_{x_j} + \bar d_{x_j}\) for patterns \(A\) and \(\bar A\), \(F(\gamma) \ge 2 d_{x_j}\) for \(B\) and \(F(\gamma) \ge 2\bar d_{x_j}\) for \(\bar B\).
(c) A simple pattern in \(x\) lasts exactly \(d_x + \bar d_x\) (\(A\), \(\bar A\)), \(2 d_x\) (\(B\)) or \(2\bar d_x\) (\(\bar B\)).


Lemma 3.4 machine-checked Relaxation. Assume (S). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\) there are non-empty multisets \(Y_1, \dots, Y_p\) with \(\sum_k |Y_k| = 2t - p\), \(c(Y_1 + \dots + Y_p) \le C\) and \(\ell(Y_k) \le F_k \le M\) for every \(k\). Hence, with integer durations, \(C \ge L(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor)\), where \[L(T) = \min\Big\{c(Y) : Y = Y_1 + \dots + Y_p,\ |Y| = 2t - p,\ Y_k \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \delta(Y_k) \le T \text{ for all } k\Big\}.\] No assumption on the flights between central cities is needed.


Sketch. Charge each pattern to whichever of its first and last central cities has the smaller \(d\), which by Lemma 3.3(a) costs at most half its flight time in load; by Corollary II there are at least \(2t - p\) patterns, at least one per plane, and their charged landings are distinct (full proof).

\(L\) is the minimisation that defines the front, without admissibility. Wherever it meets the least cost of an admissible partition, the front is known whatever the flights between central cities; this is the common case (certificates).


Proof of Proposition I under the assumption of [QS15]
Under (A1), a flight between central cities can always be replaced by a detour through \(C_G\): using the same plane, the passenger on board flies to \(C_G\) instead, and the plane flies on to the next city, arriving no later. The plan then only performs simple patterns, which we read through the passengers they carry.

Definition 4.2 Lean definition Role configuration. A role configuration assigns to each plane \(k\) three multisets of central cities, its patterns \(B\) (\(\mathrm{Dr}_k\), drop-offs), \(\bar B\) (\(\mathrm{Pk}_k\), pick-ups) and \(A\) or \(\bar A\) (\(\mathrm{Cr}_k\), crossings), with \(|\mathrm{Cr}_k|\) odd and the per-city balance \(\sum_k \mathrm{Dr}_k = \sum_k \mathrm{Pk}_k\). Its passenger count is \(\sum_k \big(|\mathrm{Dr}_k| + (|\mathrm{Cr}_k| + 1)/2\big)\), its cost is \(\sum_k c(\mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k)\), and the role load of plane \(k\) is \[\lambda_k = 2\delta(\mathrm{Dr}_k) + 2\bar\delta(\mathrm{Pk}_k) + \delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k) + \bar\delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k).\]

Under (S), \(\lambda_k = \ell(X_k)\) for the group \(X_k = \mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k\). Three lemmas connect plans, role configurations and partitions; call a plan simple if all its patterns are simple.

Lemma 4.3 informal, parts in Lean (direct selection): in a simple plan with clean journeys every journey is \(C_I \to x \to C_G\), and selecting patterns by their role in the journeys gives a role configuration with passenger count at least \(t\), cost at most \(C\) and \(\lambda_k \le F_k\).
Lemma 4.4 machine-checked (shrinking): deleting two crossings, or a \((B\bar B)\)-pairing, brings the passenger count down to exactly \(t\) without increasing anything.
Lemma 4.5 machine-checked (parity): the groups of a role configuration with passenger count \(t\) form an admissible partition of \(2t - p\) cities, with parity matrix \(h_{k,i} = (\mathrm{Dr}_k(i) + \mathrm{Pk}_k(i)) \bmod 2\).


Theorem 4.7 machine-checked Converse. Assume (S) and (A1). For every feasible plan with cost \(C\), makespan \(M\) and flight times \(F_k\), there is an admissible partition \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) of a list \(X\) of \(2t - p\) cities with \(c(X) \le C\) and \(\ell(X_k) \le F_k \le M\) for every \(k\).


Sketch. Replace every flight \(a \to b\) between central cities by \(a \to C_G \to b\): by (S) and (A1) the plane reaches \(b\) no later, the landings are unchanged, and a passenger on board is delivered in \(C_G\). Then clean the journeys (Lemma 3.1) and apply Lemmas 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 (full proof).

With Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 1.1, this proves Proposition I under (A1), in the following precise form.

Corollary 4.8 machine-checked Assume (S) and (A1). Then \[\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X, \qquad \mathcal X = \{(c(X), M(X)) : |X| = 2t - p,\ M(X) < \infty\},\] and every point of \(\mathcal F\) is attained by a plan with exactly \(2t - p\) central landings.

Table 1 lists an admissible partition for each point of the example instance. Every point uses two even groups and one \((B\bar B)\)-pairing. Groups of sizes 1 and 3 put three landings on one plane; \(\{1\}, \{1, 1, 1\}\) for instance costs 36 with makespan 12, and is dominated by \((24, 12)\).
